<p><b>Ulysses S. Grant</b> (born <b>Hiram Ulysses Grant</b>; <span class="rt-commentedText nowrap"><span class="IPA nopopups noexcerpt" lang="en-fonipa"><a href="/wiki/Help:IPA/English" title="Help:IPA/English">/<span style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><span title="/ˈ/: primary stress follows">ˈ</span><span title="&#39;h&#39; in &#39;hi&#39;">h</span><span title="/aɪ/: &#39;i&#39; in &#39;tide&#39;">aɪ</span><span title="&#39;r&#39; in &#39;rye&#39;">r</span><span title="/ə/: &#39;a&#39; in &#39;about&#39;">ə</span><span title="&#39;m&#39; in &#39;my&#39;">m</span></span><span class="wrap"> </span><span style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><span title="/juː/: &#39;u&#39; in &#39;cute&#39;">juː</span><span title="/ˈ/: primary stress follows">ˈ</span><span title="&#39;l&#39; in &#39;lie&#39;">l</span><span title="/ɪ/: &#39;i&#39; in &#39;kit&#39;">ɪ</span><span title="&#39;s&#39; in &#39;sigh&#39;">s</span><span title="/iː/: &#39;ee&#39; in &#39;fleece&#39;">iː</span><span title="&#39;z&#39; in &#39;zoom&#39;">z</span></span>/</a></span></span> <a href="/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key" title="Help:Pronunciation respelling key"><i title="English pronunciation respelling"><span style="font-size:90%">HY</span>-rəm yoo-<span style="font-size:90%">LISS</span>-eez</i></a>; April 27, 1822&#160;&#8211;&#32;July 23, 1885) was an American military officer and politician who served as the 18th <a href="/wiki/President_of_the_United_States" title="President of the United States">president of the United States</a> from 1869 to 1877. As <a href="/wiki/Commanding_General_of_the_United_States_Army" title="Commanding General of the United States Army">Commanding General</a>, he led the <a href="/wiki/Union_Army" title="Union Army">Union Army</a> to victory in the <a href="/wiki/American_Civil_War" title="American Civil War">American Civil War</a> in 1865 and thereafter briefly served as <a href="/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_War" title="United States Secretary of War">U.S. Secretary of War</a>. Later, as president, Grant was an effective civil rights executive who signed the bill that created <a href="/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice" title="United States Department of Justice">the Justice Department</a> and worked with <a href="/wiki/Radical_Republicans" title="Radical Republicans">Radical Republicans</a> to protect African Americans during <a href="/wiki/Reconstruction_era" title="Reconstruction era">Reconstruction</a>.
</p><p>Born and raised in Ohio, Grant attended <a href="/wiki/West_Point" class="mw-redirect" title="West Point">West Point</a> and graduated with the class of 1843, going on to serve with distinction in the <a href="/wiki/Mexican%E2%80%93American_War" title="Mexican–American War">Mexican–American War</a>. He resigned from the army in 1854, returning to civilian life impoverished. In 1861, shortly after the American Civil War began, Grant joined the Union Army and quickly rose to prominence after winning early Union victories in <a href="/wiki/Western_theater_of_the_American_Civil_War" title="Western theater of the American Civil War">the western theater</a>. In 1863, he led the <a href="/wiki/Vicksburg_campaign" title="Vicksburg campaign">Vicksburg campaign</a>, gaining control of the <a href="/wiki/Mississippi_River" title="Mississippi River">Mississippi River</a>, dealing a serious strategic blow to the Confederacy. President <a href="/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln" title="Abraham Lincoln">Abraham Lincoln</a> promoted him to <a href="/wiki/Lieutenant_general_(United_States)" title="Lieutenant general (United States)">lieutenant general</a> after <a href="/wiki/Chattanooga_campaign" title="Chattanooga campaign">his victory at Chattanooga</a>. For thirteen months, Grant fought <a href="/wiki/Robert_E._Lee" title="Robert E. Lee">Robert E. Lee</a> during the high-casualty <a href="/wiki/Overland_Campaign" title="Overland Campaign">Overland Campaign</a> which ended with capture of Lee's army <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Appomattox_Court_House#Surrender" title="Battle of Appomattox Court House">at Appomattox</a>, where he formally surrendered to Grant. In 1866, President <a href="/wiki/Andrew_Johnson" title="Andrew Johnson">Andrew Johnson</a> promoted Grant to <a href="/wiki/General_of_the_Army_(United_States)#Post–American_Civil_War_era" title="General of the Army (United States)">General of the Army</a>. Later, Grant openly broke with Johnson over Reconstruction policies. A war hero, drawn in by his sense of duty, Grant was unanimously nominated by the Republican Party and then <a href="/wiki/1868_United_States_presidential_election" title="1868 United States presidential election">elected president in 1868</a>.
</p><p>As president, Grant stabilized the post-war national economy, supported congressional Reconstruction and the ratification of <a href="/wiki/Fifteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Fifteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution">the Fifteenth Amendment</a>, and prosecuted the <a href="/wiki/Ku_Klux_Klan" title="Ku Klux Klan">Ku Klux Klan</a>. Under Grant, the Union was completely restored. He appointed African Americans and Jewish Americans to prominent federal offices. In 1871, he created the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Civil_Service_Commission" title="United States Civil Service Commission">first Civil Service Commission</a>, advancing the civil service more than any prior president. The <a href="/wiki/Liberal_Republican_Party_(United_States)" title="Liberal Republican Party (United States)">Liberal Republicans</a> and Democrats united behind Grant's opponent in <a href="/wiki/1872_United_States_presidential_election" title="1872 United States presidential election">the 1872 presidential election</a>, but Grant was handily reelected. The <a href="/wiki/Panic_of_1873" title="Panic of 1873">Panic of 1873</a> plunged the nation into a severe economic depression, resulting in the Democrats winning the House majority. Grant's Native American policy was to assimilate Indians into Anglo-American culture. His foreign policy was mostly peaceful: the <a href="/wiki/Alabama_Claims" title="Alabama Claims"><i>Alabama</i> Claims</a> against Great Britain were skillfully resolved without war. However, his attempted <a href="/wiki/Annexation_of_Santo_Domingo" title="Annexation of Santo Domingo">annexation of Santo Domingo</a> was rejected by the Senate. The Grant administration was often remembered primarily for a number of scandals, but modern scholarship has better appreciated Grant's appointment of reformers and prosecutions. In the heavily <a href="/wiki/1876_United_States_presidential_election" title="1876 United States presidential election">disputed 1876 presidential election</a>, Grant facilitated the approval by Congress of a peaceful compromise.
</p><p>Upon leaving the presidency, Grant undertook <a href="/wiki/World_tour_of_Ulysses_S._Grant" title="World tour of Ulysses S. Grant">a world tour</a>, meeting a number of prominent figures, and becoming the first president to circumnavigate the world. In 1880, he was unsuccessful in obtaining the Republican presidential nomination for a third term. In the final year of his life, facing severe financial reversals and dying of throat cancer, Grant wrote <a href="/wiki/Personal_Memoirs_of_U._S._Grant" title="Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant">his memoirs</a>, which were posthumously published and became a major critical and financial success. At the time of his death, he was memorialized as a symbol of national unity. Due to the "<a href="/wiki/Lost_Cause" class="mw-redirect" title="Lost Cause">Lost Cause</a>" myth spread by Confederate sympathizers around the turn of the 20th century, <a href="/wiki/Historical_reputation_of_Ulysses_S._Grant" title="Historical reputation of Ulysses S. Grant">historical assessments</a> and <a href="/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_presidents_of_the_United_States" title="Historical rankings of presidents of the United States">rankings</a> of Grant and his presidency suffered considerably before they began recovering in the 21st century. Grant's critics take a negative view of his economic mismanagement, and the corruption within his administration while his admirers emphasize his peace policy <a href="/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States" title="Native Americans in the United States">with Native Americans</a>, <a href="/wiki/Reconstruction_era#Grant&#39;s_Presidential_Reconstruction" title="Reconstruction era">vigorous enforcement of civil and voting rights for African Americans</a>, and securing North and South as a single nation within the Union.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012636_1-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012636-1">&#91;1&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" />
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Early_life_and_education">Early life and education</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Early_life_and_career_of_Ulysses_S._Grant" title="Early life and career of Ulysses S. Grant">Early life and career of Ulysses S. Grant</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Birthplace_of_Ulysses_S_Grant,_color_illustration,_cropped.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Color drawing of Grant&#39;s birthplace, a simple one-story structure, with fence and trees in front, next to the Ohio River with steamboat passing by" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Birthplace_of_Ulysses_S_Grant%2C_color_illustration%2C_cropped.jpg/220px-Birthplace_of_Ulysses_S_Grant%2C_color_illustration%2C_cropped.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="167" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Birthplace_of_Ulysses_S_Grant%2C_color_illustration%2C_cropped.jpg/330px-Birthplace_of_Ulysses_S_Grant%2C_color_illustration%2C_cropped.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Birthplace_of_Ulysses_S_Grant%2C_color_illustration%2C_cropped.jpg/440px-Birthplace_of_Ulysses_S_Grant%2C_color_illustration%2C_cropped.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1022" data-file-height="776" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Grant%27s_birthplace" class="mw-redirect" title="Grant&#39;s birthplace">Grant's birthplace</a> in <a href="/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_Ohio" title="Point Pleasant, Ohio">Point Pleasant, Ohio</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Grant's ancestors Matthew and Priscilla Grant arrived aboard the ship <i><a href="/wiki/Mary_and_John" title="Mary and John">Mary and John</a></i> at <a href="/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony" title="Massachusetts Bay Colony">Massachusetts Bay Colony</a> in 1630.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely19813_2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely19813-2">&#91;2&#93;</a></sup> Grant's great-grandfather fought in the <a href="/wiki/French_and_Indian_War" title="French and Indian War">French and Indian War</a>, and his grandfather, Noah, served in the <a href="/wiki/American_Revolution" title="American Revolution">American Revolution</a> at <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Bunker_Hill" title="Battle of Bunker Hill">Bunker Hill</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200121–22_3-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200121–22-3">&#91;3&#93;</a></sup> Afterward, Noah settled in <a href="/wiki/Pennsylvania" title="Pennsylvania">Pennsylvania</a> and married Rachel Kelley, who was of <a href="/wiki/Irish_American" class="mw-redirect" title="Irish American">Irish descent</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite20166_4-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite20166-4">&#91;4&#93;</a></sup> Their son <a href="/wiki/Jesse_Root_Grant" title="Jesse Root Grant">Jesse Root Grant</a> grew up to be a <a href="/wiki/Whig_Party_(United_States)" title="Whig Party (United States)">Whig Party</a> supporter and a fervent abolitionist.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHesseltine19574_5-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHesseltine19574-5">&#91;5&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Jesse Grant moved to <a href="/wiki/Point_Pleasant,_Ohio" title="Point Pleasant, Ohio">Point Pleasant, Ohio</a> in 1820 and found work as a <a href="/wiki/Tanner_(occupation)" class="mw-redirect" title="Tanner (occupation)">foreman in a tannery</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite20168_6-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite20168-6">&#91;6&#93;</a></sup> He soon met his future wife, <a href="/wiki/Hannah_Simpson_Grant" title="Hannah Simpson Grant">Hannah Simpson</a>, who descended from <a href="/wiki/Scotch-Irish_Americans" title="Scotch-Irish Americans">Presbyterian immigrants</a> from <a href="/wiki/Ballygawley,_County_Tyrone" title="Ballygawley, County Tyrone">Ballygawley, County Tyrone</a> in <a href="/wiki/Plantation_of_Ulster" title="Plantation of Ulster">Ireland</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-7" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-7">&#91;7&#93;</a></sup> The two were married on June 24, 1821 and their first child, Hiram Ulysses Grant was born on April 27, 1822.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely19815–6White20168–9_8-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely19815–6White20168–9-8">&#91;8&#93;</a></sup> The boy's name, Ulysses, was drawn from ballots placed in a hat. To honor his father-in-law, Jesse named the boy "Hiram Ulysses", though he would always refer to him by his middle name, "Ulysses".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimpson20142–3White20169–10_9-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimpson20142–3White20169–10-9">&#91;9&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1823, the family moved to <a href="/wiki/Georgetown,_Ohio" title="Georgetown, Ohio">Georgetown, Ohio</a>, where five more siblings were born: Simpson, Clara, Orvil, Jennie, and Mary.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELongacre20066–7_10-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELongacre20066–7-10">&#91;10&#93;</a></sup> At the age of five, Ulysses began his formal education, starting at a <a href="/wiki/Subscription_school" title="Subscription school">subscription school</a> and later in two private schools.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981497White201616,_18_11-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981497White201616,_18-11">&#91;11&#93;</a></sup> In the winter of 1836–1837, Grant was a student at <a href="/wiki/John_Brett_Richeson_House#Maysville_Academy" title="John Brett Richeson House">Maysville Seminary</a>, and in the autumn of 1838, he attended <a href="/wiki/John_Rankin_(abolitionist)" title="John Rankin (abolitionist)">John Rankin</a>'s academy.
</p><p>In his youth, Grant developed an unusual ability to ride and manage horses.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely19818,_10,_140–41White201621_12-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely19818,_10,_140–41White201621-12">&#91;12&#93;</a></sup> Grant disliked the tannery, so his father put his ability with horses to use by giving him work driving wagon loads of supplies and transporting people.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands20128White201619_13-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands20128White201619-13">&#91;13&#93;</a></sup> Unlike his siblings, Grant was not forced to attend church by his <a href="/wiki/Methodist" class="mw-redirect" title="Methodist">Methodist</a> parents.<sup id="cite_ref-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-15">&#91;a&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELongacre20066–7Waugh200914_16-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELongacre20066–7Waugh200914-16">&#91;15&#93;</a></sup> For the rest of his life, he prayed privately and never officially joined any denomination.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimpson20142–3Longacre20066–7_17-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimpson20142–3Longacre20066–7-17">&#91;16&#93;</a></sup> To others, including his own son, Grant appeared to be an <a href="/wiki/Agnostic" class="mw-redirect" title="Agnostic">agnostic</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWaugh200914_18-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaugh200914-18">&#91;17&#93;</a></sup> He inherited some of Hannah's Methodist <a href="/wiki/Works_of_Piety" class="mw-redirect" title="Works of Piety">piety</a> and quiet nature.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite201620Simpson201420_19-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201620Simpson201420-19">&#91;18&#93;</a></sup> Grant was largely apolitical before the war but wrote, "If I had ever had any political sympathies they would have been with the Whigs. I was raised in that school."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow201799–100_20-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201799–100-20">&#91;19&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Early_military_career_and_personal_life">Early military career and personal life</span></h2>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="West_Point_and_first_assignment">West Point and first assignment</span></h3>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ulysses_Grant_at_21.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Engraving of a young Grant in uniform" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Ulysses_Grant_at_21.jpg/180px-Ulysses_Grant_at_21.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="256" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Ulysses_Grant_at_21.jpg/270px-Ulysses_Grant_at_21.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Ulysses_Grant_at_21.jpg/360px-Ulysses_Grant_at_21.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1096" data-file-height="1559" /></a><figcaption>Grant as a young officer, <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr> 1845–1847</figcaption></figure>
<p>Grant's father wrote to Representative <a href="/wiki/Thomas_L._Hamer" title="Thomas L. Hamer">Thomas L. Hamer</a> requesting that he nominate Ulysses to the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Military_Academy" title="United States Military Academy">United States Military Academy</a> at <a href="/wiki/West_Point,_New_York" title="West Point, New York">West Point, New York</a>. Despite political differences with Jesse Root Grant, Hamer, a <a href="/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States)" title="Democratic Party (United States)">Democrat</a>, nominated his 17-year-old son to West Point in spring 1839 and Ulysses was accepted on July 1.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite201624–25_21-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201624–25-21">&#91;20&#93;</a></sup> Unfamiliar with Grant, however, Hamer submitted an incorrect name to West Point. As a result, Grant was enlisted at West Point under the name "U. S. Grant".<sup id="cite_ref-25" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-25">&#91;b&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198112Smith200124,_83Simon19673–4Kahan20182_26-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198112Smith200124,_83Simon19673–4Kahan20182-26">&#91;24&#93;</a></sup> As the initials "U. S." also stood for "<a href="/wiki/Uncle_Sam" title="Uncle Sam">Uncle Sam</a>", he became known amongst army colleagues as "Sam".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite201630_27-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201630-27">&#91;25&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Initially, Grant was indifferent to military life, but within a year he reexamined his desire to leave the academy and later wrote that "on the whole I like this place very much".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimpson201413–14Smith200126–28_28-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimpson201413–14Smith200126–28-28">&#91;26&#93;</a></sup> While at the academy, his greatest interest was horses, and he earned a reputation as the <a href="/wiki/Horsemanship_of_Ulysses_S._Grant" title="Horsemanship of Ulysses S. Grant">"most proficient" horseman</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198110_29-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198110-29">&#91;27&#93;</a></sup> Seeking relief from military routine, he studied under <a href="/wiki/Romanticism" title="Romanticism">Romantic</a> artist <a href="/wiki/Robert_Walter_Weir" title="Robert Walter Weir">Robert Walter Weir</a>, producing nine surviving artworks.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200127McFeely198116–17_30-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200127McFeely198116–17-30">&#91;28&#93;</a></sup> He spent more time reading books from the library than his academic texts.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198116–17Smith200126–27_31-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198116–17Smith200126–27-31">&#91;29&#93;</a></sup> On Sundays, cadets were required to march to and attend services at the academy's church, a requirement that Grant disliked.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite201641_32-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201641-32">&#91;30&#93;</a></sup> Quiet by nature, he established a few intimate friends among fellow cadets, including <a href="/wiki/Frederick_Tracy_Dent" title="Frederick Tracy Dent">Frederick Tracy Dent</a> and <a href="/wiki/James_Longstreet" title="James Longstreet">James Longstreet</a>. He was inspired both by the Commandant, Captain <a href="/wiki/Charles_Ferguson_Smith" title="Charles Ferguson Smith">Charles Ferguson Smith</a>, and by General <a href="/wiki/Winfield_Scott" title="Winfield Scott">Winfield Scott</a>, who visited the academy to review the cadets. Grant later wrote of the military life, "there is much to dislike, but more to like."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands201212–13_33-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands201212–13-33">&#91;31&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant graduated on June 30, 1843, ranked 21st out of 39 in his class and was promoted the next day to the rank <a href="/wiki/Brevet_(military)" title="Brevet (military)">brevet</a> <a href="/wiki/Second_lieutenant" title="Second lieutenant">second lieutenant</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow201727Longacre200621Cullum1850256–57_34-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201727Longacre200621Cullum1850256–57-34">&#91;32&#93;</a></sup> He planned to resign his commission after his four-year term of duty. He would later write that among the happiest days of his life were the day he left the presidency and the day he left the academy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow201728McFeely198116,_19_35-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201728McFeely198116,_19-35">&#91;33&#93;</a></sup> Despite his excellent horsemanship, he was not assigned to the cavalry, but to the <a href="/wiki/4th_Infantry_Regiment_(United_States)" title="4th Infantry Regiment (United States)">4th Infantry Regiment</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-37" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-37">&#91;c&#93;</a></sup> Grant's first assignment took him to the <a href="/wiki/Jefferson_Barracks" class="mw-redirect" title="Jefferson Barracks">Jefferson Barracks</a> near <a href="/wiki/St._Louis,_Missouri" class="mw-redirect" title="St. Louis, Missouri">St. Louis, Missouri</a>. Lt. Col. <a href="/wiki/Robert_C._Buchanan" title="Robert C. Buchanan">Robert C. Buchanan</a> fined Grant wine bottles for Grant's late returns from White Haven.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200128–29Brands201215Chernow201781_38-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200128–29Brands201215Chernow201781-38">&#91;35&#93;</a></sup> Commanded by Colonel <a href="/wiki/Stephen_W._Kearny" title="Stephen W. Kearny">Stephen W. Kearny</a>, the barracks was the nation's largest military base in the West.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200128–29_39-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200128–29-39">&#91;36&#93;</a></sup> Grant was happy with his new commander but looked forward to the end of his military service and a possible teaching career.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200130–33_40-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200130–33-40">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Marriage_and_family">Marriage and family</span></h3>
<p>In 1844, Grant accompanied Frederick Dent to Missouri and met his family, including Dent's sister <a href="/wiki/Julia_Grant" title="Julia Grant">Julia</a>. The two soon became engaged.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200130–33_40-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200130–33-40">&#91;37&#93;</a></sup> Four years later, on August 22, 1848, they were married at Julia's home in St. Louis. Grant's abolitionist father disapproved of the Dents' owning slaves, and neither of Grant's parents attended the wedding.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow201761–62White2016102Waugh200933_41-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201761–62White2016102Waugh200933-41">&#91;38&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>At the wedding, Grant was flanked by three fellow West Point graduates, all dressed in their blue uniforms, including Longstreet, Julia's cousin.<sup id="cite_ref-44" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-44">&#91;d&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200173–74Waugh200933Chernow201762White2016102_45-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200173–74Waugh200933Chernow201762White2016102-45">&#91;41&#93;</a></sup> At the end of the month, Julia was warmly received by Grant's family in <a href="/wiki/Bethel,_Ohio" title="Bethel, Ohio">Bethel, Ohio</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198120,_26Bonekemper20118Simpson201449_46-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198120,_26Bonekemper20118Simpson201449-46">&#91;42&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The couple had four children: <a href="/wiki/Frederick_Dent_Grant" title="Frederick Dent Grant">Frederick</a>, <a href="/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant_Jr." title="Ulysses S. Grant Jr.">Ulysses Jr.</a> (known as "Buck"), <a href="/wiki/Nellie_Grant" title="Nellie Grant">Ellen</a> (known as "Nellie"), and <a href="/wiki/Jesse_Root_Grant_(politician)" title="Jesse Root Grant (politician)">Jesse II</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200173_47-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200173-47">&#91;43&#93;</a></sup> After the wedding, Grant obtained a two-month extension to his leave and returned to St. Louis, where he decided that, with a wife to support, he would remain in the army.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimpson201449_48-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimpson201449-48">&#91;44&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Mexican.E2.80.93American_War"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Mexican–American_War">Mexican–American War</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Mexican%E2%80%93American_War" title="Mexican–American War">Mexican–American War</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Battle_of_Monterrey.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="An American depiction of the Battle of Monterrey within the city" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Battle_of_Monterrey.jpg/220px-Battle_of_Monterrey.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="143" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Battle_of_Monterrey.jpg/330px-Battle_of_Monterrey.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Battle_of_Monterrey.jpg/440px-Battle_of_Monterrey.jpg 2x" data-file-width="598" data-file-height="390" /></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Monterrey" title="Battle of Monterrey">Battle of Monterrey</a> during which Grant saw military action</figcaption></figure>
<p>After rising tensions with Mexico following the United States <a href="/wiki/Texas_annexation" title="Texas annexation">annexation of Texas</a>, war broke out in 1846. During the conflict, Grant distinguished himself as a daring and competent soldier.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEEncyclopedia_of_the_Mexican-American_War_2013271_49-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEncyclopedia_of_the_Mexican-American_War_2013271-49">&#91;45&#93;</a></sup> Before the war President <a href="/wiki/John_Tyler" title="John Tyler">John Tyler</a> had ordered Grant's unit to Louisiana as part of the <a href="/wiki/Army_of_Occupation_(Mexico)" title="Army of Occupation (Mexico)">Army of Occupation</a> under Major General <a href="/wiki/Zachary_Taylor" title="Zachary Taylor">Zachary Taylor</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200135–37Brands201215–17_50-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200135–37Brands201215–17-50">&#91;46&#93;</a></sup> In September 1846, Tyler's successor, <a href="/wiki/James_K._Polk" title="James K. Polk">James K. Polk</a>, unable to provoke Mexico into war at <a href="/wiki/Corpus_Christi,_Texas" title="Corpus Christi, Texas">Corpus Christi, Texas</a>, ordered Taylor to march 150 miles south to the <a href="/wiki/Rio_Grande" title="Rio Grande">Rio Grande</a>. Marching south to <a href="/wiki/Fort_Texas" class="mw-redirect" title="Fort Texas">Fort Texas</a>, to prevent a Mexican siege, Grant experienced combat for the first time on May 8, 1846, at the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Palo_Alto" title="Battle of Palo Alto">Battle of Palo Alto</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198130–31Brands201223_51-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198130–31Brands201223-51">&#91;47&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant served as regimental quartermaster, but yearned for a combat role; when finally allowed, he led a charge at the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Resaca_de_la_Palma" title="Battle of Resaca de la Palma">Battle of Resaca de la Palma</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite201680_52-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201680-52">&#91;48&#93;</a></sup> He demonstrated his equestrian ability at the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Monterrey" title="Battle of Monterrey">Battle of Monterrey</a> by volunteering to carry a dispatch past snipers, where he hung off the side of his horse, keeping the animal between him and the enemy. Before leaving the city he assured some wounded Americans he would send for help.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198133–34Brands201237_53-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198133–34Brands201237-53">&#91;49&#93;</a></sup> Polk, wary of Taylor's growing popularity, divided his forces, sending some troops (including Grant's unit) to form a new army under Major General <a href="/wiki/Winfield_Scott" title="Winfield Scott">Winfield Scott</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198134–35_54-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198134–35-54">&#91;50&#93;</a></sup> Traveling by sea, Scott's army landed at <a href="/wiki/Veracruz" title="Veracruz">Veracruz</a> and advanced toward <a href="/wiki/Mexico_City" title="Mexico City">Mexico City</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands201241–42_55-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands201241–42-55">&#91;51&#93;</a></sup> The army met the Mexican forces at the battles of <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Molino_del_Rey" title="Battle of Molino del Rey">Molino del Rey</a> and <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Chapultepec" title="Battle of Chapultepec">Chapultepec</a> outside Mexico City.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198136_56-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198136-56">&#91;52&#93;</a></sup> For his bravery at Molino del Rey, Grant was brevetted first lieutenant on September 30.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite201666Encyclopedia_of_the_Mexican-American_War_2013271_57-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201666Encyclopedia_of_the_Mexican-American_War_2013271-57">&#91;53&#93;</a></sup> At San Cosmé, Grant directed his men to drag a disassembled <a href="/wiki/Howitzer" title="Howitzer">howitzer</a> into a church steeple, then reassembled it and bombarded nearby Mexican troops.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198136_56-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198136-56">&#91;52&#93;</a></sup> His bravery and initiative earned him his brevet promotion to captain.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimpson201444Encyclopedia_of_the_Mexican-American_War_2013271_58-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimpson201444Encyclopedia_of_the_Mexican-American_War_2013271-58">&#91;54&#93;</a></sup> On September 14, 1847, Scott's army marched into the city; Mexico <a href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Guadalupe_Hidalgo" title="Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo">ceded the vast territory</a>, including <a href="/wiki/California" title="California">California</a>, to the U.S. on February 2, 1848.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200167–68,_70,_73Brands201249–52_59-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200167–68,_70,_73Brands201249–52-59">&#91;55&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>During the war, Grant established a commendable record, studied the tactics and strategies of Scott and Taylor, and emerged as a seasoned officer, writing in his memoirs that this is how he learned much about military leadership.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimpson2014458Chernow201758_60-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimpson2014458Chernow201758-60">&#91;56&#93;</a></sup> In retrospect, although he respected Scott, he identified his leadership style with Taylor's. However, Grant also wrote that the Mexican war was morally unjust and that the territorial gains were designed to expand slavery, stating, "I was bitterly opposed to the measure ... and to this day, regard the war which resulted as one of the most unjust ever waged by a stronger against a weaker nation." He opined that the Civil War was divine punishment on the U.S. for its aggression against Mexico.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198130,_31,_37–38_61-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198130,_31,_37–38-61">&#91;57&#93;</a></sup> During the war, Grant discovered his "moral courage" and began to consider a career in the army.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite201675_62-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201675-62">&#91;58&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Historians increasingly have pointed to the importance of Grant's experience as an assistant quartermaster during the war. Although he was initially averse to the position, it prepared Grant in understanding military supply routes, transportation systems, and logistics, particularly with regard to "provisioning a large, mobile army operating in hostile territory," according to biographer Ronald White.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite201680_52-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201680-52">&#91;48&#93;</a></sup> Grant came to recognize how wars could be won or lost by crucial factors that lay beyond the tactical battlefield. Serving as assistant quartermaster made Grant a complete soldier, and learning how to supply an entire army gave Grant the training to sustain large armies.<sup id="cite_ref-65" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-65">&#91;e&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite201685,_96Chernow201746_66-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite201685,_96Chernow201746-66">&#91;61&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Post-war_assignments_and_resignation">Post-war assignments and resignation</span></h3>
<p>Grant's first post-war assignments took him and Julia to <a href="/wiki/Detroit" title="Detroit">Detroit</a> on November 17, 1848, but he was soon transferred to <a href="/wiki/Madison_Barracks" title="Madison Barracks">Madison Barracks</a>, a desolate outpost in upstate New York, in bad need of supplies and repair. After four months, Grant was sent back to his quartermaster job in Detroit.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow201765_67-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201765-67">&#91;62&#93;</a></sup> When the discovery of <a href="/wiki/California_Gold_Rush" title="California Gold Rush">gold in California</a> brought droves of prospectors and settlers to the territory, Grant and the 4th infantry were ordered to reinforce the small garrison there. Grant was charged with bringing the soldiers and a few hundred civilians from New York City to Panama, <a href="/wiki/Maritime_history_of_California#To_California_via_Panama" title="Maritime history of California">overland</a> to the Pacific and then north to California. Julia, eight months pregnant with Ulysses Jr., did not accompany him.
</p><p>While Grant was in Panama, a <a href="/wiki/Cholera" title="Cholera">cholera</a> epidemic broke out and claimed the lives of many soldiers, civilians, and children. Grant established and organized a field hospital in <a href="/wiki/Panama_City" title="Panama City">Panama City</a>, and moved the worst cases to a hospital barge one mile offshore.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow201774_68-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201774-68">&#91;63&#93;</a></sup> When orderlies protested having to attend to the sick, Grant did much of the nursing himself, earning high praise from observers.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200176–78Chernow201773–74_69-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200176–78Chernow201773–74-69">&#91;64&#93;</a></sup> In August, Grant arrived in San Francisco. His next assignment sent him north to <a href="/wiki/Vancouver_Barracks" title="Vancouver Barracks">Vancouver Barracks</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Oregon_Territory" title="Oregon Territory">Oregon Territory</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200178Chernow201775_70-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200178Chernow201775-70">&#91;65&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant tried several business ventures but failed, and in one instance his business partner absconded with $800 of Grant's investment, equivalent to $21,000&#32;in 2021.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981Chernow2017_71-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981Chernow2017-71">&#91;66&#93;</a></sup> Concerning <a href="/wiki/Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Pacific_Northwest_Coast" title="Indigenous peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast">local Indians</a>, Grant assured Julia, by letter, they were harmless. After he witnessed white agents cheating Indians of their supplies, and their devastation by <a href="/wiki/Smallpox" title="Smallpox">smallpox</a> and <a href="/wiki/Measles" title="Measles">measles</a> which were transferred to them by white settlers, he developed empathy for their plight.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016487Chernow201778_72-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016487Chernow201778-72">&#91;67&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Promoted to <a href="/wiki/Captain_(U.S._Army)" class="mw-redirect" title="Captain (U.S. Army)">captain</a> on August 5, 1853, Grant was assigned to command Company F, <a href="/wiki/4th_Infantry_Regiment_(United_States)" title="4th Infantry Regiment (United States)">4th Infantry</a>, at the newly constructed <a href="/wiki/Fort_Humboldt_State_Historic_Park" title="Fort Humboldt State Historic Park">Fort Humboldt</a> in California.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198152Cullum1891171Chernow201781_73-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198152Cullum1891171Chernow201781-73">&#91;68&#93;</a></sup> Grant arrived at Fort Humboldt on January 5, 1854, commanded by Lieutenant Colonel <a href="/wiki/Robert_C._Buchanan" title="Robert C. Buchanan">Robert C. Buchanan</a>, a martinet officer, with whom Grant had earlier crossed paths at Jefferson Barracks.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow201781–83_74-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201781–83-74">&#91;69&#93;</a></sup> Separated from his wife and family, Grant began to drink.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198155Chernow201784–85_75-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198155Chernow201784–85-75">&#91;70&#93;</a></sup> Colonel Buchanan reprimanded Grant for one drinking episode and told Grant to "resign or reform." Grant told Buchanan he would "resign if I don't reform."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow201785_76-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201785-76">&#91;71&#93;</a></sup> On Sunday, Grant was found influenced by alcohol, but not incapacitated, at his company's paytable.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECullum1891171Chernow201784–85_77-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECullum1891171Chernow201784–85-77">&#91;72&#93;</a></sup> Keeping his pledge to Buchanan, Grant resigned, effective July 31, 1854.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECullum1891171Chernow201785–86_78-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECullum1891171Chernow201785–86-78">&#91;73&#93;</a></sup> Buchanan endorsed Grant's letter of resignation but did not submit any report that verified the incident.<sup id="cite_ref-84" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-84">&#91;f&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200186–87White2016118–20McFeely198155_85-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200186–87White2016118–20McFeely198155-85">&#91;79&#93;</a></sup> Grant did not face court-martial, and the War Department said: "Nothing stands against his good name."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELongacre200655–58_86-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELongacre200655–58-86">&#91;80&#93;</a></sup> Grant said years later, "the vice of intemperance (drunkenness) had not a little to do with my decision to resign."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200187–88Lewis1950328–32_87-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200187–88Lewis1950328–32-87">&#91;81&#93;</a></sup> With no means of support, Grant returned to St. Louis and reunited with his family, uncertain about his future.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands201277–78_88-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands201277–78-88">&#91;82&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span id="Civilian_struggles.2C_slavery.2C_and_politics"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Civilian_struggles,_slavery,_and_politics">Civilian struggles, slavery, and politics</span></h2>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Hardscrabble.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="A small log cabin" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Hardscrabble.jpg/220px-Hardscrabble.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="142" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Hardscrabble.jpg/330px-Hardscrabble.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/09/Hardscrabble.jpg/440px-Hardscrabble.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3475" data-file-height="2238" /></a><figcaption>"Hardscrabble", the log house built by Grant in between wars</figcaption></figure>
<p>In 1854, at age 32, Grant entered civilian life, without any money-making vocation to support his growing family. It was the beginning of seven years of financial struggles, poverty, and instability.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow201795,_106Simon2002242McFeely198160–61Brands201294–96_89-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201795,_106Simon2002242McFeely198160–61Brands201294–96-89">&#91;83&#93;</a></sup> Grant's father offered him a place in the <a href="/wiki/Galena,_Illinois" title="Galena, Illinois">Galena, Illinois</a>, branch of the family's leather business, but demanded Julia and the children stay in Missouri, with the Dents, or with the Grants in Kentucky. Grant and Julia declined the offer. For the next four years, Grant farmed with the help of Julia's slave Dan, on his brother-in-law's property, <i>Wish-ton-wish</i>, near <a href="/wiki/St._Louis" title="St. Louis">St. Louis</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198158–60White2016125_90-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198158–60White2016125-90">&#91;84&#93;</a></sup> The farm was not successful and to earn an alternate living he sold firewood on St. Louis street corners.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198161_91-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198161-91">&#91;85&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1856, the Grants moved to land on Julia's father's farm, and built a home called "Hardscrabble" on <a href="/wiki/Grant%27s_Farm" title="Grant&#39;s Farm">Grant's Farm</a>. Julia described the <a href="/wiki/Log_house" title="Log house">rustic house</a> as an "unattractive cabin", but made the dwelling as homelike as possible with the family's keepsakes and other belongings.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198158–60Chernow201794_92-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198158–60Chernow201794-92">&#91;86&#93;</a></sup> Grant's family had little money, clothes, and furniture, but always had enough food.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands201296_93-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands201296-93">&#91;87&#93;</a></sup> During the <a href="/wiki/Panic_of_1857" title="Panic of 1857">Panic of 1857</a>, which devastated Grant as it did many farmers, Grant pawned his gold watch in order to buy Christmas gifts for his family.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016128_94-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016128-94">&#91;88&#93;</a></sup> In 1858, Grant rented out Hardscrabble and moved his family to Julia's father's <a href="/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant_National_Historic_Site" title="Ulysses S. Grant National Historic Site">850-acre plantation</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198162Brands201286White2016128_95-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198162Brands201286White2016128-95">&#91;89&#93;</a></sup> That fall, after suffering from <a href="/wiki/Malaria" title="Malaria">malaria</a>, Grant finally gave up farming.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012White2016_96-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012White2016-96">&#91;90&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>That same year, Grant acquired a <a href="/wiki/History_of_slavery_in_Missouri" title="History of slavery in Missouri">slave</a> from his father-in-law, a thirty-five-year-old man named William Jones.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200194–95White2016130_97-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200194–95White2016130-97">&#91;91&#93;</a></sup> Although Grant was not an <a href="/wiki/Abolitionist" class="mw-redirect" title="Abolitionist">abolitionist</a> at the time, he disliked slavery and could not bring himself to force an enslaved man to do work.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands201286–87_98-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands201286–87-98">&#91;92&#93;</a></sup> In March 1859, Grant freed William by a <a href="/wiki/Manumission" title="Manumission">manumission</a> deed, potentially worth at least $1,000 (equivalent to $33,000 in 2022), when Grant needed the money.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200194–95McFeely198169White2016130_99-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200194–95McFeely198169White2016130-99">&#91;93&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant moved to St. Louis, taking on a partnership with Julia's cousin Harry Boggs working in the real estate business as a bill collector, again without success and with Julia's prompting ended the partnership.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198164Brands201289–90White2016129–31_100-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198164Brands201289–90White2016129–31-100">&#91;94&#93;</a></sup> In August, Grant applied for a position as county engineer, believing his education qualified him for the job. He had thirty-five notable recommendations, but the position was given on the basis of political affiliation and Grant was passed over by the <a href="/wiki/Free_Soil_Party" title="Free Soil Party">Free Soil</a> and <a href="/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States)" title="Republican Party (United States)">Republican</a> county commissioners because he was believed to share his father-in-law's <a href="/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States)" title="Democratic Party (United States)">Democratic</a> sentiments.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016131Simon19694–5_101-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016131Simon19694–5-101">&#91;95&#93;</a></sup> In the 1856 presidential election, Grant cast his first <a href="/wiki/1856_United_States_presidential_election" title="1856 United States presidential election">presidential vote</a> for Democrat <a href="/wiki/James_Buchanan" title="James Buchanan">James Buchanan</a>, later saying he was really voting against Republican <a href="/wiki/John_C._Fr%C3%A9mont" title="John C. Frémont">John C. Frémont</a> over concern that his anti-slavery position would lead to southern secession and war and because he considered Frémont to be a shameless self-promoter.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198169–70_102-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198169–70-102">&#91;96&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In April 1860, Grant and his family moved north to Galena, accepting a position in his father's leather goods business, "Grant &amp; Perkins", run by his younger brothers Simpson and Orvil. In a few months, Grant paid off his debts.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198165–66White2016133,_136_103-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198165–66White2016133,_136-103">&#91;97&#93;</a></sup> The family attended the local Methodist church and he soon established himself as a reputable citizen of Galena.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016135–37_104-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016135–37-104">&#91;98&#93;</a></sup> For the 1860 election, he could not vote because he was not yet a legal resident of Illinois, but he favored Democrat <a href="/wiki/Stephen_A._Douglas" title="Stephen A. Douglas">Stephen A. Douglas</a> over the eventual winner, <a href="/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln" title="Abraham Lincoln">Abraham Lincoln</a>, and Lincoln over the Southern Democrat, <a href="/wiki/John_C._Breckinridge" title="John C. Breckinridge">John C. Breckinridge</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198169–70Simon19694–5_105-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198169–70Simon19694–5-105">&#91;99&#93;</a></sup> He was torn between his increasingly anti-slavery views and the fact that his wife remained a staunch Democrat.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017119–20_106-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017119–20-106">&#91;100&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Civil_War">Civil War</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant_and_the_American_Civil_War" title="Ulysses S. Grant and the American Civil War">Ulysses S. Grant and the American Civil War</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ulysses_S_Grant_as_Brigadier_General,_1861.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Ulysses_S_Grant_as_Brigadier_General%2C_1861.jpg/170px-Ulysses_S_Grant_as_Brigadier_General%2C_1861.jpg" decoding="async" width="170" height="238" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Ulysses_S_Grant_as_Brigadier_General%2C_1861.jpg/255px-Ulysses_S_Grant_as_Brigadier_General%2C_1861.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Ulysses_S_Grant_as_Brigadier_General%2C_1861.jpg/340px-Ulysses_S_Grant_as_Brigadier_General%2C_1861.jpg 2x" data-file-width="758" data-file-height="1062" /></a><figcaption>Brigadier General Grant, 1861</figcaption></figure>
<p>On April 12, 1861, the <a href="/wiki/American_Civil_War" title="American Civil War">American Civil War</a> began when Confederate troops <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Sumter" title="Battle of Fort Sumter">attacked Fort Sumter</a> in <a href="/wiki/Charleston,_South_Carolina" title="Charleston, South Carolina">Charleston, South Carolina</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016140_107-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016140-107">&#91;101&#93;</a></sup> The news came as a shock in Galena, and Grant shared his neighbors' concern about the war.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012121_108-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012121-108">&#91;102&#93;</a></sup> On April 15, Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200199_109-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200199-109">&#91;103&#93;</a></sup> The next day, Grant attended a mass meeting to assess the crisis and encourage recruitment, and a speech by his father's attorney, <a href="/wiki/John_Aaron_Rawlins" title="John Aaron Rawlins">John Aaron Rawlins</a>, stirred Grant's patriotism.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016140–43Brands2012121–22McFeely198173Bonekemper201217Smith200199Chernow2017125_110-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016140–43Brands2012121–22McFeely198173Bonekemper201217Smith200199Chernow2017125-110">&#91;104&#93;</a></sup> In an April 21 letter to his father, Grant wrote out his views on the upcoming conflict: "We have a government and laws and a flag, and they must all be sustained. There are but two parties now, Traitors and Patriots."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012123_111-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012123-111">&#91;105&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Early_commands">Early commands</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Kentucky_in_the_American_Civil_War" title="Kentucky in the American Civil War">Kentucky in the American Civil War</a></div>
<p>On April 18, Grant chaired a second recruitment meeting, but turned down a captain's position as commander of the newly formed militia company, hoping his previous experience would aid him to obtain a more senior military rank.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012122–23McFeely198180Bonekemper2012_112-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012122–23McFeely198180Bonekemper2012-112">&#91;106&#93;</a></sup> His early efforts to be recommissioned, however, were rejected by Major General <a href="/wiki/George_B._McClellan" title="George B. McClellan">George B. McClellan</a> and Brigadier General <a href="/wiki/Nathaniel_Lyon" title="Nathaniel Lyon">Nathaniel Lyon</a>. On April 29, supported by Congressman <a href="/wiki/Elihu_B._Washburne" title="Elihu B. Washburne">Elihu B. Washburne</a> of Illinois, Grant was appointed military aide to Governor <a href="/wiki/Richard_Yates_(19th-century_politician)" class="mw-redirect" title="Richard Yates (19th-century politician)">Richard Yates</a> and mustered ten regiments into the <a href="/wiki/Illinois_militia" class="mw-redirect" title="Illinois militia">Illinois militia</a>. On June 14, again aided by Washburne, Grant was appointed colonel and put in charge of the <a href="/wiki/21st_Illinois_Volunteer_Infantry_Regiment" class="mw-redirect" title="21st Illinois Volunteer Infantry Regiment">21st Illinois Volunteer Infantry Regiment</a>; he appointed <a href="/wiki/John_A._Rawlins" class="mw-redirect" title="John A. Rawlins">John A. Rawlins</a> as his <a href="/wiki/Aide-de-camp" title="Aide-de-camp">aide-de-camp</a> and brought order and discipline to the regiment. Soon after, Colonel Grant and the 21st Regiment were transferred to Missouri to dislodge Confederate forces.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFlood200545–46Smith2001113Bonekemper201218–20_113-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFlood200545–46Smith2001113Bonekemper201218–20-113">&#91;107&#93;</a></sup> 
</p><p>On August 5, with Washburne's aid, Grant was appointed brigadier general of volunteers.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBonekemper201221_114-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper201221-114">&#91;108&#93;</a></sup> Major General <a href="/wiki/John_C._Fr%C3%A9mont" title="John C. Frémont">John C. Frémont</a>, Union commander of the West, passed over senior generals and appointed Grant commander of the District of Southeastern Missouri.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001117–18Bonekemper201221_115-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001117–18Bonekemper201221-115">&#91;109&#93;</a></sup> On September 2, Grant arrived at <a href="/wiki/Cairo,_Illinois" title="Cairo, Illinois">Cairo, Illinois</a>, assumed command by replacing Colonel <a href="/wiki/Richard_J._Oglesby" title="Richard J. Oglesby">Richard J. Oglesby</a>, and set up his headquarters to plan a campaign down the Mississippi, and up the Tennessee and Cumberland rivers.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016159Bonekemper201221_116-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016159Bonekemper201221-116">&#91;110&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After the Confederates moved into western Kentucky, taking Columbus, with designs on southern Illinois, Grant notified Frémont and, without waiting further for his reply, strategically advanced on <a href="/wiki/Paducah,_Kentucky" title="Paducah, Kentucky">Paducah, Kentucky</a>, taking it without a fight on September 6.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFlood200563White2016159Bonekemper201221_117-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFlood200563White2016159Bonekemper201221-117">&#91;111&#93;</a></sup> Having understood the importance to Lincoln of Kentucky's neutrality, Grant assured its citizens, "I have come among you not as your enemy, but as your friend."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198191Chernow2017153–55_118-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198191Chernow2017153–55-118">&#91;112&#93;</a></sup> On November 1, Frémont ordered Grant to "<a href="/wiki/Demonstration_(military)" title="Demonstration (military)">make demonstrations</a>" against the Confederates on both sides of the Mississippi, but prohibited him from attacking the enemy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016168_119-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016168-119">&#91;113&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Belmont_.281861.29.2C_Forts_Henry_and_Donelson_.281862.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Belmont_(1861),_Forts_Henry_and_Donelson_(1862)">Belmont (1861), Forts Henry and Donelson (1862)</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Belmont" title="Battle of Belmont">Battle of Belmont</a>, <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Henry" title="Battle of Fort Henry">Battle of Fort Henry</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Donelson" title="Battle of Fort Donelson">Battle of Fort Donelson</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Battle_of_Fort_Donelson.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Battle_of_Fort_Donelson.png/260px-Battle_of_Fort_Donelson.png" decoding="async" width="260" height="188" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Battle_of_Fort_Donelson.png/390px-Battle_of_Fort_Donelson.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/10/Battle_of_Fort_Donelson.png/520px-Battle_of_Fort_Donelson.png 2x" data-file-width="1786" data-file-height="1293" /></a><figcaption><i>Battle of Fort Donelson</i> by <a href="/wiki/Kurz_and_Allison" title="Kurz and Allison">Kurz and Allison</a>, 1887</figcaption></figure>
<p>On November 2, 1861, Lincoln removed Frémont from command, freeing Grant to attack Confederate soldiers encamped in <a href="/wiki/Cape_Girardeau" class="mw-redirect" title="Cape Girardeau">Cape Girardeau</a>, Missouri.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016168_119-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016168-119">&#91;113&#93;</a></sup> On November 5, Grant, along with Brigadier General <a href="/wiki/John_A._McClernand" class="mw-redirect" title="John A. McClernand">John A. McClernand</a>, landed 2,500 men at Hunter's Point, and on November 7 engaged the Confederates at the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Belmont" title="Battle of Belmont">Battle of Belmont</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016169–71_120-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016169–71-120">&#91;114&#93;</a></sup> The Union army took the camp, but the reinforced Confederates under Brigadier Generals <a href="/wiki/Frank_Cheatham" class="mw-redirect" title="Frank Cheatham">Frank Cheatham</a> and <a href="/wiki/Gideon_J._Pillow" class="mw-redirect" title="Gideon J. Pillow">Gideon J. Pillow</a> forced a chaotic Union retreat. <sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016172_121-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016172-121">&#91;115&#93;</a></sup> Grant had wanted to destroy Confederate strongholds at both <a href="/wiki/Belmont,_Missouri" title="Belmont, Missouri">Belmont, Missouri</a> and <a href="/wiki/Columbus,_Kentucky" title="Columbus, Kentucky">Columbus, Kentucky</a>, but was not given enough troops and was only able to disrupt their positions. Grant's troops fought their way back to their Union boats and escaped back to Cairo under fire from the fortified stronghold at Columbus. <sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016172–73Groom201294,_101–03_122-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016172–73Groom201294,_101–03-122">&#91;116&#93;</a></sup> Although Grant and his army retreated, the battle gave his volunteers much-needed confidence and experience.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198192–94_123-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198192–94-123">&#91;117&#93;</a></sup> It also showed Lincoln that Grant was a general willing to fight.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBonekemper201233,_35_124-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper201233,_35-124">&#91;118&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Columbus blocked Union access to the lower Mississippi. Grant and lieutenant colonel <a href="/wiki/James_B._McPherson" title="James B. McPherson">James B. McPherson</a> planned to bypass Columbus and with a force of 25,000 troops, move against <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Henry" title="Battle of Fort Henry">Fort Henry</a> on the <a href="/wiki/Tennessee_River" title="Tennessee River">Tennessee River</a>. They would then march ten miles east to <a href="/wiki/Fort_Donelson" title="Fort Donelson">Fort Donelson</a> on the <a href="/wiki/Cumberland_River" title="Cumberland River">Cumberland River</a>, with the aid of gunboats, opening both rivers and allowing the Union access further south. Grant presented his plan to <a href="/wiki/Henry_Halleck" title="Henry Halleck">Henry Halleck</a>, his new commander in the newly created <a href="/wiki/Department_of_Missouri" class="mw-redirect" title="Department of Missouri">Department of Missouri</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016168McFeely198194_125-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016168McFeely198194-125">&#91;119&#93;</a></sup> Halleck was considering the same strategy, but rebuffed Grant, believing he needed twice the number of troops. However, after Halleck telegraphed and consulted McClellan about the plan, he finally agreed on the condition that the attack would be conducted in close cooperation with the navy <a href="/wiki/Flag_Officer#United_States" class="mw-redirect" title="Flag Officer">Flag Officer</a>, <a href="/wiki/Andrew_H._Foote" class="mw-redirect" title="Andrew H. Foote">Andrew H. Foote</a>. <sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001138–42Groom2012101–03_126-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001138–42Groom2012101–03-126">&#91;120&#93;</a></sup> Foote's gunboats bombarded Fort Henry, leading to its surrender on February 6, 1862, before Grant's infantry even arrived.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001146_127-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001146-127">&#91;121&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant then ordered an immediate <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Donelson" title="Battle of Fort Donelson">assault on Fort Donelson</a>, which dominated the Cumberland River. Fort Donelson, unlike Fort Henry, had a force equal to Grant's army. Unaware of the garrison's strength, Grant, McClernand, and Smith positioned their divisions around the fort. The next day McClernand and Smith independently launched probing attacks on apparent weak spots but were forced to retreat by the Confederates. On February 14, Foote's gunboats began bombarding the fort, only to be repulsed by its heavy guns. Seizing the initiative, the next day, Pillow fiercely attacked and routed one of Grant's divisions, McClernand's. Union reinforcements arrived, giving Grant a total force of over 40,000 men. Grant was with Foote, four miles away when the Confederates attacked. Hearing the battle noise, Grant rode back and rallied his troop commanders, riding over seven miles of freezing roads and trenches, exchanging reports. When Grant blocked the Nashville Road, the Confederates retreated back into Fort Donelson.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAxelrod2011210_128-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAxelrod2011210-128">&#91;122&#93;</a></sup> On February 16, Foote resumed his bombardment, which signaled a general attack. Confederate generals <a href="/wiki/John_B._Floyd" title="John B. Floyd">John B. Floyd</a> and Pillow fled, leaving the fort in command of <a href="/wiki/Simon_Bolivar_Buckner" title="Simon Bolivar Buckner">Simon Bolivar Buckner</a>, who submitted to Grant's demand for "unconditional and immediate surrender".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001141–64Brands2012164–65_129-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001141–64Brands2012164–65-129">&#91;123&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant had won the first major victory for the Union, capturing Floyd's entire rebel army of more than 12,000. Halleck was angry that Grant had acted without his authorization and complained to McClellan, accusing Grant of "neglect and inefficiency". On March 3, Halleck sent a telegram to Washington complaining that he had no communication with Grant for a week. Three days later, Halleck followed up with a postscript claiming "word has just reached me that&#160;... Grant has resumed his bad habits (of drinking)."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGroom2012138,_143–44_130-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGroom2012138,_143–44-130">&#91;124&#93;</a></sup> Lincoln, regardless, promoted Grant to major general of volunteers and the Northern press treated Grant as a hero. Playing off his initials, they took to calling him "Unconditional Surrender Grant".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012164–65Smith2001125–34_131-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012164–65Smith2001125–34-131">&#91;125&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Shiloh_.281862.29_and_aftermath"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Shiloh_(1862)_and_aftermath">Shiloh (1862) and aftermath</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Shiloh" title="Battle of Shiloh">Battle of Shiloh</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Thure_de_Thulstrup_-_Battle_of_Shiloh.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Thure_de_Thulstrup_-_Battle_of_Shiloh.jpg/290px-Thure_de_Thulstrup_-_Battle_of_Shiloh.jpg" decoding="async" width="290" height="208" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Thure_de_Thulstrup_-_Battle_of_Shiloh.jpg/435px-Thure_de_Thulstrup_-_Battle_of_Shiloh.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Thure_de_Thulstrup_-_Battle_of_Shiloh.jpg/580px-Thure_de_Thulstrup_-_Battle_of_Shiloh.jpg 2x" data-file-width="9648" data-file-height="6920" /></a><figcaption><i>Battle of Shiloh</i> by <a href="/wiki/Thure_de_Thulstrup" title="Thure de Thulstrup">Thure de Thulstrup</a>, 1888</figcaption></figure>
<p>Reinstated by Halleck at the urging of Lincoln and Secretary of War <a href="/wiki/Edwin_Stanton" title="Edwin Stanton">Edwin Stanton</a>, Grant left Fort Henry and traveled by boat up the Tennessee River to rejoin his army with orders to advance with the <a href="/wiki/Army_of_the_Tennessee" title="Army of the Tennessee">Army of the Tennessee</a> into Tennessee. His main army was located at <a href="/wiki/Pittsburg_Landing" class="mw-redirect" title="Pittsburg Landing">Pittsburg Landing</a>, while 40,000 Confederate troops converged at <a href="/wiki/Corinth,_Mississippi" title="Corinth, Mississippi">Corinth, Mississippi</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016210Barney2011287_132-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016210Barney2011287-132">&#91;126&#93;</a></sup> Brigadier General <a href="/wiki/William_Tecumseh_Sherman" title="William Tecumseh Sherman">William Tecumseh Sherman</a> assured Grant that his green troops were ready for an attack. Grant agreed and wired Halleck with their assessment.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001185_133-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001185-133">&#91;127&#93;</a></sup> Grant wanted to attack the Confederates at Corinth, but Halleck ordered him not to attack until Major General <a href="/wiki/Don_Carlos_Buell" title="Don Carlos Buell">Don Carlos Buell</a> arrived with his division of 25,000.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981111–12Groom201263White2016211_134-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981111–12Groom201263White2016211-134">&#91;128&#93;</a></sup> Meanwhile, Grant prepared for an attack on the Confederate army of roughly equal strength. Instead of preparing defensive fortifications between the Tennessee River and Owl Creek, and clearing fields of fire, they spent most of their time drilling the largely inexperienced troops while Sherman dismissed reports of nearby Confederates.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGroom201262–65McFeely1981112_135-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGroom201262–65McFeely1981112-135">&#91;129&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Union inaction created the opportunity for the Confederates to attack first before Buell arrived.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016211_136-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016211-136">&#91;130&#93;</a></sup> On the morning of April 6, 1862, Grant's troops were taken by surprise when the Confederates, led by Generals <a href="/wiki/Albert_Sidney_Johnston" title="Albert Sidney Johnston">Albert Sidney Johnston</a> and <a href="/wiki/P._G._T._Beauregard" title="P. G. T. Beauregard">P. G. T. Beauregard</a>, struck first "like an Alpine avalanche" near Shiloh church, attacking five divisions of Grant's army and forcing a confused retreat toward the Tennessee River.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981111Bonekemper201251,_94Barney2011287_137-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981111Bonekemper201251,_94Barney2011287-137">&#91;131&#93;</a></sup> Johnston was killed and command fell upon Beauregard.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016217–18_138-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016217–18-138">&#91;132&#93;</a></sup> One Union line held the Confederate attack off for several hours, giving Grant time to assemble artillery and 20,000 troops near Pittsburg Landing.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBonekemper201251,_58–59,_63–64_139-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper201251,_58–59,_63–64-139">&#91;133&#93;</a></sup> The Confederates finally broke and captured a Union division, but Grant's newly assembled line held the landing, while the exhausted Confederates, lacking reinforcements, halted their advance.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981114Flood2005109,_112Bonekemper201251,_58–59,_63–64_140-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981114Flood2005109,_112Bonekemper201251,_58–59,_63–64-140">&#91;134&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The day's fighting had been costly, with thousands of casualties. That evening, heavy rain set in. Sherman found Grant standing alone under a tree in the rain. "Well, Grant, we've had the devil's own day of it, haven't we?" Sherman said. "Yes," replied Grant. "Lick 'em tomorrow, though."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017205_141-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017205-141">&#91;135&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Bolstered by 18,000 fresh troops from the divisions of Major Generals Buell and <a href="/wiki/Lew_Wallace" title="Lew Wallace">Lew Wallace</a>, Grant counterattacked at dawn the next day and regained the field, forcing the disorganized and demoralized rebels to retreat back to Corinth.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBonekemper201259,_63–64Smith2001206_142-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper201259,_63–64Smith2001206-142">&#91;136&#93;</a></sup> Halleck ordered Grant not to advance more than one day's march from Pittsburg Landing, stopping the pursuit of the Confederate Army.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981115–16_143-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981115–16-143">&#91;137&#93;</a></sup> Although Grant had won the battle, the situation was little changed, with the Union still in possession of Pittsburg Landing and the Confederates once again holed up in Corinth.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981115_144-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981115-144">&#91;138&#93;</a></sup> Grant, now realizing that the South was determined to fight and that the war would not be won with one battle, would later write, "Then, indeed, I gave up all idea of saving the Union except by complete conquest."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012187–88_145-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012187–88-145">&#91;139&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Shiloh was the costliest battle in American history to that point and the staggering 23,746 total casualties stunned the nation.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBonekemper201294White2016221_146-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper201294White2016221-146">&#91;140&#93;</a></sup> Briefly hailed a hero for routing the Confederates, Grant was soon mired in controversy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016223–24_147-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016223–24-147">&#91;141&#93;</a></sup> The Northern press castigated Grant for shockingly high casualties, and accused him of drunkenness during the battle, contrary to the accounts of officers and others with him at the time.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKaplan20151109–19White2016223–25_148-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKaplan20151109–19White2016223–25-148">&#91;142&#93;</a></sup> Discouraged, Grant considered resigning but Sherman convinced him to stay.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012188–91White2016230–31_149-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012188–91White2016230–31-149">&#91;143&#93;</a></sup> Lincoln dismissed Grant's critics, saying "I can't spare this man; he fights."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016225–26_150-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016225–26-150">&#91;144&#93;</a></sup> Ultimately, Grant's costly victory at Shiloh ended any chance for the Confederates to prevail in the Mississippi valley or regain its strategic advantage in the West.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001204Barney2011289_151-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001204Barney2011289-151">&#91;145&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Halleck arrived from St. Louis on April 11, took command, and assembled a combined army of about 120,000 men. On April 29, he relieved Grant of field command and replaced him with Major General <a href="/wiki/George_Henry_Thomas" title="George Henry Thomas">George Henry Thomas</a>. Halleck slowly marched his army to take Corinth, entrenching each night.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016229_152-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016229-152">&#91;146&#93;</a></sup> Meanwhile, Beauregard pretended to be reinforcing, sent "deserters" to the Union Army with that story, and moved his army out during the night, to Halleck's surprise when he finally <a href="/wiki/First_Battle_of_Corinth" class="mw-redirect" title="First Battle of Corinth">arrived at Corinth</a> on May 30.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016230Groom2012363–64_153-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016230Groom2012363–64-153">&#91;147&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Halleck divided his combined army and reinstated Grant as field commander of the Army of the Tennessee on July 11.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELongacre2006137White2016231_154-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELongacre2006137White2016231-154">&#91;148&#93;</a></sup> Later that year, on September 19, Grant's army defeated Confederates at the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Iuka" title="Battle of Iuka">Battle of Iuka</a>, then successfully <a href="/wiki/Second_Battle_of_Corinth" title="Second Battle of Corinth">defended Corinth</a>, inflicting heavy casualties.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012211–12_155-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012211–12-155">&#91;149&#93;</a></sup> On October 25, Grant assumed command of the District of the Tennessee.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBadeau1887126_156-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBadeau1887126-156">&#91;150&#93;</a></sup> In November, after Lincoln's preliminary <a href="/wiki/Emancipation_Proclamation" title="Emancipation Proclamation">Emancipation Proclamation</a>, Grant ordered units under his command to incorporate former slaves into the Union Army, giving them clothes, shelter, and wages for their services.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFlood2005133_157-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFlood2005133-157">&#91;151&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Vicksburg_campaign_.281862.E2.80.931863.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Vicksburg_campaign_(1862–1863)">Vicksburg campaign (1862–1863)</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Vicksburg_Campaign" class="mw-redirect" title="Vicksburg Campaign">Vicksburg Campaign</a> and <a href="/wiki/General_Order_No._11_(1862)" title="General Order No. 11 (1862)">General Order No. 11 (1862)</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:VicksburgBlockade.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/VicksburgBlockade.jpg/260px-VicksburgBlockade.jpg" decoding="async" width="260" height="190" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/VicksburgBlockade.jpg/390px-VicksburgBlockade.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/VicksburgBlockade.jpg/520px-VicksburgBlockade.jpg 2x" data-file-width="7761" data-file-height="5661" /></a><figcaption>Grant's successful gamble: Porter's gunboats night ran the Confederate gauntlet at Vicksburg on the <a href="/wiki/Mississippi_River" title="Mississippi River">Mississippi River</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The Union capture of <a href="/wiki/Vicksburg,_Mississippi" title="Vicksburg, Mississippi">Vicksburg</a>, the last Confederate stronghold on the <a href="/wiki/Mississippi_River" title="Mississippi River">Mississippi River</a>, was considered to be vital as it would split the Confederacy in two.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016243Miller2019xiiChernow2017236_158-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016243Miller2019xiiChernow2017236-158">&#91;152&#93;</a></sup> Lincoln, however, appointed McClernand for the job, rather than Grant or Sherman.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012221–23Catton2005112Chernow2017236–37_159-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012221–23Catton2005112Chernow2017236–37-159">&#91;153&#93;</a></sup> Halleck, who retained power over troop displacement, ordered McClernand to <a href="/wiki/Memphis,_Tennessee" title="Memphis, Tennessee">Memphis</a>, and placed him and his troops under Grant's authority.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFlood2005147–48White2016246Chernow2017238–39_160-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFlood2005147–48White2016246Chernow2017238–39-160">&#91;154&#93;</a></sup>
