</p><p>On November 13, 1862, Grant captured <a href="/wiki/Holly_Springs,_Mississippi" title="Holly Springs, Mississippi">Holly Springs</a> and advanced to <a href="/wiki/Corinth,_Mississippi" title="Corinth, Mississippi">Corinth</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016248Chernow2017231–32_161-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016248Chernow2017231–32-161">&#91;155&#93;</a></sup> His plan was to march south to Jackson, and attack Vicksburg overland, while Sherman would attack Vicksburg from Chickasaw Bayou.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017239_162-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017239-162">&#91;156&#93;</a></sup> However, Confederate cavalry raids on December 11 and 20, 1862, broke Union communications and recaptured Holly Springs, preventing Grant and Sherman from converging on Vicksburg.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECatton2005119,_291White2016248–49Chernow2017239–41_163-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatton2005119,_291White2016248–49Chernow2017239–41-163">&#91;157&#93;</a></sup> On December 29, a Confederate army led by <a href="/wiki/Lieutenant_General_(United_States)" class="mw-redirect" title="Lieutenant General (United States)">Lieutenant General</a> <a href="/wiki/John_C._Pemberton" title="John C. Pemberton">John C. Pemberton</a> repulsed Sherman's direct approach ascending the bluffs to Vicksburg at <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Chickasaw_Bayou" title="Battle of Chickasaw Bayou">Chickasaw Bayou</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012223,_225White2016250_164-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012223,_225White2016250-164">&#91;158&#93;</a></sup> McClernand reached Sherman's army, assumed command, and independently of Grant led a campaign that captured Confederate <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Arkansas_Post" class="mw-redirect" title="Battle of Arkansas Post">Fort Hindman</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBonekemper2012147–48_165-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper2012147–48-165">&#91;159&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Contraband fugitive <a href="/wiki/African-American" class="mw-redirect" title="African-American">African-American</a> slaves poured into Grant's district, whom he sent north to Cairo to be integrated into white society as domestic servants in Chicago. However, Lincoln ended this move when Illinois political leaders complained.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller2019206–07_166-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller2019206–07-166">&#91;160&#93;</a></sup> On his own initiative, Grant set up a pragmatic program and hired a young Presbyterian Chaplain <a href="/wiki/John_Eaton_(general)" class="mw-redirect" title="John Eaton (general)">John Eaton</a> to administer slave refuge work camps.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller2019206–09_167-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller2019206–09-167">&#91;161&#93;</a></sup> Compensated contraband freed slaves would be used to pick cotton that would be shipped north and sent to aid the Union war effort. Lincoln approved and Grant's camp program was successful.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller2019209–10_168-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller2019209–10-168">&#91;162&#93;</a></sup> Grant also worked freed black labor on a canal to bypass Vicksburg and on other points on the river, incorporating the laborers into the Union Army and Navy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016Miller2019154–55_169-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016Miller2019154–55-169">&#91;163&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant's war responsibilities included combating an illegal Northern cotton trade and civilian obstruction.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001225White2016235–36_170-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001225White2016235–36-170">&#91;164&#93;</a></sup> Smuggling of cotton was rampant, while the price of cotton skyrocketed.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017232_171-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017232-171">&#91;165&#93;</a></sup> Grant believed the smuggling funded the Confederacy and provided them with military intelligence, while Union soldiers were dying in the fields.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFlood2005143–44,_151Sarna2012a37White2016235–36_172-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFlood2005143–44,_151Sarna2012a37White2016235–36-172">&#91;166&#93;</a></sup> He had received numerous dispatches with complaints about Jewish speculators in his district.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller2019259_173-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller2019259-173">&#91;167&#93;</a></sup> He also feared the trading corrupted many of his officers who were also eager to make a profit on a bale of cotton, while the majority of those involved in illegal trading were not Jewish.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017232–33Howland1868123–24_174-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017232–33Howland1868123–24-174">&#91;168&#93;</a></sup> To combat this, Grant required two permits, one from the Treasury and one from the Union Army, to purchase cotton.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017232_171-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017232-171">&#91;165&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Battle_of_Jackson_(cropped).tif" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Battle_of_Jackson_%28cropped%29.tif/lossy-page1-260px-Battle_of_Jackson_%28cropped%29.tif.jpg" decoding="async" width="260" height="164" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Battle_of_Jackson_%28cropped%29.tif/lossy-page1-390px-Battle_of_Jackson_%28cropped%29.tif.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Battle_of_Jackson_%28cropped%29.tif/lossy-page1-520px-Battle_of_Jackson_%28cropped%29.tif.jpg 2x" data-file-width="7070" data-file-height="4466" /></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Jackson,_Mississippi" title="Battle of Jackson, Mississippi">Battle of Jackson</a>, fought on May 14, 1863, was part of the <a href="/wiki/Vicksburg_Campaign" class="mw-redirect" title="Vicksburg Campaign">Vicksburg Campaign</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p>On December 17, 1862, Grant issued a controversial <a href="/wiki/General_Order_No._11_(1862)" title="General Order No. 11 (1862)">General Order No. 11</a>, expelling "Jews, as a class", from his Union Army military district.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012218Shevitz2005256_175-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012218Shevitz2005256-175">&#91;169&#93;</a></sup> The order was fully enforced at Holly Springs (December 17) and Paducah (December 28). Confederate General Van Dorn's raid on Holly Springs (December 20), prevented many Jewish people from potential expulsion. After complaints, Lincoln rescinded the order on January 3, 1863. Grant finally stopped the order within three weeks on January 17. He would later describe issuing the order as one of his biggest regrets.<sup id="cite_ref-179" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-179">&#91;g&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001226–27_180-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001226–27-180">&#91;173&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On January 29, 1863, Grant assumed overall command. Eventually, he attempted to advance his army through water-logged terrain to bypass Vicksburg's guns.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBonekemper2012148–49_181-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper2012148–49-181">&#91;174&#93;</a></sup> The plan of attacking Vicksburg from downriver carried great risk because upon crossing the Mississippi River, his army would be beyond the reach of most of its supply lines.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016269_182-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016269-182">&#91;175&#93;</a></sup> On April 16, Grant ordered Admiral <a href="/wiki/David_Dixon_Porter" title="David Dixon Porter">David Dixon Porter</a>'s gunboats south under fire from the Vicksburg batteries to meet up with troops who had marched south down the west side of the river.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012226–28_183-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012226–28-183">&#91;176&#93;</a></sup> Grant ordered diversionary battles, confusing Pemberton and allowing Grant's army to move east across the Mississippi, landing troops at <a href="/wiki/Bruinsburg,_Mississippi" title="Bruinsburg, Mississippi">Bruinsburg</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFlood2005160_184-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFlood2005160-184">&#91;177&#93;</a></sup> Grant's army <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Jackson,_Mississippi" title="Battle of Jackson, Mississippi">captured Jackson</a>, the state capital. Advancing west, he defeated Pemberton's army at the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Champion_Hill" title="Battle of Champion Hill">Battle of Champion Hill</a> on May 16, forcing their retreat into Vicksburg.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFlood2005164–65_185-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFlood2005164–65-185">&#91;178&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After Grant's men assaulted the entrenchments twice, suffering severe losses, they settled in for <a href="/wiki/Siege_of_Vicksburg" title="Siege of Vicksburg">a siege which lasted seven weeks</a>. During quiet periods of the campaign, Grant would take to drinking on occasion.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001231_186-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001231-186">&#91;179&#93;</a></sup> The personal rivalry between McClernand and Grant continued until Grant removed him from command when he contravened Grant by publishing an order without permission.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981136_187-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981136-187">&#91;180&#93;</a></sup> Pemberton surrendered Vicksburg to Grant on July 4, 1863.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981122–38Smith2001206–57_188-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981122–38Smith2001206–57-188">&#91;181&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Vicksburg's fall gave Union forces control of the Mississippi River and split the Confederacy. By that time, Grant's political sympathies fully coincided with the <a href="/wiki/Radical_Republicans" title="Radical Republicans">Radical Republicans</a>' aggressive prosecution of the war and emancipation of the slaves.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECatton19688_189-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatton19688-189">&#91;182&#93;</a></sup> The success at Vicksburg was a morale boost for the Union war effort.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981136_187-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981136-187">&#91;180&#93;</a></sup> When Stanton suggested Grant be brought east to run the <a href="/wiki/Army_of_the_Potomac" title="Army of the Potomac">Army of the Potomac</a>, Grant demurred, writing that he knew the geography and resources of the West better and he did not want to upset the chain of command in the East.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECatton19687_190-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatton19687-190">&#91;183&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Chattanooga_.281863.29_and_promotion"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Chattanooga_(1863)_and_promotion">Chattanooga (1863) and promotion</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Chattanooga_Campaign" class="mw-redirect" title="Chattanooga Campaign">Chattanooga Campaign</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Battle_of_Missionary_Ridge_McCormick_Harvesting.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Battle_of_Missionary_Ridge_McCormick_Harvesting.jpg/290px-Battle_of_Missionary_Ridge_McCormick_Harvesting.jpg" decoding="async" width="290" height="205" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Battle_of_Missionary_Ridge_McCormick_Harvesting.jpg/435px-Battle_of_Missionary_Ridge_McCormick_Harvesting.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Battle_of_Missionary_Ridge_McCormick_Harvesting.jpg/580px-Battle_of_Missionary_Ridge_McCormick_Harvesting.jpg 2x" data-file-width="10131" data-file-height="7160" /></a><figcaption>Union troops swarm <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Missionary_Ridge" title="Battle of Missionary Ridge">Missionary Ridge</a> and defeat Bragg's army.</figcaption></figure>
<p>On October 16, 1863, Lincoln promoted Grant to major general in the regular army and assigned him command of the newly formed <a href="/wiki/Military_Division_of_the_Mississippi" title="Military Division of the Mississippi">Division of the Mississippi</a> which comprised the Armies of the <a href="/wiki/Army_of_the_Ohio" title="Army of the Ohio">Ohio</a>, the Tennessee, and the <a href="/wiki/Army_of_the_Cumberland" title="Army of the Cumberland">Cumberland</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012265Cullum1891172White2016295_191-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012265Cullum1891172White2016295-191">&#91;184&#93;</a></sup> After the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Chickamauga" title="Battle of Chickamauga">Battle of Chickamauga</a>, the Army of the Cumberland retreated into Chattanooga where they were partially besieged.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFlood2005196_192-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFlood2005196-192">&#91;185&#93;</a></sup> Grant arrived in Chattanooga on horseback, after a journey by boat from Vicksburg to Cairo, and then by train to Bridgeport, Alabama. Plans to resupply the city and break the partial siege had already been set on foot before his arrival. Forces commanded by Major General <a href="/wiki/Joseph_Hooker" title="Joseph Hooker">Joseph Hooker</a>, which had been sent from the Army of the Potomac, approached from the west and linked up with other units moving east from inside the city, capturing Brown's Ferry and opening a supply line to the railroad at Bridgeport.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981145–47Smith2001267–68Brands2012267–68_193-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981145–47Smith2001267–68Brands2012267–68-193">&#91;186&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant planned to have Sherman's Army of the Tennessee, assisted by the Army of the Cumberland, assault the northern end of <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Missionary_Ridge" title="Battle of Missionary Ridge">Missionary Ridge</a>, preparatory to rolling down it on the enemy's right flank. On November 23, Major General <a href="/wiki/George_Henry_Thomas" title="George Henry Thomas">George Henry Thomas</a> surprised the enemy in open daylight, advancing the Union lines and taking Orchard Knob, between Chattanooga and the ridge. The next day, Sherman failed to achieve his mission of getting atop Missionary Ridge, which was the key to Grant's plan of battle. Hooker's forces took <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Lookout_Mountain" title="Battle of Lookout Mountain">Lookout Mountain</a> using an ingenious maneuver to flank the enemy, in unexpected success.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFlood2005214–15_194-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFlood2005214–15-194">&#91;187&#93;</a></sup> On the 25th, Grant ordered Major General <a href="/wiki/George_Henry_Thomas" title="George Henry Thomas">George Henry Thomas</a> to advance to the rifle-pits at the case of Missionary in an effort to help Sherman, after Sherman's army failed to take Missionary Ridge from the northeast.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFlood2005216_195-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFlood2005216-195">&#91;188&#93;</a></sup> Four divisions of the Army of the Cumberland, with the center two led by Major General <a href="/wiki/Philip_Sheridan" title="Philip Sheridan">Philip Sheridan</a> and Brigadier General <a href="/wiki/Thomas_J._Wood" title="Thomas J. Wood">Thomas J. Wood</a>, chased the Confederates out of the rifle-pits at the base and, against orders, continued the charge up the 45-degree slope and captured the Confederate entrenchments along the crest, forcing a hurried retreat.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFlood2005217–18_196-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFlood2005217–18-196">&#91;189&#93;</a></sup> The decisive battle gave the Union control of Tennessee and opened <a href="/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state)" title="Georgia (U.S. state)">Georgia</a>, the Confederate heartland, to Union invasion.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981148–50_197-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981148–50-197">&#91;190&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On March 2, 1864, Lincoln promoted Grant to lieutenant general, giving him command of all Union Armies.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFlood2005232McFeely1981148Cullum1891172_198-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFlood2005232McFeely1981148Cullum1891172-198">&#91;191&#93;</a></sup> Grant's new rank had only previously been held by <a href="/wiki/George_Washington" title="George Washington">George Washington</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016313,_319_199-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016313,_319-199">&#91;192&#93;</a></sup> He arrived in Washington on March 8, and was formally commissioned by Lincoln the next day at a Cabinet meeting.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017339,_342_200-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017339,_342-200">&#91;193&#93;</a></sup> Grant developed a good working relationship with Lincoln, who allowed Grant to devise his own strategy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017343–44,_352_201-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017343–44,_352-201">&#91;194&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant established his headquarters with General <a href="/wiki/George_Meade" title="George Meade">George Meade</a>'s Army of the Potomac in <a href="/wiki/Culpeper,_Virginia" title="Culpeper, Virginia">Culpeper</a>, north-west of Richmond, and met weekly with Lincoln and Stanton in Washington.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981156Chernow2017352_202-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981156Chernow2017352-202">&#91;195&#93;</a></sup> After protest from Halleck, Grant scrapped a risky invasion plan of North Carolina, and adopted a plan of five coordinated Union offensives on five fronts in order to prevent Confederate armies from shifting troops along interior lines.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWheelan201420Simon2002243Chernow2017356–57_203-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWheelan201420Simon2002243Chernow2017356–57-203">&#91;196&#93;</a></sup> Grant and Meade would make a direct frontal attack on <a href="/wiki/Robert_E._Lee" title="Robert E. Lee">Robert E. Lee</a>'s <a href="/wiki/Army_of_Northern_Virginia" title="Army of Northern Virginia">Army of Northern Virginia</a>, while Sherman — now in command of all western armies — was to destroy <a href="/wiki/Joseph_E._Johnston" title="Joseph E. Johnston">Joseph E. Johnston</a>'s <a href="/wiki/Army_of_Tennessee" title="Army of Tennessee">Army of Tennessee</a> and take Atlanta.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECatton2005190,_193Wheelan201420Chernow2017348,_356–57_204-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatton2005190,_193Wheelan201420Chernow2017348,_356–57-204">&#91;197&#93;</a></sup> Major General <a href="/wiki/Benjamin_Butler_(politician)" class="mw-redirect" title="Benjamin Butler (politician)">Benjamin Butler</a> would advance on Lee from the southeast, up the <a href="/wiki/James_River" title="James River">James River</a>, while Major General <a href="/wiki/Nathaniel_Banks" class="mw-redirect" title="Nathaniel Banks">Nathaniel Banks</a> would capture <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Mobile_Bay" title="Battle of Mobile Bay">Mobile</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981157Wheelan201420Chernow2017356–57_205-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981157Wheelan201420Chernow2017356–57-205">&#91;198&#93;</a></sup> Major General <a href="/wiki/Franz_Sigel" title="Franz Sigel">Franz Sigel</a> was to capture granaries and rail lines in the fertile <a href="/wiki/Shenandoah_Valley" title="Shenandoah Valley">Shenandoah Valley</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981157–75Smith2001313–39,_343–68Wheelan201420Chernow2017356–57_206-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981157–75Smith2001313–39,_343–68Wheelan201420Chernow2017356–57-206">&#91;199&#93;</a></sup> Grant was now commanded in total 533,000 battle-ready troops spread out over an eighteen-mile front.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017355_207-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017355-207">&#91;200&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Overland_Campaign_.281864.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Overland_Campaign_(1864)">Overland Campaign (1864)</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Overland_Campaign" title="Overland Campaign">Overland Campaign</a></div>
<p>The Overland Campaign was a series of brutal battles fought in Virginia for seven weeks during May and June 1864.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017378_208-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017378-208">&#91;201&#93;</a></sup> Sigel's and Butler's efforts failed, and Grant was left alone to fight Lee.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017396–97_209-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017396–97-209">&#91;202&#93;</a></sup> On the morning of Wednesday, May 4, Grant led the army out from his headquarters and towards Germanna Ford.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001303,_314Chernow2017376–77_210-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001303,_314Chernow2017376–77-210">&#91;203&#93;</a></sup> They crossed the <a href="/wiki/Rapidan_River" title="Rapidan River">Rapidan</a> unopposed, while supplies were transported on four pontoon bridges.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001314Chernow2017376–77_211-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001314Chernow2017376–77-211">&#91;204&#93;</a></sup> On May 5, the Union army attacked Lee in the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_the_Wilderness" title="Battle of the Wilderness">battle of the Wilderness</a>, a three-day battle with estimated casualties of 17,666 Union and 11,125 Confederate.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017378–79,_384Bonekemper2012463_212-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017378–79,_384Bonekemper2012463-212">&#91;205&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Rather than retreat, Grant flanked Lee's army to the southeast and attempted to wedge his forces between Lee and Richmond at <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Spotsylvania_Court_House" title="Battle of Spotsylvania Court House">Spotsylvania Court House</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981165_213-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981165-213">&#91;206&#93;</a></sup> Lee's army got to Spotsylvania first and a costly battle ensued, lasting thirteen days, with heavy casualties.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017385–87,_394–95Bonekemper2012463_214-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017385–87,_394–95Bonekemper2012463-214">&#91;207&#93;</a></sup> On May 12, Grant attempted to break through Lee's <i>Muleshoe</i> salient guarded by Confederate artillery, resulting in one of the bloodiest assaults of the Civil War, known as <a href="/wiki/The_Bloody_Angle_(Spotsylvania)" class="mw-redirect" title="The Bloody Angle (Spotsylvania)">the Bloody Angle</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017389,_392–95_215-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017389,_392–95-215">&#91;208&#93;</a></sup> Unable to break Lee's lines, Grant again flanked the rebels to the southeast, meeting at <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_North_Anna" title="Battle of North Anna">North Anna</a>, where a battle lasted three days.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981169_216-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981169-216">&#91;209&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Cold_Harbor">Cold Harbor</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Cold_Harbor" title="Battle of Cold Harbor">Battle of Cold Harbor</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Mathew_B._Brady_-_Ulysses_S._Grant_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Mathew_B._Brady_-_Ulysses_S._Grant_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg/200px-Mathew_B._Brady_-_Ulysses_S._Grant_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg" decoding="async" width="200" height="192" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Mathew_B._Brady_-_Ulysses_S._Grant_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg/300px-Mathew_B._Brady_-_Ulysses_S._Grant_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Mathew_B._Brady_-_Ulysses_S._Grant_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg/400px-Mathew_B._Brady_-_Ulysses_S._Grant_-_Google_Art_Project.jpg 2x" data-file-width="4941" data-file-height="4743" /></a><figcaption>General Grant at his headquarters in <a href="/wiki/Cold_Harbor,_Virginia" title="Cold Harbor, Virginia">Cold Harbor, Virginia</a>, June 1864</figcaption></figure>
<p>Grant believed breaking through Lee's lines at its weakest point, <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Cold_Harbor" title="Battle of Cold Harbor">Cold Harbor</a>, a vital road hub that linked to Richmond, would mean the destruction of Lee's army, the capture of Richmond, and a quick end to the rebellion.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981170–71Furgurson2007235Chernow2017403_217-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981170–71Furgurson2007235Chernow2017403-217">&#91;210&#93;</a></sup> Grant already had two corps in position at Cold Harbor with Hancock's corps on the way.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017403_218-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017403-218">&#91;211&#93;</a></sup> The recent bloody Wilderness campaign had severely diminished Confederate morale and hence Grant was now willing to advance on Lee's army once again.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017403–04Bonekemper2011_219-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017403–04Bonekemper2011-219">&#91;212&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Lee's lines were extended north and east of Richmond and Petersburg for approximately ten miles, but there were several points where there were no fortifications built yet, and Cold Harbor was one of them. On June 1 and 2 both Grant and Lee were still waiting for reinforcements to arrive. Hancock's men had marched all night and arrived too exhausted for an immediate attack that morning. Grant agreed to let the men rest and postponed the attack until 5 p.m., and then again until 4:30&#160;a.m. on June 3. However, Grant and Meade did not give specific orders for the attack, leaving it up to the corps commanders to decide where they would coordinate and attack the Confederate lines, as no senior commander had yet reconnoitered the latest Confederate developments. Grant had not yet learned that overnight Lee had hastily constructed entrenchments to thwart any breach attempt at Cold Harbor.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFurgurson2007120–21_220-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFurgurson2007120–21-220">&#91;213&#93;</a></sup> Grant had put off making an attack twice and was anxious to make his move before the rest of Lee's army arrived. On the morning of June 3, the third day of the thirteen-day battle, with a force of more than 100,000 men, against Lee's 59,000, Grant attacked not realizing that Lee's army was now well entrenched, much of it obscured by trees and bushes.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017403–04_221-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017403–04-221">&#91;214&#93;</a></sup> Grant's army suffered 12,000–14,000 casualties, while Lee's army suffered 3,000–5,000 casualties, but Lee was less able to replace them.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBonekemper201141–42_222-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper201141–42-222">&#91;215&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The unprecedented number of casualties was shocking by all accounts and heightened anti-war sentiment in the North. After the battle Grant wanted to appeal to Lee under the white flag for each side to gather up their wounded, most of them Union soldiers, but Lee insisted that a total truce be enacted and while they were deliberating all but a few of the wounded died in the field.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017406–07_223-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017406–07-223">&#91;216&#93;</a></sup> Without giving an apology for the disastrous defeat in his official military report, Grant confided in his staff after the battle and years later wrote in his memoirs that he "regretted that the last assault at Cold Harbor was ever made."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBonekemper2010182Chernow2017407_224-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper2010182Chernow2017407-224">&#91;217&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Siege_of_Petersburg_.281864.E2.80.931865.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Siege_of_Petersburg_(1864–1865)">Siege of Petersburg (1864–1865)</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Siege_of_Petersburg" title="Siege of Petersburg">Siege of Petersburg</a> and <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_the_Crater" title="Battle of the Crater">Battle of the Crater</a></div>
<p>Undetected by Lee, Grant moved his army south of the James River, freed Butler from <a href="/wiki/Bermuda_Hundred_Campaign" class="mw-redirect" title="Bermuda Hundred Campaign">the Bermuda Hundred</a>, and advanced toward <a href="/wiki/Petersburg,_Virginia" title="Petersburg, Virginia">Petersburg</a>, Virginia's central railroad hub.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981157–75Smith2001313–39,_343–68_225-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981157–75Smith2001313–39,_343–68-225">&#91;218&#93;</a></sup> Beauregard defended Petersburg, and Lee's veteran reinforcements arrived on June 18, resulting in <a href="/wiki/Siege_of_Petersburg" title="Siege of Petersburg">a nine-month siege</a>. Northern resentment grew. Sheridan was assigned command of the <a href="/wiki/Union_Army_of_the_Shenandoah" class="mw-redirect" title="Union Army of the Shenandoah">Union Army of the Shenandoah</a> and Grant directed him to "follow the enemy to their death" in the Shenandoah Valley. When Sheridan suffered attacks by <a href="/wiki/John_S._Mosby" title="John S. Mosby">John S. Mosby</a>'s irregular Confederate cavalry, Grant recommended rounding up their families for imprisonment at <a href="/wiki/Fort_McHenry" title="Fort McHenry">Fort McHenry</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981178–86_226-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981178–86-226">&#91;219&#93;</a></sup> After Grant's abortive attempt to capture Petersburg, Lincoln supported Grant in his decision to continue and visited Grant's headquarters at City Point on June 21 to assess the state of the army and meet with Grant and Admiral Porter. By the time Lincoln departed his appreciation for Grant had grown.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017414White2016369–70_227-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017414White2016369–70-227">&#91;220&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>To strike at Lee in a timely capacity Grant was forced to use what resources were immediately available, and they were diminishing by the day. Grant had to commit troops to check Confederate General <a href="/wiki/Jubal_Early" title="Jubal Early">Jubal Early</a>'s raids in the Shenandoah Valley and who was getting dangerously close to Washington.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECatton1968309_228-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatton1968309-228">&#91;221&#93;</a></sup> By late July, at Petersburg, Grant reluctantly approved a plan to <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_the_Crater" title="Battle of the Crater">blow up</a> part of the enemy trenches from a tunnel filled with many tons of gunpowder. The massive explosion created a crater, 170 feet across and 30 feet deep, killing an entire Confederate regiment in an instant.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017429_229-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017429-229">&#91;222&#93;</a></sup> The poorly led Union troops under Major General <a href="/wiki/Ambrose_Burnside" title="Ambrose Burnside">Ambrose Burnside</a> and Brigadier General <a href="/wiki/James_H._Ledlie" title="James H. Ledlie">James H. Ledlie</a>, rather than encircling the crater, rushed forward and poured directly into it. Recovering from the surprise, Confederates, led by Major General <a href="/wiki/William_Mahone" title="William Mahone">William Mahone</a>,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECatton1968324_230-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatton1968324-230">&#91;223&#93;</a></sup> surrounded the crater and easily picked off Union troops within it. The Union's 3,500 casualties outnumbered the Confederates' by three-to-one. The battle marked the first time that Union black troops, who endured a large proportion of the casualties, engaged in any major battle in the east.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017398_231-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017398-231">&#91;224&#93;</a></sup> Grant admitted that the overall mining tactic had been a "stupendous failure".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981179Smith2001369–95Catton1968308–09_232-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981179Smith2001369–95Catton1968308–09-232">&#91;225&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:The_Peacemakers_1868.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/The_Peacemakers_1868.jpg/240px-The_Peacemakers_1868.jpg" decoding="async" width="240" height="180" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/The_Peacemakers_1868.jpg/360px-The_Peacemakers_1868.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/The_Peacemakers_1868.jpg/480px-The_Peacemakers_1868.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3000" data-file-height="2254" /></a><figcaption>Grant (center left) next to Lincoln with General <a href="/wiki/William_Tecumseh_Sherman" title="William Tecumseh Sherman">Sherman</a> (far left) and Admiral <a href="/wiki/David_Dixon_Porter" title="David Dixon Porter">Porter</a> (right) – <i><a href="/wiki/The_Peacemakers" title="The Peacemakers">The Peacemakers</a></i> by <a href="/wiki/George_Peter_Alexander_Healy" title="George Peter Alexander Healy">George Peter Alexander Healy</a>, 1868</figcaption></figure>
<p>Grant would later meet with Lincoln and testify at a court of inquiry against Generals Burnside and Ledlie for their incompetence.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECatton1968325_233-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatton1968325-233">&#91;226&#93;</a></sup> In his memoirs, he blamed both of them for that disastrous Union defeat.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017430_234-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017430-234">&#91;227&#93;</a></sup> Rather than fight Lee in a full-frontal attack as he had done at Cold Harbor, Grant continued to force Lee to extend his defenses south and west of Petersburg, better allowing him to capture essential railroad links.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECatton1968309_228-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatton1968309-228">&#91;221&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Union forces soon captured <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Mobile_Bay" title="Battle of Mobile Bay">Mobile Bay</a> and <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Atlanta" title="Battle of Atlanta">Atlanta</a> and now controlled the Shenandoah Valley, ensuring Lincoln's reelection in November.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECatton2005223,_228Smith2001387_235-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatton2005223,_228Smith2001387-235">&#91;228&#93;</a></sup> Sherman convinced Grant and Lincoln to allow his army to <a href="/wiki/Sherman%27s_March_to_the_Sea" title="Sherman&#39;s March to the Sea">march on Savannah</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECatton2005235Smith2001388–89_236-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatton2005235Smith2001388–89-236">&#91;229&#93;</a></sup> Sherman cut a 60-mile path of destruction unopposed, reached the Atlantic Ocean, and captured Savannah on December 22.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001388–89_237-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001388–89-237">&#91;230&#93;</a></sup> On December 16, after much prodding by Grant, the Union Army under Thomas smashed <a href="/wiki/John_Bell_Hood" title="John Bell Hood">John Bell Hood</a>'s Confederate Army at <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Nashville" title="Battle of Nashville">Nashville</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001389–90_238-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001389–90-238">&#91;231&#93;</a></sup> These campaigns left Lee's forces at Petersburg as the only significant obstacle remaining to Union victory.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001390_239-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001390-239">&#91;232&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>By March 1865, Lee was trapped. Grant had severely weakened Lee's strength, having extended his lines to 35 miles.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBonekemper2012359_240-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper2012359-240">&#91;233&#93;</a></sup> He was running out of reserves to replace the high battlefield casualties and remaining Confederate troops, no longer having confidence in their commander and under the duress to trench warfare, deserted Lee by the thousands. <sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBonekemper2012353_241-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper2012353-241">&#91;234&#93;</a></sup> On March 25, in a desperate effort, Lee sacrificed his remaining troops (4,000 Confederate casualties) at <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Stedman" title="Battle of Fort Stedman">Fort Stedman</a>, a Union victory, and considered the last Petersburg line battle.
</p>
<h3><span id="Surrender_of_Lee_and_Union_victory_.281865.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Surrender_of_Lee_and_Union_victory_(1865)">Surrender of Lee and Union victory (1865)</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main articles: <a href="/wiki/Third_Battle_of_Petersburg" title="Third Battle of Petersburg">Third Battle of Petersburg</a>, <a href="/wiki/Appomattox_Campaign" class="mw-redirect" title="Appomattox Campaign">Appomattox Campaign</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Appomattox_Court_House" title="Battle of Appomattox Court House">Battle of Appomattox Court House</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:General_Robert_E._Lee_surrenders_at_Appomattox_Court_House_1865.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/General_Robert_E._Lee_surrenders_at_Appomattox_Court_House_1865.jpg/250px-General_Robert_E._Lee_surrenders_at_Appomattox_Court_House_1865.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="152" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/General_Robert_E._Lee_surrenders_at_Appomattox_Court_House_1865.jpg/375px-General_Robert_E._Lee_surrenders_at_Appomattox_Court_House_1865.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bc/General_Robert_E._Lee_surrenders_at_Appomattox_Court_House_1865.jpg/500px-General_Robert_E._Lee_surrenders_at_Appomattox_Court_House_1865.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1600" data-file-height="973" /></a><figcaption>Defeated by Grant, Lee surrendered at the Appomattox Court House.</figcaption></figure>
<p>On April 2, Grant ordered a general assault on Lee's entrenched depleted forces. Lee abandoned Petersburg and Richmond, while Grant's conquering Union troops easily took Petersburg and captured Richmond the next day.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBonekemper2012365–66_242-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper2012365–66-242">&#91;235&#93;</a></sup> A desperate Lee, and part of his army cut and ran, attempted to link up with the remnants of <a href="/wiki/Joseph_E._Johnston" title="Joseph E. Johnston">Joseph E. Johnston</a>'s defeated army. Sheridan's cavalry, however, stopped the two armies from converging, cutting them off from their supply trains.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016403–04_243-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016403–04-243">&#91;236&#93;</a></sup> Grant was in communication with Lee before he entrusted his aide <a href="/wiki/Orville_Babcock" class="mw-redirect" title="Orville Babcock">Orville Babcock</a> to carry his last dispatch to Lee that demanded his surrender with instructions to escort him to a meeting place of Lee's choosing.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001401–03_244-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001401–03-244">&#91;237&#93;</a></sup> Grant immediately rode west, bypassing Lee's army, to join Sheridan who had captured <a href="/wiki/Appomattox_Station" title="Appomattox Station">Appomattox Station</a>, blocking Lee's escape route. On his way, Grant received a letter sent by Lee informing him Lee would surrender his army.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017504Smith2001401–03_245-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017504Smith2001401–03-245">&#91;238&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On April 9, Grant and Lee met at <a href="/wiki/Appomattox_Court_House_National_Historical_Park" title="Appomattox Court House National Historical Park">Appomattox Court House</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016405_246-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016405-246">&#91;239&#93;</a></sup> Upon receiving Lee's dispatch about the proposed meeting Grant had been jubilant. Although Grant felt depressed at the fall of "a foe who had fought so long and valiantly," he believed the Southern cause was "one of the worst for which a people ever fought."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001_247-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001-247">&#91;240&#93;</a></sup> After briefly discussing their days of old in Mexico, Grant wrote out the terms of surrender. Men and officers were to be paroled, but in addition, there was amnesty: "Each officer and man will be allowed to return to his home, not to be disturbed by U.S. authority so long as they observe their paroles and the laws in force where they may reside." Lee immediately accepted Grant's terms and signed the surrender document, without any diplomatic recognition of the Confederacy. The vanquished Lee, afterward asked Grant that his former Confederate troops keep their horses. Grant generously allowed Lee's request.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016405–06_248-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016405–06-248">&#91;241&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGoethals201592Smith2001405_249-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoethals201592Smith2001405-249">&#91;242&#93;</a></sup> Grant ordered his troops to stop all celebration, saying the "war is over; the rebels are our countrymen again."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016407_250-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016407-250">&#91;243&#93;</a></sup> Johnston's Tennessee army surrendered on April 26, 1865, <a href="/wiki/Richard_Taylor_(Confederate_general)" title="Richard Taylor (Confederate general)">Richard Taylor's</a> Alabama army on May 4, and <a href="/wiki/Edmund_Kirby_Smith" title="Edmund Kirby Smith">Kirby Smith's</a> Texas army on May 26, ending the war.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981212,_219–20Catton2005304Chernow2017510_251-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981212,_219–20Catton2005304Chernow2017510-251">&#91;244&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Lincoln.27s_assassination"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Lincoln's_assassination">Lincoln's assassination</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Assassination_of_Abraham_Lincoln" title="Assassination of Abraham Lincoln">Assassination of Abraham Lincoln</a></div>
<p>On April 14, 1865, five days after Grant's victory at Appomattox, he attended a cabinet meeting in Washington. Lincoln invited him and his wife Julia to <a href="/wiki/Ford%27s_Theatre" title="Ford&#39;s Theatre">Ford's Theatre</a> but they declined, because they had plans to travel to their home in <a href="/wiki/Burlington,_New_Jersey" title="Burlington, New Jersey">Burlington</a>. In a conspiracy that also targeted top cabinet members in one last effort to topple the Union, Lincoln was fatally shot by <a href="/wiki/John_Wilkes_Booth" title="John Wilkes Booth">John Wilkes Booth</a> at the theater and died the next morning.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981224White2016412_252-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981224White2016412-252">&#91;245&#93;</a></sup> Many, including Grant himself, thought that he, Grant, had been a target in the plot, and during the subsequent trial, the government tried to prove that Grant had been stalked by Booth's conspirator <a href="/wiki/Michael_O%27Laughlen" title="Michael O&#39;Laughlen">Michael O'Laughlen</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012375–76_253-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012375–76-253">&#91;246&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Stanton notified Grant of the president's death and summoned him back to Washington. Vice President <a href="/wiki/Andrew_Johnson" title="Andrew Johnson">Andrew Johnson</a> was <a href="/wiki/Inauguration_of_Andrew_Johnson" title="Inauguration of Andrew Johnson">sworn in</a> as president on April 15. Attending Lincoln's funeral on April 19, Grant stood alone and wept openly; he later said Lincoln was "the greatest man I have ever known".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001409–12_254-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001409–12-254">&#91;247&#93;</a></sup> Grant was determined to work with Johnson, and he privately expressed "every reason to hope" in the new president's ability to run the government "in its old channel".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981227–29White2016414_255-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981227–29White2016414-255">&#91;248&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Commanding_General">Commanding General</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant_as_commanding_general,_1865%E2%80%931869" title="Ulysses S. Grant as commanding general, 1865–1869">Ulysses S. Grant as commanding general, 1865–1869</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ulysses_S_Grant-Constant_Mayer.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Ulysses_S_Grant-Constant_Mayer.jpg/220px-Ulysses_S_Grant-Constant_Mayer.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="278" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Ulysses_S_Grant-Constant_Mayer.jpg/330px-Ulysses_S_Grant-Constant_Mayer.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a4/Ulysses_S_Grant-Constant_Mayer.jpg/440px-Ulysses_S_Grant-Constant_Mayer.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1301" data-file-height="1645" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Constant_Mayer" title="Constant Mayer">Constant Mayer</a>'s portrait of General Grant, 1866</figcaption></figure>
<p>At the war's end, Grant remained commander of the army, with duties that included dealing with <a href="/wiki/Maximilian_I_of_Mexico" title="Maximilian I of Mexico">Emperor Maximilian</a> and French troops in Mexico, enforcement of Reconstruction in the former Confederate states, and supervision of Indian wars on the western Plains.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012410–11Chernow2017556–57_256-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012410–11Chernow2017556–57-256">&#91;249&#93;</a></sup> After the <a href="/wiki/Grand_Review_of_the_Armies" title="Grand Review of the Armies">Grand Review of the Armies</a>, Lee and his generals were indicted for treason in Virginia. Johnson demanded they be put on trial, but Grant insisted that they should not be tried, citing his Appomatox amnesty. Johnson backed down, so charges against Lee were dropped.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016418_257-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016418-257">&#91;250&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001417–18_258-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001417–18-258">&#91;251&#93;</a></sup> Grant secured a house for his family in Georgetown Heights in 1865 but instructed Elihu Washburne that for political purposes his legal residence remained in Galena, Illinois.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981232–33_259-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981232–33-259">&#91;252&#93;</a></sup> That same year, Grant spoke at <a href="/wiki/Cooper_Union" title="Cooper Union">Cooper Union</a> in New York in support of Johnson's presidency. Further travels that summer took the Grants to <a href="/wiki/Albany,_New_York" title="Albany, New York">Albany, New York</a>, back to Galena, and throughout Illinois and Ohio, with enthusiastic receptions.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981233–34_260-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981233–34-260">&#91;253&#93;</a></sup> On July 25, 1866, Congress promoted Grant to the newly created rank of <a href="/wiki/General_of_the_Army_of_the_United_States" class="mw-redirect" title="General of the Army of the United States">General of the Army of the United States</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001434n_261-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001434n-261">&#91;254&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Tour_of_the_South">Tour of the South</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Reconstruction_era" title="Reconstruction era">Reconstruction era</a></div>
<p>President Johnson's Reconstruction policy included a speedy return of the former Confederates to Congress, reinstating white people to office in the South, and relegating black people to second-class citizenship.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun201710_262-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun201710-262">&#91;255&#93;</a></sup> On November 27, 1865, General Grant left Washington, sent by Johnson on a fact-finding mission to the South, to counter a pending less favorable report by Senator <a href="/wiki/Carl_Schurz" title="Carl Schurz">Carl Schurz</a> which reported that white people in the South harbored resentment of the North, and that black people suffered from violence and fraud.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimpson1988433–34_263-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimpson1988433–34-263">&#91;256&#93;</a></sup> Grant recommended continuation of the <a href="/wiki/Freedmen%27s_Bureau" title="Freedmen&#39;s Bureau">Freedmen's Bureau</a>, which Johnson opposed, but advised against using black troops, which he believed encouraged an alternative to farm labor.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001420McFeely1981238–41_264-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001420McFeely1981238–41-264">&#91;257&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant did not believe the people of the South were ready for self-rule, and that both white and black people in the South required protection by the federal government. Concerned that the war led to diminished respect for civil authorities, he continued using the Army to maintain order.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012390_265-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012390-265">&#91;258&#93;</a></sup> Grant's report on the South, which he later recanted, sympathized with Johnson's conservative Reconstruction policies.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017565–66_266-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017565–66-266">&#91;259&#93;</a></sup> Although Grant desired former Confederates be returned to Congress, he advocated eventual black citizenship. On December 19, the day after the passage of the Thirteenth Amendment was announced in the Senate, Johnson's response used Grant's report, read aloud to the Senate, to undermine Schurz's final report and Radical opposition to Johnson's policies.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981240–41Smith2001420–21Chernow2017565–66Simpson1988439_267-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981240–41Smith2001420–21Chernow2017565–66Simpson1988439-267">&#91;260&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Break_from_Johnson">Break from Johnson</span></h3>
<p>Grant was initially optimistic about Johnson, saying he was satisfied the nation had "nothing to fear" from the Johnson administration.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017533–34_268-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017533–34-268">&#91;261&#93;</a></sup> Despite differing styles, the two got along cordially and Grant attended cabinet meetings concerning Reconstruction.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017533–34_268-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017533–34-268">&#91;261&#93;</a></sup> By February 1866, the relationship began to break down.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017569_269-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017569-269">&#91;262&#93;</a></sup> Johnson opposed Grant's closure of the <i><a href="/wiki/Richmond_Examiner" title="Richmond Examiner">Richmond Examiner</a></i> for disloyal editorials and his enforcement of the <a href="/wiki/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1866" title="Civil Rights Act of 1866">Civil Rights Act of 1866</a>, passed over Johnson's veto.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017569_269-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017569-269">&#91;262&#93;</a></sup> Needing Grant's popularity, Johnson took Grant on his "<a href="/wiki/Swing_Around_the_Circle" title="Swing Around the Circle">Swing Around the Circle</a>" tour, a failed attempt to gain national support for lenient policies toward the South.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012396Simon2002244_270-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012396Simon2002244-270">&#91;263&#93;</a></sup> Grant privately called Johnson's speeches a "national disgrace" and he left the tour early.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012397–98_271-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012397–98-271">&#91;264&#93;</a></sup> On March 2, 1867, overriding Johnson's veto, Congress passed the first of three <a href="/wiki/Reconstruction_Acts" title="Reconstruction Acts">Reconstruction Acts</a>, using military officers to enforce the policy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001432–33Simon2002244_272-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001432–33Simon2002244-272">&#91;265&#93;</a></sup> Protecting Grant, Congress passed the Command of the Army Act, preventing his removal or relocation, and forcing Johnson to pass orders through Grant.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001438Simon2002244_273-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001438Simon2002244-273">&#91;266&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In August 1867, bypassing the <a href="/wiki/Tenure_of_Office_Act_(1867)" title="Tenure of Office Act (1867)">Tenure of Office Act</a>, Johnson discharged Secretary of War <a href="/wiki/Edwin_Stanton" title="Edwin Stanton">Edwin Stanton</a> without Senate approval and appointed Grant <i>ad interim</i> Secretary of War. Stanton was the only remaining cabinet member friendly to the Radicals. Although Grant initially recommended against dismissing Stanton, he accepted the position, not wanting the Army to fall under a conservative appointee who would impede Reconstruction, and managed an uneasy partnership with Johnson.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002244Chernow2017594–95_274-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002244Chernow2017594–95-274">&#91;267&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In December 1867, Congress voted to keep Stanton, who was reinstated by a Senate Committee on January 10, 1868. Grant told Johnson he was going to resign the office to avoid fines and imprisonment. Johnson, who believed the law would be overturned, said he would assume Grant's legal responsibility, and reminded Grant that he had promised him to delay his resignation until a suitable replacement was found.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016453_275-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016453-275">&#91;268&#93;</a></sup> The following Monday, not willing to wait for the law to be overturned, Grant surrendered the office to Stanton, causing confusion with Johnson.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017603_276-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017603-276">&#91;269&#93;</a></sup> With the complete backing of his cabinet, Johnson personally accused Grant of lying and "duplicity" at a stormy cabinet meeting, while a shocked and disappointed Grant felt it was Johnson who was lying.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun201735–36_277-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun201735–36-277">&#91;270&#93;</a></sup> The publication of angry messages between Grant and Johnson led to a complete break between them.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016454–55Simon2002244_278-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016454–55Simon2002244-278">&#91;271&#93;</a></sup> The controversy led to Johnson's <a href="/wiki/Impeachment_of_Andrew_Johnson" title="Impeachment of Andrew Johnson">impeachment</a> and trial in the Senate; he was acquitted by one vote.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002244Chernow2017611_279-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002244Chernow2017611-279">&#91;272&#93;</a></sup> Grant's popularity rose among the Radical Republicans and his nomination for the presidency appeared certain.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016458–59Simon2002244_280-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016458–59Simon2002244-280">&#91;273&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Election_of_1868">Election of 1868</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/1868_United_States_presidential_election" title="1868 United States presidential election">1868 United States presidential election</a></div>
<figure class="mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Grant-Colfax.png" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Grant-Colfax.png/240px-Grant-Colfax.png" decoding="async" width="240" height="169" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Grant-Colfax.png/360px-Grant-Colfax.png 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Grant-Colfax.png/480px-Grant-Colfax.png 2x" data-file-width="1200" data-file-height="845" /></a><figcaption>Grant–Colfax Republican ticket</figcaption></figure>
<p>When the Republican Party met at the <a href="/wiki/1868_Republican_National_Convention" title="1868 Republican National Convention">1868 Republican National Convention</a> in Chicago, the delegates unanimously nominated Grant for president and Speaker of the House <a href="/wiki/Schuyler_Colfax" title="Schuyler Colfax">Schuyler Colfax</a> for vice president.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002244_281-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002244-281">&#91;274&#93;</a></sup> Although Grant had preferred to remain in the army, he accepted the Republican nomination, believing that he was the only one who could unify the nation.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002244Chernow2017614_282-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002244Chernow2017614-282">&#91;275&#93;</a></sup> The Republicans advocated "equal civil and political rights to all" and <a href="/wiki/African_American" class="mw-redirect" title="African American">African American</a> enfranchisement.<sup id="cite_ref-283" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-283">&#91;276&#93;</a></sup> The Democrats, having abandoned Johnson, nominated former governor <a href="/wiki/Horatio_Seymour" title="Horatio Seymour">Horatio Seymour</a> of New York for president and <a href="/wiki/Francis_Preston_Blair_Jr." title="Francis Preston Blair Jr.">Francis P. Blair</a> of Missouri for vice president. The Democrats opposed suffrage for African Americans and advocated the immediate restoration of former Confederate states to the Union and amnesty from "all past political offenses".<sup id="cite_ref-284" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-284">&#91;277&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002244–45_285-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002244–45-285">&#91;278&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant played no overt role during the campaign and instead was joined by Sherman and Sheridan in a tour of the West that summer.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun201746_286-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun201746-286">&#91;279&#93;</a></sup> However, the Republicans adopted his words "Let us have peace" as their campaign slogan.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981264–67_287-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981264–67-287">&#91;280&#93;</a></sup> Grant's 1862 <a href="/wiki/General_Order_No._11_(1862)" title="General Order No. 11 (1862)">General Order No. 11</a> became an issue during the <a href="/wiki/1868_U.S._presidential_election" class="mw-redirect" title="1868 U.S. presidential election">presidential campaign</a>; he sought to distance himself from the order, saying "I have no prejudice against sect or race, but want each individual to be judged by his own merit."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001459–60_288-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001459–60-288">&#91;281&#93;</a></sup> The Democrats and their Klan supporters focused mainly on ending Reconstruction, intimidating black people and Republicans, and returning control of the South to the white Democrats and the planter class, alienating <a href="/wiki/War_Democrats" class="mw-redirect" title="War Democrats">War Democrats</a> in the North.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001468–69_289-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001468–69-289">&#91;282&#93;</a></sup> An example was the murder of Republican Congressman <a href="/wiki/James_M._Hinds" title="James M. Hinds">James M. Hinds</a> in Arkansas by a Klansman in October 1868, as Hinds campaigned for Grant. Grant won the popular vote by 300,000 votes out of 5,716,082 votes cast, receiving an <a href="/wiki/Electoral_College_(United_States)" class="mw-redirect" title="Electoral College (United States)">Electoral College</a> landslide of 214 votes to Seymour's 80.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001461_290-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001461-290">&#91;283&#93;</a></sup> Seymour received a majority of white voters, but Grant was aided by 500,000 votes cast by black people,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002245_291-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002245-291">&#91;284&#93;</a></sup> winning him 52.7 percent of the popular vote.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun201755_292-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun201755-292">&#91;285&#93;</a></sup> He lost Louisiana and Georgia, primarily due to <a href="/wiki/Ku_Klux_Klan" title="Ku Klux Klan">Ku Klux Klan</a> violence against African-American voters.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFoner2014243–44_293-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFoner2014243–44-293">&#91;286&#93;</a></sup> At the age of 46, Grant was the youngest president yet elected, and the first president after the nation had outlawed slavery.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981284Smith2001461White2016471_294-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981284Smith2001461White2016471-294">&#91;287&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span id="Presidency_.281869.E2.80.931877.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Presidency_(1869–1877)">Presidency (1869–1877)</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Presidency_of_Ulysses_S._Grant" title="Presidency of Ulysses S. Grant">Presidency of Ulysses S. Grant</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ugrant.jpeg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/Ugrant.jpeg/220px-Ugrant.jpeg" decoding="async" width="220" height="286" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/Ugrant.jpeg/330px-Ugrant.jpeg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/Ugrant.jpeg/440px-Ugrant.jpeg 2x" data-file-width="2306" data-file-height="3000" /></a><figcaption>Official White House portrait of President Grant by <a href="/wiki/Henry_Ulke" title="Henry Ulke">Henry Ulke</a>, 1875</figcaption></figure>
<p>On March 4, 1869, Grant was sworn in as the eighteenth President of the United States by Chief Justice <a href="/wiki/Salmon_P._Chase" title="Salmon P. Chase">Salmon P. Chase</a>. In his inaugural address, Grant urged the ratification of the <a href="/wiki/Fifteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Fifteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution">Fifteenth Amendment</a>, while large numbers of African Americans attended his inauguration.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016472_295-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016472-295">&#91;288&#93;</a></sup> He also urged that bonds issued during the Civil War should be paid in gold, called for "proper treatment" of <a href="/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States" title="Native Americans in the United States">Native Americans</a> and encouraged their "civilization and ultimate citizenship".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPatrick1968166McFeely1981305Simon2002246,_250_296-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatrick1968166McFeely1981305Simon2002246,_250-296">&#91;289&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant's <a href="/wiki/Template:Cabinet_of_President_Ulysses_S._Grant" title="Template:Cabinet of President Ulysses S. Grant">cabinet appointments</a> sparked both criticism and approval.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001465–66White2016475,_530Chernow2017635–36Simon2002246_297-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001465–66White2016475,_530Chernow2017635–36Simon2002246-297">&#91;290&#93;</a></sup> He appointed <a href="/wiki/Elihu_B._Washburne" title="Elihu B. Washburne">Elihu B. Washburne</a> Secretary of State and <a href="/wiki/John_A._Rawlins" class="mw-redirect" title="John A. Rawlins">John A. Rawlins</a> Secretary of War.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002246–47_298-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002246–47-298">&#91;291&#93;</a></sup> Washburne resigned, and Grant appointed him Minister to France. Grant then appointed former New York Senator <a href="/wiki/Hamilton_Fish" title="Hamilton Fish">Hamilton Fish</a> Secretary of State.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002246–47_298-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002246–47-298">&#91;291&#93;</a></sup> Rawlins died in office, and Grant appointed <a href="/wiki/William_W._Belknap" title="William W. Belknap">William W. Belknap</a> Secretary of War.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016507,_564Simon2002246–47_299-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016507,_564Simon2002246–47-299">&#91;292&#93;</a></sup> Grant appointed New York businessman <a href="/wiki/Alexander_T._Stewart" class="mw-redirect" title="Alexander T. Stewart">Alexander T. Stewart</a> Secretary of Treasury, but Stewart was found legally ineligible to hold office by a 1789 law.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan201846–47_300-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan201846–47-300">&#91;293&#93;</a></sup> Grant then appointed Massachusetts Representative <a href="/wiki/George_S._Boutwell" title="George S. Boutwell">George S. Boutwell</a> Secretary of Treasury.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002246–47_298-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002246–47-298">&#91;291&#93;</a></sup> Philadelphia businessman <a href="/wiki/Adolph_E._Borie" title="Adolph E. Borie">Adolph E. Borie</a> was appointed Secretary of Navy, but found the job stressful and resigned.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan201848_301-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan201848-301">&#91;294&#93;</a></sup> Grant then appointed New Jersey's attorney general, <a href="/wiki/George_M._Robeson" title="George M. Robeson">George M. Robeson</a>, Secretary of Navy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017628Simon2002246–47Kahan201848_302-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017628Simon2002246–47Kahan201848-302">&#91;295&#93;</a></sup> Former Ohio Governor <a href="/wiki/Jacob_D._Cox" class="mw-redirect" title="Jacob D. Cox">Jacob D. Cox</a> (Interior), former Maryland Senator <a href="/wiki/John_Creswell" title="John Creswell">John Creswell</a> (Postmaster-General), and <a href="/wiki/Ebenezer_Rockwood_Hoar" class="mw-redirect" title="Ebenezer Rockwood Hoar">Ebenezer Rockwood Hoar</a> (Attorney General) rounded out the cabinet.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001446,_469–70Kahan201847–48_303-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001446,_469–70Kahan201847–48-303">&#91;296&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant nominated Sherman to succeed him as general-in-chief and gave him control over war bureau chiefs.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016474–75_304-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016474–75-304">&#91;297&#93;</a></sup> When Rawlins took over the War Department he complained to Grant that Sherman was given too much authority. Grant reluctantly revoked his own order, upsetting Sherman and damaging their wartime friendship. <a href="/wiki/James_Longstreet" title="James Longstreet">James Longstreet</a>, a former Confederate general who had endorsed Grant's nomination, was nominated for the position of Surveyor of Customs of the port of New Orleans; this was met with general amazement, and seen as a genuine effort to unite the North and South.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001472White2016474–75_305-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001472White2016474–75-305">&#91;298&#93;</a></sup> In March 1872, Grant signed legislation that established <a href="/wiki/Yellowstone_National_Park" title="Yellowstone National Park">Yellowstone National Park</a>, the first national park.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017376_306-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017376-306">&#91;299&#93;</a></sup> Grant was sympathetic to women's rights; including support of female suffrage, saying he wanted "equal rights to all citizens".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017749–50Kahan2018xiiCalhoun2017384–85_307-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017749–50Kahan2018xiiCalhoun2017384–85-307">&#91;300&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>To make up for his infamous General Order No. 11, Grant appointed more than fifty Jewish people to federal office, including consuls, district attorneys, and deputy postmasters.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan201876Chernow2017643–44Sarna2012aix–xiv_308-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan201876Chernow2017643–44Sarna2012aix–xiv-308">&#91;301&#93;</a></sup> He appointed <a href="/wiki/Edward_S._Salomon" title="Edward S. Salomon">Edward S. Salomon</a> territorial governor of Washington, the first time an American Jewish man occupied a governor's seat. Grant was sympathetic to the plight of persecuted Jewish people. In November 1869, reports surfaced of the Russian <a href="/wiki/Tsar" title="Tsar">Tsar</a> <a href="/wiki/Alexander_II_of_Russia" title="Alexander II of Russia">Alexander II</a> penalizing 2,000 Jewish families for smuggling by expelling them to the interior of the country. In response, Grant publicly supported the Jewish American <i>B'nai B'rith</i> petition against the Tsar. In December 1869, Grant appointed a Jewish journalist as Consul to Romania, to protect Jewish people there from "severe oppression".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan201876Chernow2017643–44Sarna2012aix–xiv_308-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan201876Chernow2017643–44Sarna2012aix–xiv-308">&#91;301&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1875, Grant proposed a constitutional amendment that limited religious indoctrination in public schools.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017512_309-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017512-309">&#91;302&#93;</a></sup> Instruction of "religious, atheistic, or pagan tenets", would be banned, while funding "for the benefit or in aid, directly or indirectly, of any religious sect or denomination", would be prohibited. Schools would be for all children "irrespective of sex, color, birthplace, or religions".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017512–13Smith2001570_310-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017512–13Smith2001570-310">&#91;303&#93;</a></sup> Grant's views were incorporated into the <a href="/wiki/Blaine_Amendment" title="Blaine Amendment">Blaine Amendment</a>, but it was defeated by the Senate.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017513_311-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017513-311">&#91;304&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In October 1871, under the <a href="/wiki/Morrill_Anti-Bigamy_Act" title="Morrill Anti-Bigamy Act">Morrill Act</a>, using federal marshals, Grant rounded up and prosecuted hundreds of <a href="/wiki/Utah_Territory" title="Utah Territory">Utah Territory</a> <a href="/wiki/Mormon_polygamists" class="mw-redirect" title="Mormon polygamists">Mormon polygamists</a>, including Mormon leader <a href="/wiki/Brigham_Young" title="Brigham Young">Brigham Young</a>, who was indicted for "lewd and <a href="/wiki/Lascivious" class="mw-redirect" title="Lascivious">lascivious</a> cohabitation".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTE&#39;&#39;The_New_York_Times&#39;&#39;1871Ertman2010Kahan2018301_312-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTE&#39;&#39;The_New_York_Times&#39;&#39;1871Ertman2010Kahan2018301-312">&#91;305&#93;</a></sup> Grant had called polygamy a "crime against decency and morality".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan2018132_313-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan2018132-313">&#91;306&#93;</a></sup> In 1874, Grant signed into law the <a href="/wiki/Poland_Act" title="Poland Act">Poland Act</a>, which made Mormon polygamists subject to trial in U.S. District Courts and limited Mormons on juries.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan2018132_313-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan2018132-313">&#91;306&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Beginning in March 1873, under the <a href="/wiki/Comstock_Act" class="mw-redirect" title="Comstock Act">Comstock Act</a>, Grant prosecuted, through the Postal Department, immoral and indecent <a href="/wiki/Pornography" title="Pornography">pornographers</a>, in addition to <a href="/wiki/Abortionists" class="mw-redirect" title="Abortionists">abortionists</a>. To administer the prosecutions, Grant put in charge a vigorous anti-vice activist and reformer <a href="/wiki/Anthony_Comstock" title="Anthony Comstock">Anthony Comstock</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECarpenter200184–85_314-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarpenter200184–85-314">&#91;307&#93;</a></sup> Comstock headed a federal commission and was empowered to seize and destroy obscene material and hand out arrest warrants to offenders of the law.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan2018132_313-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan2018132-313">&#91;306&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Reconstruction">Reconstruction</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Reconstruction_era" title="Reconstruction era">Reconstruction era</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Amos_T_Akerman_-_crop_and_minor_retouch.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Amos_T_Akerman_-_crop_and_minor_retouch.jpg/180px-Amos_T_Akerman_-_crop_and_minor_retouch.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="238" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Amos_T_Akerman_-_crop_and_minor_retouch.jpg/270px-Amos_T_Akerman_-_crop_and_minor_retouch.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Amos_T_Akerman_-_crop_and_minor_retouch.jpg/360px-Amos_T_Akerman_-_crop_and_minor_retouch.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1952" data-file-height="2584" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Amos_T._Akerman" title="Amos T. Akerman">Amos T. Akerman</a>, appointed Attorney General by Grant, who vigorously prosecuted the <a href="/wiki/Ku_Klux_Klan" title="Ku Klux Klan">Ku Klux Klan</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>Grant was considered an effective civil rights president, concerned about the plight of <a href="/wiki/African_Americans" title="African Americans">African Americans</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan201861_315-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan201861-315">&#91;308&#93;</a></sup> On March 18, 1869, Grant signed into law equal rights for black people, to serve on juries and hold office, in Washington D.C., and in 1870 he signed into law the Naturalization Act that gave foreign black people citizenship.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan201861_315-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan201861-315">&#91;308&#93;</a></sup> During his first term, <a href="/wiki/Reconstruction_Era" class="mw-redirect" title="Reconstruction Era">Reconstruction</a> took precedence.
