Republicans controlled most Southern states, propped up by Republican-controlled Congress, northern money, and southern military occupation.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEScher201583Simon2002247_316-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScher201583Simon2002247-316">&#91;309&#93;</a></sup> Grant advocated the ratification of the <a href="/wiki/Fifteenth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Fifteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution">Fifteenth Amendment</a> that said states could not disenfranchise <a href="/wiki/African_Americans" title="African Americans">African Americans</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002_317-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002-317">&#91;310&#93;</a></sup> Within a year, the three remaining states—Mississippi, Virginia, and Texas—adopted the new amendment—and were admitted to Congress.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012435,_465Chernow2017686–87Simon2002247_318-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012435,_465Chernow2017686–87Simon2002247-318">&#91;311&#93;</a></sup> Grant put military pressure on Georgia to reinstate its black legislators and adopt the new amendment.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012465_319-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012465-319">&#91;312&#93;</a></sup> Georgia complied, and on February 24, 1871, its senators were seated in Congress, with all the former Confederate states represented, the Union was completely restored under Grant.<sup id="cite_ref-321" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-321">&#91;h&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002246_322-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002246-322">&#91;314&#93;</a></sup> Under Grant, for the first time in American history, Black-American males served in the United States Congress, all from the Southern states.<sup id="cite_ref-323" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-323">&#91;315&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1870, to enforce Reconstruction, Congress and Grant created the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Justice_Department" class="mw-redirect" title="United States Justice Department">Justice Department</a> that allowed the Attorney General and the new Solicitor General to prosecute the Klan.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001543–45Brands2012474_324-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001543–45Brands2012474-324">&#91;316&#93;</a></sup> Congress and Grant passed a series of three Enforcement Acts, designed to protect black people and Reconstruction governments.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan201864–65Calhoun2017317–19_325-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan201864–65Calhoun2017317–19-325">&#91;317&#93;</a></sup> Using the powers of the Enforcement Acts, Grant crushed the Ku Klux Klan.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFoner2019119–21_326-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFoner2019119–21-326">&#91;318&#93;</a></sup> By October, Grant suspended <i>habeas corpus</i> in part of South Carolina and sent federal troops to help marshals, who initiated prosecutions.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002248_327-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002248-327">&#91;319&#93;</a></sup> Grant's Attorney General, <a href="/wiki/Amos_T._Akerman" title="Amos T. Akerman">Amos T. Akerman</a>, who replaced Hoar, was zealous to destroy the Klan.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan201866_328-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan201866-328">&#91;320&#93;</a></sup> Akerman and South Carolina's U.S. marshal arrested over 470 Klan members, while hundreds of Klansmen, including the wealthy leaders, fled the state.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001547Calhoun2017324_329-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001547Calhoun2017324-329">&#91;321&#93;</a></sup> By 1872, the Klan's power had collapsed, and African Americans voted in record numbers in elections in the South.<sup id="cite_ref-331" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-331">&#91;i&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001547–48_332-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001547–48-332">&#91;323&#93;</a></sup> Attorney General <a href="/wiki/George_Henry_Williams" title="George Henry Williams">George H. Williams</a>, Akerman's replacement, in the Spring of 1873, suspended prosecutions of the Klan in North Carolina and South Carolina, but prior to the election of 1874, he changed course and prosecuted the Klan.<sup id="cite_ref-336" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-336">&#91;j&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan2018122_337-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan2018122-337">&#91;327&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>During Grant's second term, the North retreated from Reconstruction, while southern conservatives called "<a href="/wiki/Redeemers" title="Redeemers">Redeemers</a>" formed armed groups, the <a href="/wiki/Red_Shirts_(Southern_United_States)" class="mw-redirect" title="Red Shirts (Southern United States)">Red Shirts</a> and the <a href="/wiki/White_League" title="White League">White League</a>, who openly used violence, intimidation, voter fraud, and racist appeals to overturn Republican rule.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERichter201272,_527–28,_532Kahan2018121–22_338-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERichter201272,_527–28,_532Kahan2018121–22-338">&#91;328&#93;</a></sup> Northern apathy toward black people, the depressed economy and Grant's scandals made it politically difficult for the Grant administration to maintain support for Reconstruction. Power shifted when the House was taken over by the Democrats in the election of 1874.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001552–53Kahan2018121–22_339-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001552–53Kahan2018121–22-339">&#91;329&#93;</a></sup> Grant ended the <a href="/wiki/Brooks%E2%80%93Baxter_War" title="Brooks–Baxter War">Brooks–Baxter War</a>, bringing Reconstruction in Arkansas to a peaceful conclusion. He sent troops to New Orleans in the wake of the <a href="/wiki/Colfax_massacre" title="Colfax massacre">Colfax massacre</a> and disputes over the election of Governor <a href="/wiki/William_Pitt_Kellogg" title="William Pitt Kellogg">William Pitt Kellogg</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012538–41Foner2014528_340-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012538–41Foner2014528-340">&#91;330&#93;</a></sup> Grant recalled Sheridan and most of the federal troops from Louisiana.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012553_341-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012553-341">&#91;331&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>By 1875, Redeemer Democrats had taken control of all but three Southern states. As violence against black Southerners escalated once more, Grant's Attorney General <a href="/wiki/Edwards_Pierrepont" title="Edwards Pierrepont">Edwards Pierrepont</a> told Republican Governor <a href="/wiki/Adelbert_Ames" title="Adelbert Ames">Adelbert Ames</a> of Mississippi that the people were "tired of the autumnal outbreaks in the South", and declined to intervene directly, instead of sending an emissary to negotiate a peaceful election.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981420–22_342-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981420–22-342">&#91;332&#93;</a></sup> Grant later regretted not issuing a proclamation to help Ames, having been told Republicans in Ohio would bolt the party if Grant intervened in Mississippi.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017816–17_343-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017816–17-343">&#91;333&#93;</a></sup> Grant told Congress in January 1875 he could not "see with indifference Union men or Republicans ostracized, persecuted, and murdered."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012552_344-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012552-344">&#91;334&#93;</a></sup> Congress refused to strengthen the laws against violence but instead passed a sweeping law to guarantee black people access to public facilities.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981418–19_345-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981418–19-345">&#91;335&#93;</a></sup> Grant signed it as the <a href="/wiki/Civil_Rights_Act_of_1875" title="Civil Rights Act of 1875">Civil Rights Act of 1875</a>, but there was little enforcement and the Supreme Court ruled the law unconstitutional in 1883.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981418–19Franklin1974235_346-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981418–19Franklin1974235-346">&#91;336&#93;</a></sup> In October 1876, Grant dispatched troops to South Carolina to keep Republican Governor <a href="/wiki/Daniel_Henry_Chamberlain" title="Daniel Henry Chamberlain">Daniel Henry Chamberlain</a> in office.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012570_347-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012570-347">&#91;337&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After Grant left office in 1877, the nation returned to compromise. Grant's Republican successor, President <a href="/wiki/Rutherford_B._Hayes" title="Rutherford B. Hayes">Rutherford B. Hayes</a>, was conciliatory toward the South and favored "local control" of civil rights on the condition that Democrats make an honorary pledge to confirm the constitutional amendments that protected black people.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESproat1974163–65Calhoun2017561–62_348-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESproat1974163–65Calhoun2017561–62-348">&#91;338&#93;</a></sup> During <a href="/wiki/Compromise_of_1877" title="Compromise of 1877">Republican negotiations with Democrats</a>, that Grant took no direct part in, the Republicans received the White House for Hayes in return for ending enforcement of racial equality for black people and removing federal troops from the last three states.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001603–04Sproat1974163–65Calhoun2017561–62_349-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001603–04Sproat1974163–65Calhoun2017561–62-349">&#91;339&#93;</a></sup> As promised, Hayes withdrew federal troops from South Carolina and Louisiana, which marked the end of Reconstruction.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017853–54Smith2001603–04Sproat1974163–65_350-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017853–54Smith2001603–04Sproat1974163–65-350">&#91;340&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Financial_affairs">Financial affairs</span></h3>
<p>Soon after taking office, Grant took conservative steps to return the nation's currency to a more secure footing.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002249_351-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002249-351">&#91;341&#93;</a></sup> During the Civil War, Congress had authorized the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Department_of_the_Treasury" title="United States Department of the Treasury">Treasury</a> to issue banknotes that, unlike the rest of the currency, were not backed by gold or silver. The "<a href="/wiki/United_States_Note" title="United States Note">greenback</a>" notes, as they were known, were necessary to pay the unprecedented war debts, but they also caused inflation and forced gold-backed money out of circulation; Grant was determined to return the national <a href="/wiki/Economy" title="Economy">economy</a> to pre-war monetary standards.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981279_352-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981279-352">&#91;342&#93;</a></sup> On March 18, 1869, he signed the <a href="/wiki/Public_Credit_Act_of_1869" title="Public Credit Act of 1869">Public Credit Act of 1869</a> that guaranteed bondholders would be repaid in "coin or its equivalent", while greenbacks would gradually be redeemed by the Treasury and replaced by notes backed by specie. The act committed the government to the full return of the <a href="/wiki/Gold_standard" title="Gold standard">gold standard</a> within ten years.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016476–78Simon2002248BurdekinSiklos201324–25_353-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016476–78Simon2002248BurdekinSiklos201324–25-353">&#91;343&#93;</a></sup> This followed a policy of "hard currency, economy and gradual reduction of the national debt." Grant's own ideas about the economy were simple, and he relied on the advice of wealthy and financially successful businessmen that he courted.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002249_351-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002249-351">&#91;341&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Gold_corner_conspiracy">Gold corner conspiracy</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Black_Friday_(1869)" title="Black Friday (1869)">Black Friday (1869)</a></div>
<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Black_Friday_1869.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Black_Friday_1869.jpg/250px-Black_Friday_1869.jpg" decoding="async" width="250" height="218" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Black_Friday_1869.jpg/375px-Black_Friday_1869.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5b/Black_Friday_1869.jpg/500px-Black_Friday_1869.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1024" data-file-height="893" /></a><figcaption>Photograph of the blackboard in the New York City Gold Room on <a href="/wiki/Black_Friday_(1869)" title="Black Friday (1869)">Black Friday</a>, showing the collapse of the price of gold</figcaption></figure>
<p>In April 1869, two railroad tycoons <a href="/wiki/Jay_Gould" title="Jay Gould">Jay Gould</a> and <a href="/wiki/James_Fisk_(financier)" title="James Fisk (financier)">Jim Fisk</a> conspired a plot to corner the gold market in New York, the nation's financial capital.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002248Chernow2017672Calhoun2017125Kahan201854_354-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002248Chernow2017672Calhoun2017125Kahan201854-354">&#91;344&#93;</a></sup> They both controlled the Erie Railroad, and a high price of gold would allow foreign agriculture buyers to purchase exported crops, shipped east over the Erie's routes.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017125–28Kahan201854_355-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017125–28Kahan201854-355">&#91;345&#93;</a></sup> Boutwell's bi-weekly policy of selling gold from the Treasury, however, kept gold artificially low.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017128_356-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017128-356">&#91;346&#93;</a></sup> Unable to corrupt Boutwell, the two schemers built a relationship with Grant's brother-in-law, <a href="/wiki/Abel_Corbin" title="Abel Corbin">Abel Corbin</a>, and gained access to Grant.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012437–43McFeely1974134Chernow2017673Calhoun2017128–29Kahan201855_357-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012437–43McFeely1974134Chernow2017673Calhoun2017128–29Kahan201855-357">&#91;347&#93;</a></sup> Gould bribed Assistant Treasurer <a href="/wiki/Daniel_Butterfield" title="Daniel Butterfield">Daniel Butterfield</a> $10,000 to gain insider information into the Treasury.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981136,_323–24Chernow2017674Kahan201855–56_358-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981136,_323–24Chernow2017674Kahan201855–56-358">&#91;348&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In July, Grant reduced the sale of Treasury gold to $2,000,000 per month and subsequent months.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017130_359-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017130-359">&#91;349&#93;</a></sup> Fisk played a role in August in New York, having a letter from Gould, he told Grant his gold policy would destroy the nation.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017131_360-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017131-360">&#91;350&#93;</a></sup> By September, Grant, who was naive in matters of finance, was convinced that a low gold price would help farmers, and the sale of gold for September was not increased.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012437–43Simon2002248Calhoun2017130_361-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012437–43Simon2002248Calhoun2017130-361">&#91;351&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On September 23, when the gold price reached <style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1154941027">.mw-parser-output .frac{white-space:nowrap}.mw-parser-output .frac .num,.mw-parser-output .frac .den{font-size:80%;line-height:0;vertical-align:super}.mw-parser-output .frac .den{vertical-align:sub}.mw-parser-output .sr-only{border:0;clip:rect(0,0,0,0);clip-path:polygon(0px 0px,0px 0px,0px 0px);height:1px;margin:-1px;overflow:hidden;padding:0;position:absolute;width:1px}</style><span class="frac" role="math">143<span class="sr-only">+</span><span class="num">1</span>&#8260;<span class="den">8</span></span>, Boutwell rushed to the White House and talked with Grant.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017140–41_362-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017140–41-362">&#91;352&#93;</a></sup> The following day, September 24, known as <a href="/wiki/Black_Friday_(1869)" title="Black Friday (1869)">Black Friday</a>, Grant ordered Boutwell to sell, whereupon Boutwell wired Butterfield in New York, to sell $4,000,000 in gold.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017141_363-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017141-363">&#91;353&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Bull_market" class="mw-redirect" title="Bull market">bull market</a> at Gould's Gold Room collapsed, the price of gold plummeted from 160 to <link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1154941027"><span class="frac" role="math">133<span class="sr-only">+</span><span class="num">1</span>&#8260;<span class="den">3</span></span>, a <a href="/wiki/Bear_market" class="mw-redirect" title="Bear market">bear market</a> panic ensued, Gould and Fisk fled for their own safety, while severe economic damages lasted months.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012445,_636Chernow2017677–88Calhoun2017141_364-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012445,_636Chernow2017677–88Calhoun2017141-364">&#91;354&#93;</a></sup> By January 1870, the economy resumed its post-war recovery.<sup id="cite_ref-366" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-366">&#91;k&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981328Smith2001490_367-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981328Smith2001490-367">&#91;356&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Foreign_affairs">Foreign affairs</span></h3>
<p>Grant had limited foreign policy experience, acquired during his service in the Mexican-American war. As a result, he relied heavily on his talented Secretary of State <a href="/wiki/Hamilton_Fish" title="Hamilton Fish">Hamilton Fish</a>. Grant and Fish had a reserved but cordial friendship. There were no foreign-policy disasters and no wars to engage in. Besides Grant himself, the main players in foreign affairs were Secretary Fish and the chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee <a href="/wiki/Charles_Sumner" title="Charles Sumner">Charles Sumner</a>. They had to cooperate to get a treaty ratified. Sumner, who hated Grant, led the opposition to Grant's plan to annex Santo Domingo despite the fact that he previously fully supported the annexation of Alaska.
<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017310–11,_380–81_368-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017310–11,_380–81-368">&#91;357&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Fundamentally, Grant had an expansionist impulse to protect American interests abroad and was a strong advocate of the <a href="/wiki/Monroe_Doctrine" title="Monroe Doctrine">Monroe Doctrine</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan201875–76_369-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan201875–76-369">&#91;358&#93;</a></sup> He also had an idealist side to his foreign policy. For instance, Grant appointed a Jewish lawyer, <a href="/wiki/Benjamin_F._Peixotto" title="Benjamin F. Peixotto">Benjamin F. Peixotto</a>, U.S. <a href="/wiki/Consul_(representative)" title="Consul (representative)">Consul</a> in <a href="/wiki/Bucharest" title="Bucharest">Bucharest</a>, in response to the <a href="/wiki/United_Principalities_of_Moldavia_and_Wallachia" title="United Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia">Romanian</a> persecution of <a href="/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_Romania" title="History of the Jews in Romania">Jews</a>. Grant said that respect "for human rights is the first duty for those set as rulers" over the nations.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan201876_370-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan201876-370">&#91;359&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Hamilton_Fish_Brady_Edited.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Formal photographic portrait of bearded man" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Hamilton_Fish_Brady_Edited.jpg/180px-Hamilton_Fish_Brady_Edited.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="248" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Hamilton_Fish_Brady_Edited.jpg/270px-Hamilton_Fish_Brady_Edited.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fb/Hamilton_Fish_Brady_Edited.jpg/360px-Hamilton_Fish_Brady_Edited.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1094" data-file-height="1506" /></a><figcaption>Secretary of State <a href="/wiki/Hamilton_Fish" title="Hamilton Fish">Hamilton Fish</a> and Grant successfully settled the <a href="/wiki/Alabama_Claims" title="Alabama Claims">Alabama Claims</a> by treaty and arbitration.</figcaption></figure>
<h4><span id="Treaty_of_Washington_.281871.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Treaty_of_Washington_(1871)">Treaty of Washington (1871)</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Washington_(1871)" title="Treaty of Washington (1871)">Treaty of Washington (1871)</a></div>
<p>The most pressing diplomatic problem in 1869 was the settlement of the <a href="/wiki/Alabama_Claims" title="Alabama Claims"><i>Alabama</i> claims</a>, depredations caused to the Union merchant ships by the Confederate warship <a href="/wiki/CSS_Alabama" title="CSS Alabama">CSS&#160;<i>Alabama</i></a>, built in a British shipyard in violation of neutrality rules.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002249Smith2001491Kahan201878_371-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002249Smith2001491Kahan201878-371">&#91;360&#93;</a></sup> Secretary Hamilton Fish played the central role in formulating and implementing the <a href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Washington_(1871)" title="Treaty of Washington (1871)">Treaty of Washington</a> and the Geneva arbitration (1872).<sup id="cite_ref-wPQtP_372-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-wPQtP-372">&#91;361&#93;</a></sup> Senator <a href="/wiki/Charles_Sumner" title="Charles Sumner">Charles Sumner</a>, Chairman of the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Senate_Committee_on_Foreign_Relations" title="United States Senate Committee on Foreign Relations">Senate Foreign Relations Committee</a> led the demand for reparations, with talk of British Columbia as payment.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981352–54_373-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981352–54-373">&#91;362&#93;</a></sup> Sumner, along with other U.S. politicians, argued that British complicity in allowing the delivery of arms to the Confederacy via <a href="/wiki/Blockade_runners_of_the_American_Civil_War" title="Blockade runners of the American Civil War">blockade runners</a> prolonged the war by two years.<sup id="cite_ref-374" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-374">&#91;363&#93;</a></sup> Fish and Treasurer George Boutwell convinced Grant that peaceful relations with Britain were essential, and the two nations agreed to negotiate along those lines.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001508–11_375-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001508–11-375">&#91;364&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>To avoid jeopardizing negotiations, Grant refrained from recognizing Cuban rebels who were fighting for independence from Spain, which would have been inconsistent with American objections to the British granting belligerent status to Confederates.<sup id="cite_ref-376" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-376">&#91;l&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002249_351-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002249-351">&#91;341&#93;</a></sup> A commission in Washington produced a treaty whereby an international tribunal would settle the damage amounts; the British admitted regret, but not fault.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001512–15Simon2002249_377-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001512–15Simon2002249-377">&#91;365&#93;</a></sup> The Senate, including Grant critics Sumner and <a href="/wiki/Carl_Schurz" title="Carl Schurz">Carl Schurz</a>, approved the Treaty of Washington, which settled disputes over fishing rights and maritime boundaries, by a 50–12 vote, signed on May 8, 1871.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001249Simon2002512–15Calhoun2017344_378-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001249Simon2002512–15Calhoun2017344-378">&#91;366&#93;</a></sup> The <i>Alabama</i> claims settlement would be Grant's most successful foreign policy achievement that secured peace with Great Britain and the United States.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun20177_379-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun20177-379">&#91;367&#93;</a></sup> The settlement (<i>$15,500,000</i>) of the <i>Alabama</i> Claims resolved troubled Anglo-American issues and turned Britain into America's strongest ally.<sup id="cite_ref-380" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-380">&#91;368&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span id="Korean_expedition_.281871.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Korean_expedition_(1871)">Korean expedition (1871)</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/United_States_expedition_to_Korea" title="United States expedition to Korea">United States expedition to Korea</a></div>
<p>In 1871, a U.S. expedition was sent to <a href="/wiki/Korea" title="Korea">Korea</a> for two main reasons. The first was to open up trade with the country which, at the time, had a policy that excluded trading with foreign powers. The second was to learn the fate of the U.S. merchant ship, the <a href="/wiki/General_Sherman_incident" title="General Sherman incident">SS <i>General Sherman</i></a>, which had disappeared after sailing up the <a href="/wiki/Taedong_River" title="Taedong River">Taedong River</a> in August 1866.<sup id="cite_ref-Korea1871_381-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Korea1871-381">&#91;369&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In May 1871, Grant dispatched an American land and naval force consisting of five U.S. warships and over 1,200 men, under the command of Admiral <a href="/wiki/John_Rodgers_(admiral)" title="John Rodgers (admiral)">John Rodgers</a>, in order to support a diplomatic delegation, led by American ambassador to China, <a href="/wiki/Frederick_Low" title="Frederick Low">Frederick Low</a>, which was sent to negotiate trade and political relations with the Korean government.<sup id="cite_ref-Korea1871_381-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Korea1871-381">&#91;369&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On June 1, the American ships entered the Ganghwa Straits on the <a href="/wiki/Han_River_(Korea)" title="Han River (Korea)">Han River</a> and, as foreign ships were barred from entering the river, onshore Korean garrisons fired upon them. Though no damage was done to the ships, Admiral Rogers gave the Koreans ten days to apologize for what he regarded as an unprovoked assault; they refused. On June 10, about 650 Americans landed and captured several forts culminating in the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Ganghwa" title="Battle of Ganghwa">Battle of Ganghwa</a>, at which over 200 Korean troops were killed with a loss of only three American soldiers. Despite the victory, however, the expedition failed to open up trade as Grant had hoped and merely strengthened Korea's <a href="/wiki/Isolationism#Korea" title="Isolationism">isolationist policy</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-382" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-382">&#91;370&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span id="Santo_Domingo_.28Dominican_Republic.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Santo_Domingo_(Dominican_Republic)">Santo Domingo (Dominican Republic)</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Annexation_of_Santo_Domingo" title="Annexation of Santo Domingo">Annexation of Santo Domingo</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Annexation_demonstration_in_San_Domingo_City-the_Seybo_regiment_in_the_citadel,_bearing_the_U.S._colors_LCCN93515587.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Annexation_demonstration_in_San_Domingo_City-the_Seybo_regiment_in_the_citadel%2C_bearing_the_U.S._colors_LCCN93515587.jpg/220px-Annexation_demonstration_in_San_Domingo_City-the_Seybo_regiment_in_the_citadel%2C_bearing_the_U.S._colors_LCCN93515587.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="168" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Annexation_demonstration_in_San_Domingo_City-the_Seybo_regiment_in_the_citadel%2C_bearing_the_U.S._colors_LCCN93515587.jpg/330px-Annexation_demonstration_in_San_Domingo_City-the_Seybo_regiment_in_the_citadel%2C_bearing_the_U.S._colors_LCCN93515587.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Annexation_demonstration_in_San_Domingo_City-the_Seybo_regiment_in_the_citadel%2C_bearing_the_U.S._colors_LCCN93515587.jpg/440px-Annexation_demonstration_in_San_Domingo_City-the_Seybo_regiment_in_the_citadel%2C_bearing_the_U.S._colors_LCCN93515587.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1536" data-file-height="1176" /></a><figcaption>Santo Domingo City; watercolor by James E. Taylor, 1871</figcaption></figure>
<p>In 1869, Grant initiated his plan, later to become an obsession, to annex the <a href="/wiki/Dominican_Republic" title="Dominican Republic">Dominican Republic</a>, then called Santo Domingo.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017555,_660–61Kahan201875–76Calhoun2017199_383-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017555,_660–61Kahan201875–76Calhoun2017199-383">&#91;371&#93;</a></sup> Grant believed acquisition of the <a href="/wiki/Caribbean" title="Caribbean">Caribbean</a> island and Samaná Bay would increase the United States' natural resources, and strengthen U.S. naval protection to enforce the <a href="/wiki/Monroe_Doctrine" title="Monroe Doctrine">Monroe Doctrine</a>, safeguard against British obstruction of U.S. shipping and protect a future oceanic canal, stop slavery in Cuba and Brazil, while black people in the United States would have a safe haven from "the crime of Klu Kluxism".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017661–62Kahan201875–76Calhoun2017199–200,_206Brands2012454–55_384-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017661–62Kahan201875–76Calhoun2017199–200,_206Brands2012454–55-384">&#91;372&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Joseph W. Fabens, an American speculator who represented <a href="/wiki/Buenaventura_B%C3%A1ez" title="Buenaventura Báez">Buenaventura Báez</a>, the president of the Dominican Republic, met with Secretary Fish and proposed annexation,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan201890–91Calhoun2017204_385-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan201890–91Calhoun2017204-385">&#91;373&#93;</a></sup> whose island inhabitants sought American protection.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017661_386-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017661-386">&#91;374&#93;</a></sup> Fish wanted nothing to do with the island, but he dutifully brought up Faben's proposal to Grant at a cabinet meeting.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESchmiel2014_387-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchmiel2014-387">&#91;375&#93;</a></sup> On July 17, Grant sent his military White House aide <a href="/wiki/Orville_E._Babcock" title="Orville E. Babcock">Orville E. Babcock</a> to evaluate the islands' resources, local conditions, and Báez's terms for annexation, but was given no diplomatic authority.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017207,_210–11Kahan201891_388-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017207,_210–11Kahan201891-388">&#91;376&#93;</a></sup> When Babcock returned to Washington with two unauthorized annexation treaties, Grant, however, approved and pressured his cabinet to accept them.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001500–02Chernow2017663–64Calhoun2017220_389-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001500–02Chernow2017663–64Calhoun2017220-389">&#91;377&#93;</a></sup> Grant ordered Fish to draw up formal treaties, sent to Báez by Babcock's return to the island nation. The Dominican Republic would be annexed for $1.5&#160;million and Samaná Bay would be lease-purchased for $2&#160;million. General <a href="/wiki/Delos_Bennett_Sackett" title="Delos Bennett Sackett">D.B. Sackett</a> and General <a href="/wiki/Rufus_Ingalls" title="Rufus Ingalls">Rufus Ingalls</a> accompanied Babcock.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017224_390-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017224-390">&#91;378&#93;</a></sup> On November 29, President Báez signed the treaties. On December 21, the treaties were placed before Grant and his cabinet.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan201891Calhoun2017223,_226_391-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan201891Calhoun2017223,_226-391">&#91;379&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant's grand plan to annex Santo Domingo, a black and mixed-race nation, into the United States, however, would be hostilely obstructed by Senator <a href="/wiki/Charles_Sumner" title="Charles Sumner">Charles Sumner</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017665_392-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017665-392">&#91;380&#93;</a></sup> On December 31, Grant met with Sumner, unannounced, at Sumner's Washington D.C. home to gain his support for annexation. Grant left confident Sumner approved, but what Sumner actually said was controversially disputed, by various witnesses. Without appealing to the American public, to his detriment, Grant submitted the treaties on January 10, 1870, to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, chaired by the stubborn and imperious Sumner, for ratification, but Sumner purposefully shelved the bills.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017660–65Calhoun2017226–34,_254_393-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017660–65Calhoun2017226–34,_254-393">&#91;381&#93;</a></sup> Prompted by Grant to stop stalling the treaties, Sumner's committee took action but rejected the bills by a 5-to-2 vote. Sumner opposed annexation and reportedly said the Dominicans were "a turbulent, treacherous race" in a closed session of the Senate.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017237–38_394-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017237–38-394">&#91;382&#93;</a></sup> Sumner sent the treaties for a full Senate vote, while Grant personally lobbied other senators. Despite Grant's efforts, the Senate defeated the treaties, on Thursday, June 30, by a 28–28 vote when a 2/3 majority was required.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016509–12Pletcher1998167Simon2002McFeely1981339–40_395-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016509–12Pletcher1998167Simon2002McFeely1981339–40-395">&#91;383&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant was outraged, and on July 1, 1870, he sacked his appointed Minister to Great Britain, <a href="/wiki/John_Lothrop_Motley" title="John Lothrop Motley">John Lothrop Motley</a>, Sumner's close friend and ally.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017254,_258Kahan201894_396-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017254,_258Kahan201894-396">&#91;384&#93;</a></sup> In January 1871, Grant signed a joint resolution to send a commission to investigate annexation.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012461Kahan201894–95_397-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012461Kahan201894–95-397">&#91;385&#93;</a></sup> For this undertaking, he chose three neutral parties, with <a href="/wiki/Frederick_Douglass" title="Frederick Douglass">Frederick Douglass</a> to be secretary of the commission, that gave Grant the moral high ground from Sumner.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017715–16_398-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017715–16-398">&#91;386&#93;</a></sup> Although the commission approved its findings, the Senate remained opposed, forcing Grant to abandon further efforts.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012461Smith2001505–06_399-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012461Smith2001505–06-399">&#91;387&#93;</a></sup> Seeking retribution, in March 1871, Grant maneuvered to have Sumner deposed from his powerful Senate chairmanship, replaced by Grant ally <a href="/wiki/Simon_Cameron" title="Simon Cameron">Simon Cameron</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002250McFeely1981349–52Kahan201895_400-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002250McFeely1981349–52Kahan201895-400">&#91;388&#93;</a></sup> The stinging controversy over Santo Domingo overshadowed Grant's foreign diplomacy.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun20177_379-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun20177-379">&#91;367&#93;</a></sup> Critics complained of Grant's reliance on military personnel to implement his policies.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017224_390-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017224-390">&#91;378&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Cuba_and_Virginius_Affair">Cuba and Virginius Affair</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Virginius_Affair" title="Virginius Affair">Virginius Affair</a></div>
<p>American policy under Grant was to remain neutral during the <a href="/wiki/Ten_Years%27_War" title="Ten Years&#39; War">Ten Years' War</a> (1868–78), a series of long bloody revolts that were taking place in Cuba against Spanish rule. On the recommendation of Fish and Senator Sumner, Grant refused to recognize the belligerence of the rebels, and in effect endorsed Spanish colonial rule there, while calling for the abolition of slavery in Cuba.<sup id="cite_ref-vCrUE_401-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-vCrUE-401">&#91;389&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHamilton_Fish_(1808–1893)_402-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHamilton_Fish_(1808–1893)-402">&#91;390&#93;</a></sup> This was done to protect American commerce and to keep peace with Spain.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHamilton_Fish_(1808–1893)_402-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHamilton_Fish_(1808–1893)-402">&#91;390&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>This fragile policy, however, was severely broken in October 1873, when a Spanish cruiser captured a merchant ship, <a href="/wiki/Virginius_Affair" title="Virginius Affair"><i>Virginius</i></a>, flying the U.S. flag, carrying supplies and men to aid the insurrection. Treating them as pirates, without trial, Spanish authorities executed 53 prisoners, including eight American citizens. American Captain Joseph Frye was executed and his crew was executed and decapitated and their lifeless bodies were mutilated, trampled by horses. Many enraged Americans protested and called for war with Spain. Grant ordered U.S. Navy Squadron warships to converge on Cuba, off of <a href="/wiki/Key_West,_Florida" class="mw-redirect" title="Key West, Florida">Key West</a>, supported by the <a href="/wiki/USS_Kansas_(1863)" title="USS Kansas (1863)">USS <i>Kansas</i></a>. On November 27, Fish reached a diplomatic resolution in which Spain's president, <a href="/wiki/Emilio_Castelar_y_Ripoll" class="mw-redirect" title="Emilio Castelar y Ripoll">Emilio Castelar y Ripoll</a>, expressed his regret, surrendered the <i>Virginius</i> and the surviving captives. A year later, Spain paid a cash indemnity of $80,000 to the families of the executed Americans.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017426–31_403-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017426–31-403">&#91;391&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTENevins1936667–94_404-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTENevins1936667–94-404">&#91;392&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h4><span class="mw-headline" id="Free_trade_with_Hawaii">Free trade with Hawaii</span></h4>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Reciprocity_Treaty_of_1875" title="Reciprocity Treaty of 1875">Reciprocity Treaty of 1875</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Kalakaua_Grant_state_visit_1874.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="reception line" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Kalakaua_Grant_state_visit_1874.jpg/220px-Kalakaua_Grant_state_visit_1874.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="162" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Kalakaua_Grant_state_visit_1874.jpg/330px-Kalakaua_Grant_state_visit_1874.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Kalakaua_Grant_state_visit_1874.jpg/440px-Kalakaua_Grant_state_visit_1874.jpg 2x" data-file-width="7393" data-file-height="5440" /></a><figcaption>King <a href="/wiki/Kal%C4%81kaua" title="Kalākaua">Kalākaua of Hawaii</a> meets President Grant at the White House on his <a href="/wiki/Kal%C4%81kaua%27s_1874%E2%80%9375_state_visit_to_the_United_States" title="Kalākaua&#39;s 1874–75 state visit to the United States">state visit</a>, 1874.</figcaption></figure>
<p>In the face of strong opposition from Democrats, Grant and Fish secured a free trade treaty in 1875 with the <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hawaii" class="mw-redirect" title="Kingdom of Hawaii">Kingdom of Hawaii</a>, incorporating the Pacific islands' sugar industry into the United States' economic sphere.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017539–40_405-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017539–40-405">&#91;393&#93;</a></sup> To secure the trade agreement, King <a href="/wiki/Kal%C4%81kaua" title="Kalākaua">Kalākaua</a> of the <a href="/wiki/Hawaiian_Kingdom" title="Hawaiian Kingdom">Hawaiian Kingdom</a> made a 91-day <a href="/wiki/Kal%C4%81kaua%27s_1874%E2%80%9375_state_visit_to_the_United_States" title="Kalākaua&#39;s 1874–75 state visit to the United States">state visit</a>, the first reigning monarch of any nation to set foot in the United States.<sup id="cite_ref-406" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-406">&#91;394&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Southern Democrats, wanting to protect American rice and sugar producers, tried to squash a bill to implement the Hawaiian treaty. The Democrats, in opposition, because the treaty was believed to be an island annexation attempt, referred to the Hawaiians as an "inferior" non-white race. Despite opposition, the implementation bill passed Congress.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017539–40_405-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017539–40-405">&#91;393&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The treaty gave free access to the <a href="/wiki/United_States" title="United States">United States</a> market for sugar and other products grown in the <a href="/wiki/Kingdom_of_Hawaii" class="mw-redirect" title="Kingdom of Hawaii">Kingdom of Hawaii</a> starting in September 1876. In return, the United States gained lands in the area known as Pu&#x2bb;u Loa for what would eventually become known as the <a href="/wiki/Pearl_Harbor" title="Pearl Harbor">Pearl Harbor</a> naval base. The treaty led to large investment by Americans in <a href="/wiki/Sugar_plantations_in_Hawaii" title="Sugar plantations in Hawaii">sugarcane plantations in Hawaii</a>, strengthening the country's business interests in the islands.<sup id="cite_ref-407" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-407">&#91;395&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Federal_Indian_policy">Federal Indian policy</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Native_American_policy_of_the_Ulysses_S._Grant_administration" title="Native American policy of the Ulysses S. Grant administration">Native American policy of the Ulysses S. Grant administration</a></div>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Black_Hills_Land_Claim" class="mw-redirect" title="Black Hills Land Claim">Black Hills Land Claim</a>, <a href="/wiki/Black_Hills_Gold_Rush" title="Black Hills Gold Rush">Black Hills Gold Rush</a>, and <a href="/wiki/Great_Sioux_War" class="mw-redirect" title="Great Sioux War">Great Sioux War</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ely_S._Parker.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Formal photographic portrait of a sitting mustached man" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Ely_S._Parker.jpg/180px-Ely_S._Parker.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="218" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Ely_S._Parker.jpg/270px-Ely_S._Parker.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Ely_S._Parker.jpg/360px-Ely_S._Parker.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1175" data-file-height="1421" /></a><figcaption><a href="/wiki/Ely_Samuel_Parker" class="mw-redirect" title="Ely Samuel Parker">Ely Samuel Parker</a>, appointed by President Grant as the first <a href="/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States" title="Native Americans in the United States">Native American</a> (<i><a href="/wiki/Seneca_people" title="Seneca people">Seneca</a></i>) Commissioner of <a href="/wiki/Bureau_of_Indian_Affairs" title="Bureau of Indian Affairs">Indian Affairs</a></figcaption></figure>
<p>When Grant took office in 1869, the nation's policy towards <a href="/wiki/Native_Americans_in_the_United_States" title="Native Americans in the United States">Native Americans</a> was in chaos, affecting more than 250,000 Native Americans being governed by 370 treaties.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016487_408-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016487-408">&#91;396&#93;</a></sup> Grant's religious faith influenced his "peace" policy toward Native Americans, believing that the "Creator" did not place races of men on earth for the "stronger" to destroy the "weaker".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016491_409-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016491-409">&#91;397&#93;</a></sup> President Grant was mostly an assimilationist, wanting Indians to adopt European customs, education, English language, Christianity, private property, clothing, and to accept democratic government, which would lead to eventual Indian citizenship.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017830–31_410-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017830–31-410">&#91;398&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-ReferenceA_411-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ReferenceA-411">&#91;399&#93;</a></sup> At Grant's 1869 Inauguration, Grant said "the proper treatment of the original occupants of the land, the Indian, is one deserving of careful study. I will favor any course towards them which tends to their civilization, Christianization and ultimate citizenship."<sup id="cite_ref-ReferenceA_411-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ReferenceA-411">&#91;399&#93;</a></sup> Grant appointed <a href="/wiki/Ely_S._Parker" title="Ely S. Parker">Ely S. Parker</a>, an assimilated <a href="/wiki/Seneca_people" title="Seneca people">Seneca</a> and member of his wartime staff, to serve as the <a href="/wiki/Bureau_of_Indian_Affairs" title="Bureau of Indian Affairs">Commissioner of Indian Affairs</a>, the first Native American to serve in this position, surprising many around him. <sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016490–91Simon2002250Smith2001472–73_412-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016490–91Simon2002250Smith2001472–73-412">&#91;400&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-ReferenceA_411-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ReferenceA-411">&#91;399&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In April 1869, Grant signed legislation establishing an unpaid <a href="/wiki/Board_of_Indian_Commissioners" title="Board of Indian Commissioners">Board of Indian Commissioners</a> to reduce corruption and oversee the implementation of what was called Grant's Indian "Peace" policy,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002250Smith2001535Simon2002250_413-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002250Smith2001535Simon2002250-413">&#91;401&#93;</a></sup> aimed to replace entrepreneurs serving as Native American agents with missionaries and aimed to protect Native Americans on reservations and educate them in farming.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981308–09Brands2012502_414-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981308–09Brands2012502-414">&#91;402&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1870, a setback in Grant's policy occurred over the <a href="/wiki/Marias_Massacre" title="Marias Massacre">Marias Massacre</a>, causing public outrage.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017270_415-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017270-415">&#91;403&#93;</a></sup> In 1871, Grant ended the sovereign tribal treaty system; by law individual Native Americans were deemed <a href="/wiki/Ward_(law)" title="Ward (law)">wards</a> of the federal government.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWaltmann1971327_416-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaltmann1971327-416">&#91;404&#93;</a></sup> Grant's Indian policy was undermined by Parker's resignation in 1871, denominational infighting among Grant's chosen religious agents, and entrenched economic interests.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002250_417-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002250-417">&#91;405&#93;</a></sup> Grant's Indian policy was also lampooned by an 1871 <a href="/wiki/Thomas_Nast" title="Thomas Nast">Thomas Nast</a> cartoon that depicted Grant as "Robinson Crusoe" forcing an Indian chief, "his man Friday", into tightly fitted western attire.<sup id="cite_ref-ReferenceA_411-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ReferenceA-411">&#91;399&#93;</a></sup> Nonetheless, Indian wars declined overall during Grant's first term, and on October 1, 1872, Major General <a href="/wiki/Oliver_Otis_Howard" title="Oliver Otis Howard">Oliver Otis Howard</a> negotiated peace with the <a href="/wiki/Apache" title="Apache">Apache</a> leader <a href="/wiki/Cochise" title="Cochise">Cochise</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECoffey2011Kahan201871–72_418-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoffey2011Kahan201871–72-418">&#91;406&#93;</a></sup> On December 28, 1872, another setback took place to Grant's policy when General <a href="/wiki/George_Crook" title="George Crook">George Crook</a> and the 5th Cavalry massacred about 75 Yavapai Apache Indians at <a href="/wiki/Skeleton_Cave_(Arizona)" title="Skeleton Cave (Arizona)">Skeleton Cave, Arizona</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-419" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-419">&#91;407&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>During his second term, Grant's Indian policy fell apart.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan2018127_420-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan2018127-420">&#91;408&#93;</a></sup> On April 11, 1873, Major General <a href="/wiki/Edward_Canby" title="Edward Canby">Edward Canby</a> was killed in Northern California south of <a href="/wiki/Tule_Lake" title="Tule Lake">Tule Lake</a> by <a href="/wiki/Modoc_people" title="Modoc people">Modoc</a> leader <a href="/wiki/Kintpuash" title="Kintpuash">Kintpuash</a>, in a failed peace conference to end the <a href="/wiki/Modoc_War" title="Modoc War">Modoc War</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001532–35Coffey2011_421-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001532–35Coffey2011-421">&#91;409&#93;</a></sup> Grant ordered restraint after Canby's death. The army captured Kintpuash, who was convicted of Canby's murder and hanged on October 3 at <a href="/wiki/Fort_Klamath" title="Fort Klamath">Fort Klamath</a>, while the remaining Modoc tribe was relocated to the <a href="/wiki/Indian_Territory" title="Indian Territory">Indian Territory</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001532–35Coffey2011_421-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001532–35Coffey2011-421">&#91;409&#93;</a></sup> In 1874, the army defeated the <a href="/wiki/Comanche" title="Comanche">Comanche</a> at the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_Palo_Duro_Canyon" title="Battle of Palo Duro Canyon">Battle of Palo Duro Canyon</a>, forcing them to finally settle at the <a href="/wiki/Fort_Sill" title="Fort Sill">Fort Sill</a> reservation in 1875.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECoffey2011604–05_422-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoffey2011604–05-422">&#91;410&#93;</a></sup> Grant <a href="/wiki/Pocket_veto" title="Pocket veto">pocket-vetoed</a> a bill in 1874 protecting bison and instead supported Interior Secretary <a href="/wiki/Columbus_Delano" title="Columbus Delano">Columbus Delano</a>, who correctly believed the killing of bison would force <a href="/wiki/Plains_Indians" title="Plains Indians">Plains Native Americans</a> to abandon their nomadic lifestyle.<sup id="cite_ref-424" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-424">&#91;m&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTETaylor20113187–88Pritchard19995_425-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaylor20113187–88Pritchard19995-425">&#91;412&#93;</a></sup> In April 1875, another setback occurred to Grant's policy. The U.S. Army led by Lt. Austin Henly massacred 27 Cheyenne Indians, including 19 men, and 8 women and children, on the Sappa Creek, in Kansas.<sup id="cite_ref-426" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-426">&#91;413&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-427" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-427">&#91;414&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>With the lure of gold discovered in the <a href="/wiki/Black_Hills_Gold_Rush" title="Black Hills Gold Rush">Black Hills</a> and the westward force of <a href="/wiki/Manifest_Destiny" class="mw-redirect" title="Manifest Destiny">Manifest Destiny</a>, white settlers trespassed on <a href="/wiki/Treaty_of_Fort_Laramie_(1868)" title="Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868)">Sioux protected lands</a> used for religious and marital ceremonies. <a href="/wiki/Red_Cloud" title="Red Cloud">Red Cloud</a> reluctantly entered negotiations on May 26, 1875, but other Sioux chiefs readied for war.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017830–31Brands2012564_428-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017830–31Brands2012564-428">&#91;415&#93;</a></sup> Grant told the Sioux leaders to make "arrangements to allow white persons to go into the Black Hills." Antagonistic toward Native American culture, Grant told them their children would attend schools, speak English, and prepare "for the life of white men."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017830–31_410-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017830–31-410">&#91;398&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Battle_of_the_Big_Horn_LCCN2003656850.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Battle_of_the_Big_Horn_LCCN2003656850.jpg/220px-Battle_of_the_Big_Horn_LCCN2003656850.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="171" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Battle_of_the_Big_Horn_LCCN2003656850.jpg/330px-Battle_of_the_Big_Horn_LCCN2003656850.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Battle_of_the_Big_Horn_LCCN2003656850.jpg/440px-Battle_of_the_Big_Horn_LCCN2003656850.jpg 2x" data-file-width="8628" data-file-height="6722" /></a><figcaption>The <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_the_Little_Big_Horn" class="mw-redirect" title="Battle of the Little Big Horn">Battle of the Little Big Horn</a>, 1876</figcaption></figure>
<p>On November 3, 1875, Grant held a meeting at the White House and, under advice from Sheridan, agreed not to enforce keeping out miners from the Black Hills, thereby forcing Native Americans onto the Sioux reservation.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017832Calhoun2017546_429-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017832Calhoun2017546-429">&#91;416&#93;</a></sup> Sheridan told Grant that the U.S. Army was undermanned and the territory involved was vast, requiring great numbers of soldiers to enforce the treaty.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001538_430-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001538-430">&#91;417&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>During the <a href="/wiki/Great_Sioux_War_of_1876" title="Great Sioux War of 1876">Great Sioux War</a> that started after <a href="/wiki/Sitting_Bull" title="Sitting Bull">Sitting Bull</a> refused to relocate to agency land, warriors led by <a href="/wiki/Crazy_Horse" title="Crazy Horse">Crazy Horse</a> massacred <a href="/wiki/George_Armstrong_Custer" title="George Armstrong Custer">George Armstrong Custer</a> and 268 of his men at the <a href="/wiki/Battle_of_the_Little_Big_Horn" class="mw-redirect" title="Battle of the Little Big Horn">Battle of the Little Big Horn</a>. The slaughter took place during the <a href="/wiki/Centennial_Exposition" title="Centennial Exposition">Centennial</a>, and the Indian victory was announced to the nation on July 4, while angry white settlers demanded retribution. Grant castigated Custer in the press, saying "I regard Custer's massacre as a sacrifice of troops, brought on by Custer himself, that was wholly unnecessary—wholly unnecessary."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012565–66Donovan2008115,_322–23_431-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012565–66Donovan2008115,_322–23-431">&#91;418&#93;</a></sup> Previously, Custer had infuriated Grant when he testified against Grant's brother Orville during a House investigation into trading post graft on March&#160;1, 1876.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBehnckeBloomfield2020181–84_432-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBehnckeBloomfield2020181–84-432">&#91;419&#93;</a></sup> In September and October 1876, Grant persuaded the tribes to relinquish the Black Hills. Congress ratified the agreement three days before Grant left office in 1877.<sup id="cite_ref-435" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-435">&#91;n&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017549_436-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017549-436">&#91;422&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Election_of_1872_and_second_term">Election of 1872 and second term</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/1872_United_States_presidential_election" title="1872 United States presidential election">1872 United States presidential election</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Grant_Liberal_Gratitude.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="A Thomas Nast cartoon depicting Grant steering a ship and being challenged by opponents during the presidential election of 1872." src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/Grant_Liberal_Gratitude.jpg/220px-Grant_Liberal_Gratitude.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="268" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/Grant_Liberal_Gratitude.jpg/330px-Grant_Liberal_Gratitude.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/Grant_Liberal_Gratitude.jpg/440px-Grant_Liberal_Gratitude.jpg 2x" data-file-width="900" data-file-height="1097" /></a><figcaption>Cartoon by <a href="/wiki/Thomas_Nast" title="Thomas Nast">Thomas Nast</a> on Grant's opponents in the reelection campaign</figcaption></figure>
<p>Grant's first administration was mixed with both success and failure.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFoner2014499–500Kahan2018103_437-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFoner2014499–500Kahan2018103-437">&#91;423&#93;</a></sup> In 1871, to placate reformers, he created the America's first <a href="/wiki/United_States_Civil_Service_Commission" title="United States Civil Service Commission">Civil Service Commission</a>, chaired by reformer <a href="/wiki/George_William_Curtis" title="George William Curtis">George William Curtis</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPatrick1968172–73Simon2002250Smith2001589–90Kahan2018105,_106_438-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPatrick1968172–73Simon2002250Smith2001589–90Kahan2018105,_106-438">&#91;424&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Liberal_Republican_Party_(United_States)" title="Liberal Republican Party (United States)">Liberal Republicans</a>, composed of reformers, men who supported low tariffs, and those who opposed Grant's prosecution of the Klan, broke from Grant and the Republican Party.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002250Chernow2017734–35Kahan2018105–06Brands2012488–89_439-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002250Chernow2017734–35Kahan2018105–06Brands2012488–89-439">&#91;425&#93;</a></sup> The Liberals, who personally disliked Grant, detested his alliance with Senator <a href="/wiki/Simon_Cameron" title="Simon Cameron">Simon Cameron</a> and Senator <a href="/wiki/Roscoe_Conkling" title="Roscoe Conkling">Roscoe Conkling</a>, considered to be spoilsmen politicians.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan2018104–06_440-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan2018104–06-440">&#91;426&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1872, the Liberals nominated <a href="/wiki/Horace_Greeley" title="Horace Greeley">Horace Greeley</a>, a leading Republican <i>New York Tribune</i> editor and a fierce enemy of Grant, for president, and Missouri governor <a href="/wiki/Benjamin_Gratz_Brown" class="mw-redirect" title="Benjamin Gratz Brown">B. Gratz Brown</a>, for vice president.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002250–51Brands2012495Chernow2017740–41_441-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002250–51Brands2012495Chernow2017740–41-441">&#91;427&#93;</a></sup> The Liberals denounced <a href="/wiki/Grantism" title="Grantism">Grantism</a>, corruption, nepotism, and inefficiency, demanded the withdrawal of federal troops from the South, literacy tests for black people to vote, and amnesty for Confederates.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWang1997103–04Simon2002250Chernow2017735,_740_442-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWang1997103–04Simon2002250Chernow2017735,_740-442">&#91;428&#93;</a></sup> The Democrats adopted the Greeley-Brown ticket and the Liberals party platform.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012495_443-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012495-443">&#91;429&#93;</a></sup> Greeley, whose Tribune gave him wider name recognition and a louder campaign voice, pushed the themes that the Grant administration was failed and corrupt.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017361,_375_444-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017361,_375-444">&#91;430&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Republicans nominated Grant for reelection, with Senator <a href="/wiki/Henry_Wilson" title="Henry Wilson">Henry Wilson</a> of Massachusetts replacing Colfax as the vice presidential nominee.<sup id="cite_ref-446" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-446">&#91;o&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017743_447-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017743-447">&#91;432&#93;</a></sup> The Republicans shrewdly borrowed from the Liberals' party platform, including "extended amnesty, lowered tariffs, and embraced civil service reform."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016532_448-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016532-448">&#91;433&#93;</a></sup> Grant lowered customs duties, gave amnesty to former Confederates, and implemented a civil service merit system, neutralizing the opposition.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017372–73,_387_449-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017372–73,_387-449">&#91;434&#93;</a></sup> To placate the burgeoning <a href="/wiki/Women%27s_suffrage_in_the_United_States" title="Women&#39;s suffrage in the United States">suffragist</a> movement, the Republicans' platform mentioned that women's rights would be treated with "respectful consideration."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017749–50_450-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017749–50-450">&#91;435&#93;</a></sup> Concerning Southern policy, Greeley advocated that local government control be given to white people, while Grant advocated federal protection of black people.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFoner2014Calhoun2017_451-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFoner2014Calhoun2017-451">&#91;436&#93;</a></sup> Grant was supported by <a href="/wiki/Frederick_Douglass" title="Frederick Douglass">Frederick Douglass</a>, prominent abolitionists, and Indian reformers.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016535_452-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016535-452">&#91;437&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant won reelection easily thanks to federal prosecution of the Klan, a strong economy, debt reduction, lowered tariffs, and tax reductions.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981384Simon2002250–51Chernow2017749_453-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981384Simon2002250–51Chernow2017749-453">&#91;438&#93;</a></sup> He received 56% of the vote to Greeley's 44% and an Electoral College landslide of 286 to 66.<sup id="cite_ref-455" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-455">&#91;p&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-456" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-456">&#91;440&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002250–51Brands2012499_457-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002250–51Brands2012499-457">&#91;441&#93;</a></sup> A majority of African Americans in the South voted for Grant, while Democratic opposition remained mostly peaceful.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFoner2014508_458-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFoner2014508-458">&#91;442&#93;</a></sup> Grant lost in six former slave states that wanted to see an end to Reconstruction.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGoethals201598_459-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoethals201598-459">&#91;443&#93;</a></sup> He proclaimed the victory as a personal vindication of his presidency, but inwardly he felt betrayed by the Liberals.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002250–51_460-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002250–51-460">&#91;444&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant was sworn in for his second term by <a href="/wiki/Salmon_P._Chase" title="Salmon P. Chase">Salmon P. Chase</a> on March 4, 1873. In his second inaugural address, he reiterated the problems still facing the nation and focused on what he considered the chief issues of the day: freedom and fairness for all Americans while emphasizing the benefits of citizenship for freed slaves. Grant concluded his address with the words, "My efforts in the future will be directed towards the restoration of good feelings between the different sections of our common community".<sup id="cite_ref-462" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-462">&#91;q&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016540–41_463-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016540–41-463">&#91;446&#93;</a></sup> In 1873, Wilson suffered a stroke; never fully recovering, he died in office on November 22, 1875.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016545Diller19961545_464-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016545Diller19961545-464">&#91;447&#93;</a></sup> With Wilson's loss, Grant relied on Fish's guidance more than ever.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981385_465-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981385-465">&#91;448&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-466" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-466">&#91;r&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Panic_of_1873_and_loss_of_House">Panic of 1873 and loss of House</span></h3>
<p>Grant continued to work for a strong dollar, signing into law the <a href="/wiki/Coinage_Act_of_1873" title="Coinage Act of 1873">Coinage Act of 1873</a>, which effectively ended the legal basis for <a href="/wiki/Bimetallism" title="Bimetallism">bimetallism</a> (the use of both silver and gold as money), establishing the gold standard in practice.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEVenable201166–68_467-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVenable201166–68-467">&#91;449&#93;</a></sup> The Coinage Act discontinued the <a href="/wiki/Seated_Liberty_dollar" title="Seated Liberty dollar">standard silver dollar</a> and established the <a href="/wiki/Gold_dollar" title="Gold dollar">gold dollar</a> as the sole monetary standard; because the gold supply did not increase as quickly as the population, the result was deflation. Silverites, who wanted more money in circulation to raise the prices that farmers received, denounced the move as the "Crime of 1873", claiming the deflation made debts more burdensome for farmers.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWeinstein1967307–26_468-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeinstein1967307–26-468">&#91;450&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Grant_Inflation_Bill_Veto.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="A cartoon depicting Grant after vetoing the Inflation bill." src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Grant_Inflation_Bill_Veto.jpg/220px-Grant_Inflation_Bill_Veto.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="151" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Grant_Inflation_Bill_Veto.jpg/330px-Grant_Inflation_Bill_Veto.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b8/Grant_Inflation_Bill_Veto.jpg/440px-Grant_Inflation_Bill_Veto.jpg 2x" data-file-width="1000" data-file-height="688" /></a><figcaption>Grant is congratulated for vetoing the "inflation bill" in 1874.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Economic turmoil renewed during Grant's second term. In September 1873, <a href="/wiki/Jay_Cooke_%26_Company" title="Jay Cooke &amp; Company">Jay Cooke &amp; Company</a>, a New York brokerage house, collapsed after it failed to sell all of the bonds issued by <a href="/wiki/Jay_Cooke" title="Jay Cooke">Cooke</a>'s <a href="/wiki/Northern_Pacific_Railway" title="Northern Pacific Railway">Northern Pacific Railway</a>. The collapse rippled through Wall Street, and other banks and brokerages that owned railroad stocks and bonds were also ruined.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012517_469-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012517-469">&#91;451&#93;</a></sup> On September 20, the <a href="/wiki/New_York_Stock_Exchange" title="New York Stock Exchange">New York Stock Exchange</a> suspended trading for ten days.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981393_470-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981393-470">&#91;452&#93;</a></sup> Grant, who knew little about finance, traveled to New York to consult leading businessmen and bankers for advice on how to resolve the crisis, which became known as the <a href="/wiki/Panic_of_1873" title="Panic of 1873">Panic of 1873</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001576–79_471-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001576–79-471">&#91;453&#93;</a></sup> Grant believed that, as with the collapse of the Gold Ring in 1869, the panic was merely an economic fluctuation that affected bankers and brokers.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012518_472-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012518-472">&#91;454&#93;</a></sup> He instructed the Treasury to buy $10&#160;million in government bonds, injecting cash into the system. The purchases curbed the panic on Wall Street, but an industrial depression, later called the <a href="/wiki/Long_Depression" title="Long Depression">Long Depression</a>, nonetheless swept the nation.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001576–79_471-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001576–79-471">&#91;453&#93;</a></sup> Many of the nation's railroads—89 out of 364—went bankrupt.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981391Smith2001375–77_473-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981391Smith2001375–77-473">&#91;455&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Congress hoped inflation would stimulate the economy and passed The <a href="/wiki/Thomas_W._Ferry" title="Thomas W. Ferry">Ferry</a> Bill, which became known as the "Inflation Bill" in 1874.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017779_474-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017779-474">&#91;456&#93;</a></sup> Many farmers and workingmen favored the bill, which would have added $64&#160;million in greenbacks to circulation, but some Eastern bankers opposed it because it would have weakened the dollar.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981395_475-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981395-475">&#91;457&#93;</a></sup> Belknap, Williams, and Delano told Grant a veto would hurt Republicans in the November elections. Grant believed the bill would destroy the credit of the nation, and he vetoed it despite their objections. Grant's veto placed him in the conservative faction of the Republican Party and was the beginning of the party's commitment to a gold-backed dollar.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001580–81_476-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001580–81-476">&#91;458&#93;</a></sup> Grant later pressured Congress for a bill to further strengthen the dollar by gradually reducing the number of greenbacks in circulation. When the Democrats gained a majority in the House after the <a href="/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives_elections,_1874" class="mw-redirect" title="United States House of Representatives elections, 1874">1874 elections</a>, the <a href="/wiki/Lame_duck_(politics)" title="Lame duck (politics)">lame-duck</a> Republican Congress did so before the Democrats took office.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016545,_550_477-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016545,_550-477">&#91;459&#93;</a></sup> On January 14, 1875, Grant signed the <a href="/wiki/Specie_Payment_Resumption_Act" title="Specie Payment Resumption Act">Specie Payment Resumption Act</a>, which required gradual reduction of the number of greenbacks allowed to circulate and declared that they would be redeemed for gold beginning on January 1, 1879.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001580–82Brands2012554_478-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001580–82Brands2012554-478">&#91;460&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Reforms_and_scandals">Reforms and scandals</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Reforms_of_the_Ulysses_S._Grant_administration" title="Reforms of the Ulysses S. Grant administration">Reforms of the Ulysses S. Grant administration</a> and <a href="/wiki/Scandals_of_the_Ulysses_S._Grant_administration" title="Scandals of the Ulysses S. Grant administration">Scandals of the Ulysses S. Grant administration</a></div>
<p>The post-Civil War economy brought on massive industrial wealth and government expansion. Speculation, lifestyle extravagance, and corruption in federal offices were rampant.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWoodward1957156White2016538,_541_479-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWoodward1957156White2016538,_541-479">&#91;461&#93;</a></sup> All of Grant's executive departments were investigated by Congress.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1974133–34Chernow2017825_480-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1974133–34Chernow2017825-480">&#91;462&#93;</a></sup> Grant by nature was honest, trusting, gullible, and extremely loyal to his chosen friends. His responses to malfeasance were mixed, at times appointing cabinet reformers, but also at times defending culprits.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001587,_92McFeely1981407–15White2016538–39Chernow2017672Kahan2018119_481-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001587,_92McFeely1981407–15White2016538–39Chernow2017672Kahan2018119-481">&#91;463&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Cover_of_Harper%27s_Weekly_Dec_7,_1872.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Cover_of_Harper%27s_Weekly_Dec_7%2C_1872.jpg/180px-Cover_of_Harper%27s_Weekly_Dec_7%2C_1872.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="276" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Cover_of_Harper%27s_Weekly_Dec_7%2C_1872.jpg/270px-Cover_of_Harper%27s_Weekly_Dec_7%2C_1872.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Cover_of_Harper%27s_Weekly_Dec_7%2C_1872.jpg/360px-Cover_of_Harper%27s_Weekly_Dec_7%2C_1872.jpg 2x" data-file-width="748" data-file-height="1148" /></a><figcaption>Cartoonist <a href="/wiki/Thomas_Nast" title="Thomas Nast">Thomas Nast</a> praises Grant for rejecting demands by Pennsylvania politicians to suspend civil service rules.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Grant in his first term appointed Secretary of Interior <a href="/wiki/Jacob_D._Cox" class="mw-redirect" title="Jacob D. Cox">Jacob D.
