Cox</a>, who implemented civil service reform: he fired unqualified clerks, and took other measures.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017730Schmiel2014205,_213Calhoun2017293_482-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017730Schmiel2014205,_213Calhoun2017293-482">&#91;464&#93;</a></sup> On October 3, 1870, Cox resigned office under a dispute with Grant over handling of a mining claim.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017730–31Schmiel2014214–15Calhoun2017284–86_483-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017730–31Schmiel2014214–15Calhoun2017284–86-483">&#91;465&#93;</a></sup> Authorized by Congress on March 3, 1871, Grant created and appointed the first <a href="/wiki/United_States_Civil_Service_Commission" title="United States Civil Service Commission">Civil Service Commission</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001589–90Simon2002250Calhoun2017372_484-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001589–90Simon2002250Calhoun2017372-484">&#91;466&#93;</a></sup> Grant's Commission created rules for competitive exams, the end of mandatory political assessments, classifying positions into grades, and appointees were chosen from the top three performing federal applicants.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017731Calhoun2017372_485-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017731Calhoun2017372-485">&#91;467&#93;</a></sup> The rules took effect on January 1, 1872, but Department heads, and others were exempted.<sup id="cite_ref-487" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-487">&#91;s&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017372_488-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017372-488">&#91;469&#93;</a></sup> Grant, more than any previous president, elevated the federal civil service, but his critics refused to acknowledge this.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017372_488-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017372-488">&#91;469&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In November 1871, Grant's appointed New York Collector, and Conkling ally, <a href="/wiki/Thomas_Murphy_(Collector)" title="Thomas Murphy (Collector)">Thomas Murphy</a>, resigned. Grant replaced Murphy with another Conkling ally, <a href="/wiki/Chester_A._Arthur" title="Chester A. Arthur">Chester A. Arthur</a>, who implemented Boutwell's reforms.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017366–67,_735–37McFeely1974144–45Kahan2018114_489-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017366–67,_735–37McFeely1974144–45Kahan2018114-489">&#91;470&#93;</a></sup> A Senate committee investigated the New York Customs House from January 3, 1872, to June 4, 1872. Previous Grant appointed collectors Murphy and <a href="/wiki/Moses_H._Grinnell" title="Moses H. Grinnell">Moses H. Grinnell</a> charged lucrative fees for warehouse space, without the legal requirement of listing the goods.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMartinez_(March_15,_2021)_490-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartinez_(March_15,_2021)-490">&#91;471&#93;</a></sup> This led to Grant firing warehouse owner George K. Leet, for pocketing the exorbitant freight fees and splitting the profits.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017368–69McFeely1974144–45Kahan2018114_491-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017368–69McFeely1974144–45Kahan2018114-491">&#91;472&#93;</a></sup>Boutwell's reforms included stricter record-keeping and that goods be stored on company docks.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMartinez_(March_15,_2021)_490-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartinez_(March_15,_2021)-490">&#91;471&#93;</a></sup> Grant ordered prosecutions in New York by Attorney General <a href="/wiki/George_Henry_Williams" title="George Henry Williams">George H. Williams</a> and Secretary of Treasury Boutwell of persons accepting and paying for bribes.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017369_492-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017369-492">&#91;473&#93;</a></sup> Although exonerated, Grant was derided for his association with Conkling's New York patronage machine.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017735–37Kahan2018114_493-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017735–37Kahan2018114-493">&#91;474&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On March 3, 1873, Grant signed into law an <a href="/wiki/Salary_Grab_Act" title="Salary Grab Act">appropriation act</a> that increased pay for federal employees, Congress (retroactive), the judiciary, and the president.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002251Calhoun2017402–09_494-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002251Calhoun2017402–09-494">&#91;475&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMartinez_(March_15,_2021)_490-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartinez_(March_15,_2021)-490">&#91;471&#93;</a></sup> Grant's annual salary doubled from $25,000 to $50,000. Critics derided Congress' two year retroactive, "services rendered", $4,000 lump sum payment for each Congressman, and the law was partially repealed. Grant, however, kept his much needed pay raise, while his personal reputation remained intact.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002251Smith2001552–53Calhoun2017_495-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002251Smith2001552–53Calhoun2017-495">&#91;476&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMartinez_(March_15,_2021)_490-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartinez_(March_15,_2021)-490">&#91;471&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 1872, Grant signed into law an act that ended private moiety (<i>tax collection</i>) contracts, but an attached rider allowed three more contracts.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017446_496-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017446-496">&#91;477&#93;</a></sup> Boutwell's assistant secretary <a href="/wiki/William_Adams_Richardson" title="William Adams Richardson">William A. Richardson</a>, hired <a href="/wiki/John_B._Sanborn" title="John B. Sanborn">John B. Sanborn</a> to go after "individuals and cooperations" who allegedly evaded taxes. Retained by Richardson (as Secretary), Sanborn aggressively collected $213,000, while splitting $156,000 to others, including Richardson, and the Republican Party campaign committee.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001578McFeely1974147Chernow2017782Calhoun2017446–47_497-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001578McFeely1974147Chernow2017782Calhoun2017446–47-497">&#91;478&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMartinez_(March_15,_2021)_490-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartinez_(March_15,_2021)-490">&#91;471&#93;</a></sup> During an 1874 Congressional investigation, Richardson denied involvement, but Sanborn said he met with Richardson six times over the contracts.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1974147–48Chernow2017782White2016_498-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1974147–48Chernow2017782White2016-498">&#91;479&#93;</a></sup> Congress severely condemned Richardson's permissive manner. Grant appointed Richardson judge of the <a href="/wiki/United_States_Court_of_Claims" title="United States Court of Claims">Court of Claims</a>, and replaced him with reformer <a href="/wiki/Benjamin_Helm_Bristow" class="mw-redirect" title="Benjamin Helm Bristow">Benjamin Bristow</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1974147–48Chernow2017782Calhoun2017446–48_499-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1974147–48Chernow2017782Calhoun2017446–48-499">&#91;480&#93;</a></sup> In June, Grant and Congress abolished the <a href="/wiki/Anti-Moiety_Acts" title="Anti-Moiety Acts">moiety system</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1974133–34_500-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1974133–34-500">&#91;481&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Bristow effectively cleaned house, tightened up the Treasury's investigation force, implemented civil service, and fired hundreds of corrupt appointees.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012556–57Kohn2000417Nevins192956McFeely1974148White2016557,_560Calhoun2017494_501-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012556–57Kohn2000417Nevins192956McFeely1974148White2016557,_560Calhoun2017494-501">&#91;482&#93;</a></sup> Bristow discovered Treasury receipts were low, and launched an investigation that uncovered the notorious <a href="/wiki/Whiskey_Ring" title="Whiskey Ring">Whiskey Ring</a>, that involved collusion between distillers and Treasury officials to evade paying the Treasury millions in tax revenues.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017494,_496_502-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017494,_496-502">&#91;483&#93;</a></sup> Much of this money was being pocketed while some of it went into Republican coffers.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002252Chernow2017798_503-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002252Chernow2017798-503">&#91;484&#93;</a></sup> In mid-April, Bristow informed Grant of the ring. On May 10, Bristow struck hard and broke the ring.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017496–97_504-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017496–97-504">&#91;485&#93;</a></sup> Federal marshals raided 32 installations nationwide and arrested 350 men; 176 indictments were obtained, leading to 110 convictions and $3,150,000 in fines returned to the Treasury.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1974156Smith2001584Brands2012556–57White2016754Calhoun2017_505-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1974156Smith2001584Brands2012556–57White2016754Calhoun2017-505">&#91;486&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Whiskeyring.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="&quot;Uncle Sam&quot; cartoon tapping a Louisville whiskey barrel, captioned &quot;probe away&quot;" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Whiskeyring.jpg/180px-Whiskeyring.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="186" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Whiskeyring.jpg/270px-Whiskeyring.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Whiskeyring.jpg/360px-Whiskeyring.jpg 2x" data-file-width="600" data-file-height="619" /></a><figcaption><i><a href="/wiki/Harper%27s_Weekly" title="Harper&#39;s Weekly">Harper's Weekly</a></i><br /> cartoon on Bristow's Whiskey Ring investigation</figcaption></figure>
<p>Grant appointed <a href="/wiki/David_Patterson_Dyer" title="David Patterson Dyer">David Dyer</a>, under Bristow's recommendation, <a href="/wiki/United_States_Attorney" title="United States Attorney">federal attorney</a> to prosecute the Ring in St. Louis, who indicted Grant's old friend General <a href="/wiki/John_McDonald_(Union_Civil_War_General)" class="mw-redirect" title="John McDonald (Union Civil War General)">John McDonald</a>, supervisor of Internal Revenue.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017498_506-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017498-506">&#91;487&#93;</a></sup> Grant endorsed Bristow's investigation writing on a letter "Let no guilty man escape..."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017499_507-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017499-507">&#91;488&#93;</a></sup> Bristow's investigation discovered Babcock received kickback payments, and that Babcock had secretly forewarned McDonald, the ring's mastermind boss, of the coming investigation.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002252White2016562Calhoun201777–78_508-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002252White2016562Calhoun201777–78-508">&#91;489&#93;</a></sup> On November 22, the jury convicted McDonald.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017515_509-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017515-509">&#91;490&#93;</a></sup> On December 9, Babcock was indicted, however, Grant refused to believe in Babcock's guilt, was ready to testify in Babcock's favor, but Fish warned that doing so would put Grant in the embarrassing position of testifying against a case prosecuted by his own administration.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017805–06Calhoun2017518,_522–23_510-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017805–06Calhoun2017518,_522–23-510">&#91;491&#93;</a></sup> Instead, Grant remained in Washington and on February 12, 1876, gave a deposition in Babcock's defense, expressing that his confidence in his secretary was "unshaken".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001592–93White2016564Simon2002_511-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001592–93White2016564Simon2002-511">&#91;492&#93;</a></sup> Grant's testimony silenced all but his strongest critics.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001592_512-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001592-512">&#91;493&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The St. Louis jury acquitted Babcock, and Grant allowed him to remain at the White House. However, after Babcock was indicted in a frame up of a Washington reformer, called the Safe Burglary Conspiracy, Grant finally dismissed him from the White House. Babcock kept his position of Superintendent of Public Buildings in Washington.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001591–93Simon2002252Calhoun2017527_513-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001591–93Simon2002252Calhoun2017527-513">&#91;494&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMartinez_(March_15,_2021)_490-5" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMartinez_(March_15,_2021)-490">&#91;471&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The Interior Department under Secretary <a href="/wiki/Columbus_Delano" title="Columbus Delano">Columbus Delano</a>, whom Grant appointed to replace Cox, was rife with fraud and corruption. The exception was Delano's effective oversight of <a href="/wiki/Yellowstone" class="mw-redirect" title="Yellowstone">Yellowstone</a>. Grant reluctantly forced Delano's resignation. Surveyor General Silas Reed had set up corrupt contracts that benefited Delano's son, John Delano.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1974149–50_514-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1974149–50-514">&#91;495&#93;</a></sup> Grant's Secretary of Interior <a href="/wiki/Zachariah_Chandler" title="Zachariah Chandler">Zachariah Chandler</a>, who succeeded Delano in 1875, implemented reforms, fired corrupt agents and ended profiteering.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002250Patrick1968172White2016560_515-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002250Patrick1968172White2016560-515">&#91;496&#93;</a></sup> When Grant was informed by Postmaster <a href="/wiki/Marshall_Jewell" title="Marshall Jewell">Marshall Jewell</a> of a potential Congressional investigation into an extortion scandal involving Attorney General <a href="/wiki/George_Henry_Williams" title="George Henry Williams">George H. Williams</a>' wife, Grant fired Williams and appointed reformer <a href="/wiki/Edwards_Pierrepont" title="Edwards Pierrepont">Edwards Pierrepont</a> in his place. Grant's new cabinet appointments temporarily appeased reformers.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016557Chernow2017787–88_516-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016557Chernow2017787–88-516">&#91;497&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>After the Democrats took control of the House in 1875, more corruption in federal departments was exposed.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981429White2016554_517-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981429White2016554-517">&#91;498&#93;</a></sup> Among the most damaging scandal involved Secretary of War <a href="/wiki/William_W._Belknap" title="William W. Belknap">William W. Belknap</a>, who took quarterly <a href="/wiki/Kickbacks" class="mw-redirect" title="Kickbacks">kickbacks</a> from the <a href="/wiki/Trader_post_scandal" title="Trader post scandal">Fort Sill tradership</a>, which led to his resignation in February 1876.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012560–61Donovan2008104Simon2002252Chernow2017_518-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012560–61Donovan2008104Simon2002252Chernow2017-518">&#91;499&#93;</a></sup> Belknap was impeached by the House but was acquitted by the Senate.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002252_519-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002252-519">&#91;500&#93;</a></sup> Grant's own brother Orvil set up "silent partnerships" and received kickbacks from four trading posts.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017819–20_520-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017819–20-520">&#91;501&#93;</a></sup> Congress discovered that Secretary of Navy Robeson had been bribed by a naval contractor, but no articles of impeachment were drawn up.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1974153_521-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1974153-521">&#91;502&#93;</a></sup> In his December 5, 1876, Eighth Annual Message, Grant apologized to the nation: "Failures have been errors of judgement, not of intent."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981441–42_522-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981441–42-522">&#91;503&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Election_of_1876">Election of 1876</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/1876_United_States_presidential_election" title="1876 United States presidential election">1876 United States presidential election</a></div>
<p>The abandonment of Reconstruction by the nation played a central role during the Election of 1876.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002252–53_523-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002252–53-523">&#91;504&#93;</a></sup> Mounting investigations into corruption by the House, controlled by the Democrats, politically discredited Grant's presidency.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981440–41Patrick1968255Simon2002252–53_524-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981440–41Patrick1968255Simon2002252–53-524">&#91;505&#93;</a></sup> Grant, by a public letter in 1875, chose not to run for a third term, while the Republicans chose Governor <a href="/wiki/Rutherford_B._Hayes" title="Rutherford B. Hayes">Rutherford B. Hayes</a> of Ohio, a reformer, at their convention.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002McFeely1981440–41Smith2001586,_596_525-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002McFeely1981440–41Smith2001586,_596-525">&#91;506&#93;</a></sup> The Democrats nominated Governor <a href="/wiki/Samuel_J._Tilden" title="Samuel J. Tilden">Samuel J. Tilden</a> of New York. Voting irregularities in three Southern states caused the election that year to remain undecided for several months.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001597–98_526-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001597–98-526">&#91;507&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-527" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-527">&#91;508&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant told Congress to settle the matter through legislation and assured both sides that he would not use the army to force a result, except to curb violence. On January 29, 1877, he signed legislation forming an <a href="/wiki/Electoral_Commission_(United_States)" title="Electoral Commission (United States)">Electoral Commission</a> to decide the matter.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001601–03_528-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001601–03-528">&#91;509&#93;</a></sup> Hayes was ruled elected President by the commission; to forestall Democratic protests, Republicans agreed to the <a href="/wiki/Compromise_of_1877" title="Compromise of 1877">Compromise of 1877</a>, in which the last troops were withdrawn from Southern capitals. With Reconstruction dead, an 80-year era of <a href="/wiki/Jim_Crow" class="mw-redirect" title="Jim Crow">Jim Crow</a> segregation was launched.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001604Chernow2017858_529-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001604Chernow2017858-529">&#91;510&#93;</a></sup> Grant's "calm visage" throughout the election crisis appeased the nation.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001603–04_530-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001603–04-530">&#91;511&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>To the chagrin of Grant, President Hayes appointed Reconstruction critics, including Liberal Republican icon Carl Schurz to Secretary of Interior.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017852–54_531-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017852–54-531">&#91;512&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span id="Post-presidency_.281877.E2.80.931885.29"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Post-presidency_(1877–1885)">Post-presidency (1877–1885)</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Post-presidency_of_Ulysses_S._Grant" title="Post-presidency of Ulysses S. Grant">Post-presidency of Ulysses S. Grant</a></div>
<p>After leaving the White House, Grant said he "was never so happy in my life". The Grants left Washington for New York, to attend the birth of their daughter Nellie's child, staying at Hamilton Fish's residence. Calling themselves "<a href="/wiki/Waif" title="Waif">waifs</a>", the Grants toured <a href="/wiki/Cincinnati" title="Cincinnati">Cincinnati</a>, <a href="/wiki/St._Louis" title="St. Louis">St. Louis</a>, Chicago, and <a href="/wiki/Galena,_Illinois" title="Galena, Illinois">Galena</a>, without a clear idea of where they would live afterward.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017862White2016587_532-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017862White2016587-532">&#91;513&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="World_tour_and_diplomacy">World tour and diplomacy</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/World_tour_of_Ulysses_S._Grant" title="World tour of Ulysses S. Grant">World tour of Ulysses S. Grant</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:World_tour_of_Ulysses_S_Grant,_1879,_map.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/World_tour_of_Ulysses_S_Grant%2C_1879%2C_map.jpg/330px-World_tour_of_Ulysses_S_Grant%2C_1879%2C_map.jpg" decoding="async" width="330" height="155" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/World_tour_of_Ulysses_S_Grant%2C_1879%2C_map.jpg/495px-World_tour_of_Ulysses_S_Grant%2C_1879%2C_map.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/07/World_tour_of_Ulysses_S_Grant%2C_1879%2C_map.jpg/660px-World_tour_of_Ulysses_S_Grant%2C_1879%2C_map.jpg 2x" data-file-width="3451" data-file-height="1617" /></a><figcaption>Map of Grant's world tour by J. S. Kemp, 1879</figcaption></figure>
<p>For some years, Grant had entertained the idea of taking a long-deserved vacation after his presidency and, after liquidating one of his investments to finance the venture, the Grants set out on a world tour that lasted approximately two and a half years.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981448–49White2016587_533-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981448–49White2016587-533">&#91;514&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant's voyage abroad was funded by a Nevada-based mining company investment he made that earned him $25,000 (equivalent to $687,000 in 2022).<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001387_534-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001387-534">&#91;515&#93;</a></sup> Preparing for the tour, they arrived in Philadelphia on May 10, 1877, and were honored with celebrations during the week before their departure. On May 16, Grant and his wife left for England aboard the <a href="/wiki/SS_Indiana_(1873)" title="SS Indiana (1873)">SS <i>Indiana</i></a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016590_535-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016590-535">&#91;516&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>During the tour, the Grants made stops in Europe, Africa, India, and points in the <a href="/wiki/Middle_East" title="Middle East">Middle East</a> and <a href="/wiki/Far_East" title="Far East">Far East</a>, meeting with notable dignitaries such as <a href="/wiki/Queen_Victoria" title="Queen Victoria">Queen Victoria</a>, <a href="/wiki/Alexander_II_of_Russia" title="Alexander II of Russia">Tsar Alexander II</a>, <a href="/wiki/Pope_Leo_XIII" title="Pope Leo XIII">Pope Leo XIII</a>, <a href="/wiki/Otto_von_Bismarck" title="Otto von Bismarck">Otto von Bismarck</a>, <a href="/wiki/Li_Hongzhang" title="Li Hongzhang">Li Hongzhang</a>, <a href="/wiki/Emperor_Meiji" title="Emperor Meiji">Emperor Meiji</a> and others.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017872_536-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017872-536">&#91;517&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>As a courtesy to Grant by the <a href="/wiki/Rutherford_B._Hayes" title="Rutherford B. Hayes">Hayes administration</a>, his touring party received federal transportation on three U.S. Navy ships: a five-month tour of the <a href="/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea" title="Mediterranean Sea">Mediterranean</a> on the <a href="/wiki/USS_Vandalia_(1876)" title="USS Vandalia (1876)">USS <i>Vandalia</i></a>, travel from Hong Kong to China on the <a href="/wiki/USS_Ashuelot" title="USS Ashuelot">USS <i>Ashuelot</i></a>, and transportation from China to Japan on the <a href="/wiki/USS_Richmond_(1860)" title="USS Richmond (1860)">USS <i>Richmond</i></a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016597–602,_608–10_537-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016597–602,_608–10-537">&#91;518&#93;</a></sup> During the tour, the Hayes administration encouraged Grant to assume a public unofficial diplomatic role to represent the United States and strengthen American interests abroad, while resolving issues for some countries in the process.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECampbell2016xi–xii,_2–3_538-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECampbell2016xi–xii,_2–3-538">&#91;519&#93;</a></sup> Homesick, the Grants left Japan sailing on the <a href="/wiki/SS_City_of_Tokio" title="SS City of Tokio">SS <i>City of Tokio</i></a> escorted by a Japanese man-of-war, crossed the Pacific and landed in San Francisco on September 20, 1879, greeted by cheering crowds.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001613Chernow2017881–83_539-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001613Chernow2017881–83-539">&#91;520&#93;</a></sup> Before returning home to Philadelphia, Grant stopped at Chicago for a reunion with General Sherman and the Army of the Tennessee.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012598_540-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012598-540">&#91;521&#93;</a></sup> Grant's tour demonstrated to Europe and Asia that the United States was an emerging world power.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017871_541-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017871-541">&#91;522&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<div style="clear:both;"></div>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Third_term_attempt">Third term attempt</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/1880_Republican_National_Convention" title="1880 Republican National Convention">1880 Republican National Convention</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ulysses_S._Grant_Trapeze_Cartoon_Keppler_Puck_1880.tif" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Grant, shown in a cartoon as an acrobat hanging from rings, holding up multiple politician/acrobats" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Ulysses_S._Grant_Trapeze_Cartoon_Keppler_Puck_1880.tif/lossy-page1-180px-Ulysses_S._Grant_Trapeze_Cartoon_Keppler_Puck_1880.tif.jpg" decoding="async" width="180" height="277" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Ulysses_S._Grant_Trapeze_Cartoon_Keppler_Puck_1880.tif/lossy-page1-270px-Ulysses_S._Grant_Trapeze_Cartoon_Keppler_Puck_1880.tif.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Ulysses_S._Grant_Trapeze_Cartoon_Keppler_Puck_1880.tif/lossy-page1-360px-Ulysses_S._Grant_Trapeze_Cartoon_Keppler_Puck_1880.tif.jpg 2x" data-file-width="765" data-file-height="1177" /></a><figcaption>Cartoonist <a href="/wiki/Joseph_Ferdinand_Keppler" class="mw-redirect" title="Joseph Ferdinand Keppler">Joseph Keppler</a> lampooned Grant and his associates.<br /> <i><a href="/wiki/Puck_(magazine)" title="Puck (magazine)">Puck</a></i>, 1880</figcaption></figure>
<p><a href="/wiki/Stalwarts" class="mw-redirect" title="Stalwarts">Stalwarts</a>, led by Grant's old political ally, <a href="/wiki/Roscoe_Conkling" title="Roscoe Conkling">Roscoe Conkling</a>, saw Grant's renewed popularity as an opportunity to regain power, and sought to nominate him for the presidency in <a href="/wiki/1880_United_States_presidential_election" title="1880 United States presidential election">1880</a>. Opponents called it a violation of the unofficial two-term rule in use since George Washington. Grant said nothing publicly but wanted the job and encouraged his men.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHesseltine1957432–39_542-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHesseltine1957432–39-542">&#91;523&#93;</a></sup> Washburne urged him to run; Grant demurred, saying he would be happy for the Republicans to win with another candidate, though he preferred <a href="/wiki/James_G._Blaine" title="James G. Blaine">James G. Blaine</a> to <a href="/wiki/John_Sherman" title="John Sherman">John Sherman</a>. Even so, Conkling and <a href="/wiki/John_A._Logan" title="John A. Logan">John A. Logan</a> began to organize delegates in Grant's favor. When <a href="/wiki/1880_Republican_National_Convention" title="1880 Republican National Convention">the convention</a> convened in Chicago in June, there were more delegates pledged to Grant than to any other candidate, but he was still short of a majority vote to get the nomination.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012600–01_543-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012600–01-543">&#91;524&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>At the convention, Conkling nominated Grant with an eloquent speech, the most famous line being: "When asked which state he hails from, our sole reply shall be, he hails from Appomattox and its famous apple tree."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012600–01_543-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012600–01-543">&#91;524&#93;</a></sup> With 370 votes needed for the nomination, the first ballot had Grant at 304, Blaine at 284, Sherman at 93, and the rest to minor candidates.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981479–81_544-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981479–81-544">&#91;525&#93;</a></sup> Subsequent ballots followed, with roughly the same result; neither Grant nor Blaine could win. After thirty-six ballots, Blaine's delegates deserted him and combined with those of other candidates to nominate a compromise candidate: Representative and former Union general <a href="/wiki/James_A._Garfield" title="James A. Garfield">James A. Garfield</a> of Ohio.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012602_545-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012602-545">&#91;526&#93;</a></sup> A procedural motion made the vote unanimous for Garfield, who accepted the nomination.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001617_546-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001617-546">&#91;527&#93;</a></sup> Grant gave speeches for Garfield but declined to criticize the Democratic nominee, <a href="/wiki/Winfield_Scott_Hancock" title="Winfield Scott Hancock">Winfield Scott Hancock</a>, a general who had served under him in the Army of the Potomac.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012604–05_547-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012604–05-547">&#91;528&#93;</a></sup> Garfield won the election. Grant gave Garfield his public support and pushed him to include Stalwarts in his administration.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012607–09_548-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012607–09-548">&#91;529&#93;</a></sup> On July 2, 1881, Garfield was shot by an assassin and died on September 19. On learning of Garfield's death from a reporter, Grant wept bitterly.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012613–14_549-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012613–14-549">&#91;530&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span class="mw-headline" id="Business_failures">Business failures</span></h3>
<p>In the 19th century, there were no federal <a href="/wiki/Former_Presidents_Act" title="Former Presidents Act">presidential pensions</a>, and the Grants' personal income was limited to $6,000 a year.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBunting2004151_550-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBunting2004151-550">&#91;531&#93;</a></sup> Grant's world tour had been costly, and he had depleted most of his savings, while he needed to earn money and find a new home.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012611_551-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012611-551">&#91;532&#93;</a></sup> Wealthy friends bought him a house on Manhattan's <a href="/wiki/Upper_East_Side" title="Upper East Side">Upper East Side</a>, and to make an income, Grant, Jay Gould, and former Mexican Finance Secretary <a href="/wiki/Mat%C3%ADas_Romero" title="Matías Romero">Matías Romero</a> chartered the <a href="/wiki/Mexican_Southern_Railroad" title="Mexican Southern Railroad">Mexican Southern Railroad</a>, with plans to build a railroad from Oaxaca to Mexico City. Grant urged <a href="/wiki/Chester_A._Arthur" title="Chester A. Arthur">Chester A. Arthur</a>, who had succeeded Garfield as president in 1881, to negotiate a free trade treaty with Mexico. Arthur and the Mexican government agreed, but the United States Senate rejected the treaty in 1883. The railroad was similarly unsuccessful, falling into bankruptcy the following year.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981486–89_552-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981486–89-552">&#91;533&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>At the same time, Grant's son Buck had opened a Wall Street brokerage house with <a href="/wiki/Ferdinand_Ward" title="Ferdinand Ward">Ferdinand Ward</a>. Although a conniving man who swindled numerous wealthy men, Ward was at the time regarded as a rising star on Wall Street. The firm, Grant &amp; Ward, was initially successful.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981488–91Ward2012_553-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981488–91Ward2012-553">&#91;534&#93;</a></sup> In 1883, Grant joined the firm and invested $100,000 (~$2.52&#160;million in 2021) of his own money.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012619_554-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012619-554">&#91;535&#93;</a></sup> Grant, however, warned Ward that if his firm engaged in government business he would dissolve their partnership.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017917–18_555-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017917–18-555">&#91;536&#93;</a></sup> To encourage investment, Ward paid investors abnormally high interest, by pledging the company's securities on multiple loans in a process called <a href="/wiki/Rehypothecation" class="mw-redirect" title="Rehypothecation">rehypothecation</a>, which would now be understood as a <a href="/wiki/Ponzi_scheme" title="Ponzi scheme">Ponzi scheme</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981488–91_556-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981488–91-556">&#91;537&#93;</a></sup> Ward, in collusion with banker James D. Fish and kept secret from <a href="/wiki/Bank_examiner" title="Bank examiner">bank examiners</a>, retrieved the firm's securities from the company's bank vault.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016627–29_557-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016627–29-557">&#91;538&#93;</a></sup> When the trades went bad, multiple loans came due, all backed up by the same collateral.<sup id="cite_ref-grant-and-ward_558-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-grant-and-ward-558">&#91;539&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Historians agree that the elder Grant was likely unaware of Ward's intentions, but it is unclear how much Buck Grant knew. In May 1884, enough investments went bad to convince Ward that the firm would soon be bankrupt. Ward, who assumed Grant was "a child in business matters",<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017917_559-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017917-559">&#91;540&#93;</a></sup> told him of the impending failure, but assured Grant that this was a temporary shortfall.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012620–21White2016627–29_560-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012620–21White2016627–29-560">&#91;541&#93;</a></sup> Grant approached businessman <a href="/wiki/William_Henry_Vanderbilt" title="William Henry Vanderbilt">William Henry Vanderbilt</a>, who gave him a personal loan of $150,000.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981492–93_561-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981492–93-561">&#91;542&#93;</a></sup> Grant invested the money in the firm, but it was not enough to save it from failure. The fall of Grant &amp; Ward set off the <a href="/wiki/Panic_of_1884" title="Panic of 1884">Panic of 1884</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-grant-and-ward_558-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-grant-and-ward-558">&#91;539&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Vanderbilt offered to forgive Grant's debt entirely, an offer Grant refused.<sup id="cite_ref-562" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-562">&#91;543&#93;</a></sup> Essentially penniless, but compelled by a sense of personal honor he repaid what he could with his Civil War mementos and the sale or transfer of all other assets.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPerry2004xxix_563-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerry2004xxix-563">&#91;544&#93;</a></sup> Vanderbilt took title to Grant's home, although he allowed the Grants to continue to reside there, and pledged to donate the souvenirs to the federal government and insisted the debt had been paid in full.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016632–33Brands2012620–21_564-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016632–33Brands2012620–21-564">&#91;545&#93;</a></sup> Grant was distraught over Ward's deception and asked privately how he could ever "trust any human being again."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001621_565-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001621-565">&#91;546&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In March 1885, as his health was failing, he testified against both Ward and Fish.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBadeau1887447MackowskiWhite2015169_566-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBadeau1887447MackowskiWhite2015169-566">&#91;547&#93;</a></sup> Ward was convicted of <a href="/wiki/Grand_larceny" class="mw-redirect" title="Grand larceny">fraud</a> in October 1885, months after Grant's death, and served six and a half years in prison.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012620–21_567-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012620–21-567">&#91;548&#93;</a></sup> After the collapse of Grant &amp; Ward, there was an outpouring of sympathy for Grant.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017925–26_568-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017925–26-568">&#91;549&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h3><span id="Memoirs.2C_military_pension.2C_illness_and_death"></span><span class="mw-headline" id="Memoirs,_military_pension,_illness_and_death">Memoirs, military pension, illness and death</span></h3>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Main article: <a href="/wiki/Personal_Memoirs_of_U._S._Grant" title="Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant">Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:US_Grant_in_1885.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Grant sitting in a porch chair wrapped in blankets" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/US_Grant_in_1885.jpg/220px-US_Grant_in_1885.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="259" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/US_Grant_in_1885.jpg/330px-US_Grant_in_1885.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/US_Grant_in_1885.jpg/440px-US_Grant_in_1885.jpg 2x" data-file-width="884" data-file-height="1040" /></a><figcaption>Grant working on <a href="/wiki/Personal_Memoirs_of_U._S._Grant" title="Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant">his memoirs</a>, less than a month before his death</figcaption></figure>
<p>In the summer of 1884, Grant complained of a sore throat but put off seeing a doctor until late October, when he learned it was cancer, possibly caused by his frequent cigar smoking.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016636Waugh2009277_569-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016636Waugh2009277-569">&#91;550&#93;</a></sup> Grant chose not to reveal the seriousness of his condition to his wife, who soon found out from Grant's doctor.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016637_570-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016637-570">&#91;551&#93;</a></sup> Before being diagnosed, Grant attended a Methodist service for Civil War veterans in <a href="/wiki/Ocean_Grove,_New_Jersey" title="Ocean Grove, New Jersey">Ocean Grove, New Jersey</a>, on August 4, 1884, receiving a standing ovation from more than ten thousand veterans and others; it would be his last public appearance.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981495–96_571-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981495–96-571">&#91;552&#93;</a></sup> In March of the following year, <i><a href="/wiki/The_New_York_Times" title="The New York Times">The New York Times</a></i> announced that Grant was dying of cancer, and a nationwide public concern for the former president began.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012622–62Smith2001625_572-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012622–62Smith2001625-572">&#91;553&#93;</a></sup> Knowing of Grant and Julia's financial difficulties, Congress sought to honor him and restored him to the rank of General of the Army with full retirement pay—Grant's assumption of the presidency in 1869 had required that he resign his commission and forfeit his (and his widow's) pension.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001625White2016641_573-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001625White2016641-573">&#91;554&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant was nearly broke and worried constantly about leaving his wife a suitable amount of money to live on. He approached <i><a href="/wiki/The_Century_Magazine" title="The Century Magazine">The Century Magazine</a></i> and wrote a number of articles on his Civil War campaigns at the rate of $500 (equivalent to $16,000&#32;in 2022) each. The articles were well received by critics, and the editor, <a href="/wiki/Robert_Underwood_Johnson" title="Robert Underwood Johnson">Robert Underwood Johnson</a>, suggested that Grant write a book of memoirs, as Sherman and others had done.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981_574-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981-574">&#91;555&#93;</a></sup> The magazine offered him a book contract with a 10% royalty. However, Grant's friend <a href="/wiki/Mark_Twain" title="Mark Twain">Mark Twain</a>, one of the few who understood how precarious Grant's financial condition actually was, made him an offer for his memoirs that paid an unheard-of 70% royalty.<sup id="cite_ref-grant-and-ward_558-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-grant-and-ward-558">&#91;539&#93;</a></sup> To provide for his family, Grant worked intensely on his memoirs at his home in New York City. His former staff member <a href="/wiki/Adam_Badeau" title="Adam Badeau">Adam Badeau</a> assisted him with much of the research, while his son <a href="/wiki/Frederick_Dent_Grant" title="Frederick Dent Grant">Frederick</a> located documents and did much of the fact-checking.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012625_575-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012625-575">&#91;556&#93;</a></sup> Because of the summer heat and humidity, his doctors recommended that he move upstate to <a href="/wiki/Grant_Cottage_State_Historic_Site" title="Grant Cottage State Historic Site">a cottage</a> at the top of <a href="/wiki/Mount_McGregor_(mountain)" title="Mount McGregor (mountain)">Mount McGregor</a>, offered by a family friend.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016646_576-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016646-576">&#91;557&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>On July 18, 1885, Grant finished his memoir; he lived for only five more days.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012629–30_577-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012629–30-577">&#91;558&#93;</a></sup> Grant's memoirs treat his early life and time in the Mexican–American War briefly and include the events of his life up to the end of the Civil War.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001627_578-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001627-578">&#91;559&#93;</a></sup> The <i><a href="/wiki/Personal_Memoirs_of_U._S._Grant" title="Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant">Personal Memoirs of U. S. Grant</a></i> was a critical and commercial success. Julia Grant eventually received about $450,000 in royalties (equivalent to $14,700,000&#32;in 2022). The memoir has been highly regarded by the public, military historians, and literary critics.<sup id="cite_ref-grant-and-ward_558-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-grant-and-ward-558">&#91;539&#93;</a></sup> Grant portrayed himself in the persona of the honorable Western hero, whose strength lies in his honesty and straightforwardness. He candidly depicted his battles against both the Confederates and internal army foes.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERussell1990189–209_579-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussell1990189–209-579">&#91;560&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Grant_Funeral_Train3.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Drawing of a steam engine and train approaching station with an honor guard at attention" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Grant_Funeral_Train3.jpg/220px-Grant_Funeral_Train3.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="164" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Grant_Funeral_Train3.jpg/330px-Grant_Funeral_Train3.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Grant_Funeral_Train3.jpg/440px-Grant_Funeral_Train3.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2680" data-file-height="2000" /></a><figcaption>Grant's funeral train at West Point</figcaption></figure>
<p>After a year-long struggle with throat cancer, surrounded by his family, Grant died at 8:08&#160;a.m. in the Mount McGregor cottage on July 23, 1885, at the age of 63.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981517_580-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981517-580">&#91;561&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Sheridan, then Commanding General of the Army, ordered a day-long tribute to Grant on all military posts, and President <a href="/wiki/Grover_Cleveland" title="Grover Cleveland">Grover Cleveland</a> ordered a thirty-day nationwide period of mourning. After private services, the honor guard placed Grant's body on a special <a href="/wiki/Funeral_train" title="Funeral train">funeral train</a>, which traveled to West Point and New York City. A quarter of a million people viewed it in the two days before the funeral.<sup id="cite_ref-grant-and-ward_558-4" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-grant-and-ward-558">&#91;539&#93;</a></sup> Tens of thousands of men, many of them veterans from the <a href="/wiki/Grand_Army_of_the_Republic" title="Grand Army of the Republic">Grand Army of the Republic</a> (GAR), marched with Grant's casket drawn by two dozen black stallions to <a href="/wiki/Riverside_Park_(Manhattan)" title="Riverside Park (Manhattan)">Riverside Park</a> in the <a href="/wiki/Morningside_Heights,_Manhattan" class="mw-redirect" title="Morningside Heights, Manhattan">Morningside Heights</a> neighborhood of <a href="/wiki/Upper_Manhattan" title="Upper Manhattan">Upper Manhattan</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017955_581-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017955-581">&#91;562&#93;</a></sup> His pallbearers included Union generals Sherman and Sheridan, Confederate generals <a href="/wiki/Simon_Bolivar_Buckner" title="Simon Bolivar Buckner">Simon Bolivar Buckner</a> and <a href="/wiki/Joseph_E._Johnston" title="Joseph E. Johnston">Joseph E. Johnston</a>, Admiral <a href="/wiki/David_Dixon_Porter" title="David Dixon Porter">David Dixon Porter</a>, and Senator <a href="/wiki/John_A._Logan" title="John A. Logan">John A. Logan</a>, the head of the GAR.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012633–35_582-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012633–35-582">&#91;563&#93;</a></sup> Following the casket in the seven-mile-long (11&#160;km) procession were President Cleveland, two former living presidents Hayes and Arthur, all of the president's cabinet, as well as justices of the Supreme Court.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200119_583-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200119-583">&#91;564&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Attendance at the New York funeral topped 1.5&#160;million.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012633–35_582-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012633–35-582">&#91;563&#93;</a></sup> Ceremonies were held in other major cities around the country, while Grant was eulogized in the press and likened to George Washington and Abraham Lincoln.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWaugh2009215–59_584-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaugh2009215–59-584">&#91;565&#93;</a></sup> Grant's body was laid to rest in Riverside Park, first in a temporary tomb, and then—twelve years later, on April 17, 1897—in the General Grant National Memorial, also known as "<a href="/wiki/Grant%27s_Tomb" title="Grant&#39;s Tomb">Grant's Tomb</a>", the largest <a href="/wiki/Mausoleum" title="Mausoleum">mausoleum</a> in North America.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012633–35_582-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012633–35-582">&#91;563&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Historical_reputation">Historical reputation</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">Further information: <a href="/wiki/Historical_reputation_of_Ulysses_S._Grant" title="Historical reputation of Ulysses S. Grant">Historical reputation of Ulysses S. Grant</a> and <a href="/wiki/Historical_rankings_of_presidents_of_the_United_States" title="Historical rankings of presidents of the United States">Historical rankings of presidents of the United States</a></div>
<figure class="mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ulysses_Grant_3.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/Ulysses_Grant_3.jpg/200px-Ulysses_Grant_3.jpg" decoding="async" width="200" height="287" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/Ulysses_Grant_3.jpg/300px-Ulysses_Grant_3.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/Ulysses_Grant_3.jpg/400px-Ulysses_Grant_3.jpg 2x" data-file-width="623" data-file-height="893" /></a><figcaption>Maj. General Grant, <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;">&#8201;1863</span></figcaption></figure>
<p>Grant was hailed across the North as the winning general in the American Civil War and overall his military reputation has held up quite well. Achieving great national fame for his victories at <a href="/wiki/Vicksburg_campaign" title="Vicksburg campaign">Vicksburg</a> and the surrender at <a href="/wiki/Appomattox_campaign" title="Appomattox campaign">Appomattox</a>, he was widely credited as the General who "saved the Union". Grant was the most successful general, Union or Confederate, to dominate the Civil War.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBonekemper2012xiii_585-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper2012xiii-585">&#91;566&#93;</a></sup> Criticized by the South for using excessive force, his overall military reputation stands intact.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBonekemper2011White2016287–88_586-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBonekemper2011White2016287–88-586">&#91;567&#93;</a></sup> Grant's drinking was often exaggerated by the press and falsely stereotyped by many of his rivals and critics.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198155,_77Waugh200939–40_587-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198155,_77Waugh200939–40-587">&#91;568&#93;</a></sup> During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Grant's reputation was damaged by the "<a href="/wiki/Lost_Cause" class="mw-redirect" title="Lost Cause">Lost Cause</a>" movement and the <a href="/wiki/Dunning_School" title="Dunning School">Dunning School</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981521–22White2016xxiiiCalhoun2017587_588-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981521–22White2016xxiiiCalhoun2017587-588">&#91;569&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Views of Grant reached new lows as he was seen as an unsuccessful president and an unskilled, if lucky, general.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012b45_589-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012b45-589">&#91;570&#93;</a></sup> In the 1950s, some historians made a reassessment of Grant's military career, shifting the analysis of Grant as the victor by brute force to that of successful, skillful, modern strategist and commander.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTERafuse2007851_590-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTERafuse2007851-590">&#91;571&#93;</a></sup> Historian <a href="/wiki/William_S._McFeely" title="William S. McFeely">William S. McFeely</a>'s biography, <i>Grant</i> (1981), won the <a href="/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize" title="Pulitzer Prize">Pulitzer Prize</a>, and brought renewed scholarly interest in Grant. McFeely believed Grant was an "ordinary American" trying to "make his mark" during the 19th century. <sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981xii,_xiii,_522White2016xxiv_591-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981xii,_xiii,_522White2016xxiv-591">&#91;572&#93;</a></sup> In the 21st century, Grant's reputation improved markedly among historians after the publication of <i>Grant</i> (2001), by historian <a href="/wiki/Jean_Edward_Smith" title="Jean Edward Smith">Jean Edward Smith</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-C-SPAN_Survey_on_Presidents_PDF_2017_592-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-C-SPAN_Survey_on_Presidents_PDF_2017-592">&#91;573&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-C-SPAN_Survey_on_Presidents_2017_2001_593-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-C-SPAN_Survey_on_Presidents_2017_2001-593">&#91;574&#93;</a></sup> Opinions of Grant's presidency demonstrate a better appreciation of Grant's personal integrity, Reconstruction efforts, and peace policy towards Indians, even when they fell short.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWaugh20092Stiles2016_594-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWaugh20092Stiles2016-594">&#91;575&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-595" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-595">&#91;576&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p><a href="/wiki/H._W._Brands" title="H. W. Brands">H. W. Brands</a>' <i>The Man Who Saved the Union</i> (2012), <a href="/wiki/Ronald_C._White" title="Ronald C. White">Ronald C. White</a>'s <i>American Ulysses</i> (2016), and <a href="/wiki/Ron_Chernow" title="Ron Chernow">Ron Chernow</a>'s <i><a href="/wiki/Grant_(book)" title="Grant (book)">Grant</a></i> (2017) continued the elevation of Grant's historical reputation.<sup id="cite_ref-nJvNx_596-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-nJvNx-596">&#91;577&#93;</a></sup> White said that Grant "demonstrated a distinctive sense of humility, moral courage, and determination", and as president he "stood up for African Americans, especially fighting against voter suppression perpetrated by the Ku Klux Klan".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEHunt2017_597-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHunt2017-597">&#91;578&#93;</a></sup> White believed that Grant was "an exceptional person and leader".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016xxiv_598-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016xxiv-598">&#91;579&#93;</a></sup> <a href="/wiki/Charles_W._Calhoun" title="Charles W. Calhoun">Charles W. Calhoun</a>'s <i>The Presidency of Ulysses S. Grant</i> (2017) noted Grant's successes in office but asked whether Grant's revived reputation was found in the "popular consciousness".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun20175–6,_592_599-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun20175–6,_592-599">&#91;580&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<figure class="mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Ulysses_S_Grant_by_Brady_c1870-restored.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Ulysses_S_Grant_by_Brady_c1870-restored.jpg/200px-Ulysses_S_Grant_by_Brady_c1870-restored.jpg" decoding="async" width="200" height="250" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Ulysses_S_Grant_by_Brady_c1870-restored.jpg/300px-Ulysses_S_Grant_by_Brady_c1870-restored.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Ulysses_S_Grant_by_Brady_c1870-restored.jpg/400px-Ulysses_S_Grant_by_Brady_c1870-restored.jpg 2x" data-file-width="2014" data-file-height="2518" /></a><figcaption>President Grant, <abbr title="circa">c.</abbr><span style="white-space:nowrap;">&#8201;1870</span></figcaption></figure>
<p>Historians still debate how effective Grant was at halting corruption.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEWhite2016539_600-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhite2016539-600">&#91;581&#93;</a></sup> Before the current rehabilitation of Grant's reputation, the scandals during his administration stigmatized his political reputation.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017592_601-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTECalhoun2017592-601">&#91;582&#93;</a></sup> Militarily evaluated, Grant was a modern general and "a skillful leader who had a natural grasp of tactics and strategy".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEAxelrod2011205_602-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAxelrod2011205-602">&#91;583&#93;</a></sup> Grant's successful Civil War military strategies have been recognized and adapted into successful business practices.<sup class="noprint Inline-Template Template-Fact" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed" title="Wikipedia:Citation needed"><span title="This claim needs references to reliable sources. (August 2023)">citation needed</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>
</p><p>Historian Robert Farley writes that the "Cult of Lee" and the <a href="/wiki/Dunning_School" title="Dunning School">Dunning School</a>'s resentment of Grant for his defeat of Lee at <a href="/wiki/Appomattox_campaign" title="Appomattox campaign">Appomattox</a> and his strong enforcement of Reconstruction resulted in Grant's shoddy treatment by historians. Farley said the cult of Lee had "little room for Grant, in no small part because Grant was the only president to vigorously pursue Reconstruction and the first to treat blacks as both human and American".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFarley_2021_603-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFarley_2021-603">&#91;584&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In a 2021 <a href="/wiki/C-SPAN" title="C-SPAN">C-SPAN</a> survey ranking presidents from worst to best, Grant was ranked 20 out of 44 presidents. He was given "more credit for Reconstruction and his diplomacy than condemnation for his alleged corruption" during his presidency.<sup id="cite_ref-604" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-604">&#91;585&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2022, the <a href="/wiki/Bicentennial_(disambiguation)" class="mw-redirect mw-disambig" title="Bicentennial (disambiguation)">bicentenary</a> of Grant's birth, a posthumous promotion to the rank of <a href="/wiki/General_of_the_Armies_of_the_United_States" class="mw-redirect" title="General of the Armies of the United States">General of the Armies of the United States</a> was authorized for Grant as part of the <a href="/wiki/National_Defense_Authorization_Act_for_Fiscal_Year_2023" title="National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023">2023 Defense Authorization Bill</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-HR_7776_605-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-HR_7776-605">&#91;586&#93;</a></sup> Preceded by George Washington and <a href="/wiki/John_J._Pershing" title="John J. Pershing">John J. Pershing</a>, Grant will become the third person to hold this rank if the authorization is acted on by the president.<sup id="cite_ref-606" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-606">&#91;587&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-607" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-607">&#91;588&#93;</a></sup> On Grant's 200th birthday, April 27, 2022, a celebration was held at the <a href="/wiki/Grant%27s_Tomb" title="Grant&#39;s Tomb">General Grant National Memorial</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-608" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-608">&#91;589&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Memorials_and_presidential_library">Memorials and presidential library</span></h2>
<link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1033289096"><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable">See also: <a href="/wiki/Cultural_depictions_of_Ulysses_S._Grant" title="Cultural depictions of Ulysses S. Grant">Cultural depictions of Ulysses S. Grant</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:General_Grant_National_Memorial_New_York_November_2016_003.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img alt="Neoclassical structure with dome" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/General_Grant_National_Memorial_New_York_November_2016_003.jpg/220px-General_Grant_National_Memorial_New_York_November_2016_003.jpg" decoding="async" width="220" height="165" class="mw-file-element" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/General_Grant_National_Memorial_New_York_November_2016_003.jpg/330px-General_Grant_National_Memorial_New_York_November_2016_003.jpg 1.5x, //upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/04/General_Grant_National_Memorial_New_York_November_2016_003.jpg/440px-General_Grant_National_Memorial_New_York_November_2016_003.jpg 2x" data-file-width="5000" data-file-height="3750" /></a><figcaption>Grant's Tomb at dusk, 2016</figcaption></figure>
<p>Several memorials honor Grant. In addition to Grant's Tomb, there is the <a href="/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant_Memorial" title="Ulysses S. Grant Memorial">Ulysses S. Grant Memorial</a> at the foot of <a href="/wiki/Capitol_Hill" title="Capitol Hill">Capitol Hill</a> in Washington, D.C.<sup id="cite_ref-px4FP_609-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-px4FP-609">&#91;590&#93;</a></sup> Created by sculptor <a href="/wiki/Henry_Merwin_Shrady" class="mw-redirect" title="Henry Merwin Shrady">Henry Merwin Shrady</a> and architect <a href="/wiki/Edward_Pearce_Casey" title="Edward Pearce Casey">Edward Pearce Casey</a>, and dedicated in 1922, it overlooks the <a href="/wiki/Capitol_Reflecting_Pool" title="Capitol Reflecting Pool">Capitol Reflecting Pool</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-Ulysses_S._Grant_Memorial_610-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Ulysses_S._Grant_Memorial-610">&#91;591&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>The <a href="/wiki/Ulysses_S._Grant_National_Historic_Site" title="Ulysses S. Grant National Historic Site">Ulysses S. Grant National Historic Site</a> near St. Louis, and several other sites in Ohio and Illinois memorialize Grant's life.<sup id="cite_ref-ZktCM_611-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-ZktCM-611">&#91;592&#93;</a></sup> The <a href="/wiki/Grant_Cottage_State_Historic_Site" title="Grant Cottage State Historic Site">U.S. Grant Cottage State Historic Site</a>, located at the top of <a href="/wiki/Mount_McGregor_(mountain)" title="Mount McGregor (mountain)">Mount McGregor</a> in <a href="/wiki/Wilton,_New_York" title="Wilton, New York">Wilton, New York</a>, preserves the house in which he completed his memoirs and died.<sup id="cite_ref-bAhNe_612-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-bAhNe-612">&#91;593&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-Urlsi_613-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Urlsi-613">&#91;594&#93;</a></sup> There are smaller memorials in Chicago's <a href="/wiki/Lincoln_Park" title="Lincoln Park">Lincoln Park</a> and Philadelphia's <a href="/wiki/Fairmount_Park" title="Fairmount Park">Fairmount Park</a>. Named in his honor are <a href="/wiki/Grant_Park_(Chicago)" title="Grant Park (Chicago)">Grant Park</a>, as well as <a href="/wiki/Grant_County,_Indiana" title="Grant County, Indiana">several counties in western and midwestern states</a>. On June 3, 1891, a bronze statue of Grant by Danish sculptor <a href="/wiki/Johannes_Gelert" title="Johannes Gelert">Johannes Gelert</a> was dedicated at Grant Park in Galena, Illinois.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEPriceHendricks200745_614-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPriceHendricks200745-614">&#91;595&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-VtkVr_615-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-VtkVr-615">&#91;596&#93;</a></sup> From 1890 to 1940, part of what is now <a href="/wiki/Kings_Canyon_National_Park" title="Kings Canyon National Park">Kings Canyon National Park</a> was called <i>General Grant National Park</i>, named for the <a href="/wiki/General_Grant_tree" class="mw-redirect" title="General Grant tree">General Grant sequoia</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-zzzHY_616-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-zzzHY-616">&#91;597&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In May 2012, the Ulysses S. Grant Foundation, on the institute's fiftieth anniversary, selected <a href="/wiki/Mississippi_State_University#Mitchell_Memorial_Library" title="Mississippi State University">Mississippi State University</a> as the permanent location for Grant's <a href="/wiki/Presidential_library_system" title="Presidential library system">presidential library</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-617" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-617">&#91;598&#93;</a></sup> Historian <a href="/wiki/John_Y._Simon" title="John Y. Simon">John Y. Simon</a> edited Grant's letters into a 32-volume scholarly edition published by <a href="/wiki/Southern_Illinois_University_Press" title="Southern Illinois University Press">Southern Illinois University Press</a>.<sup id="cite_ref-jJugU_618-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-jJugU-618">&#91;599&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>Grant's image has appeared on the front of the <a href="/wiki/United_States_fifty-dollar_bill" title="United States fifty-dollar bill">United States fifty-dollar bill</a> since 1913. In 1921, the Ulysses S. Grant Centenary Association was founded with the goal of coordinating special observances and erecting monuments in recognition of Grant's historical role. The venture was financed by the minting of 10,000 gold dollars and 250,000 half dollars. <a href="/wiki/Grant_Memorial_coinage" title="Grant Memorial coinage">The coins</a> were minted and issued in 1922, commemorating the <a href="/wiki/Centenary" class="mw-redirect" title="Centenary">centenary</a> of Grant's birth.<sup id="cite_ref-7gWys_619-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-7gWys-619">&#91;600&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-yI5mO_620-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-yI5mO-620">&#91;601&#93;</a></sup> Grant has also appeared on <a href="/wiki/U.S._presidents_on_U.S._postage_stamps#Ulysses_S._Grant" class="mw-redirect" title="U.S. presidents on U.S. postage stamps">several U.S. postage stamps</a>, the first one issued in 1890, five years after his death.<sup id="cite_ref-621" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-621">&#91;602&#93;</a></sup>
</p><p>In 2020, during <a href="/wiki/George_Floyd_protests" title="George Floyd protests">George Floyd protests</a> protesters toppled a bronze <a href="/wiki/Bust_of_Ulysses_S._Grant_(San_Francisco)" title="Bust of Ulysses S. Grant (San Francisco)">bust of Grant</a> at <a href="/wiki/San_Francisco" title="San Francisco">San Francisco</a>'s <a href="/wiki/Golden_Gate_Park" title="Golden Gate Park">Golden Gate Park</a> in response to his brief ownership of a slave. The toppling of Grant's statue prompted a response from historian <a href="/wiki/Greg_Downs_(writer)" title="Greg Downs (writer)">Gregory Downs</a> who, noting Grant's enforcement of civil rights and prosecution of the Klan, remarked, "When the mob members tore down Grant's bust, they unknowingly built upon a 150-year effort to erase and defame him."<sup id="cite_ref-622" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-622">&#91;603&#93;</a></sup>
</p>
