<h2><span class="mw-headline" id="Notes">Notes</span></h2>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1011085734">.mw-parser-output .reflist{font-size:90%;margin-bottom:0.5em;list-style-type:decimal}.mw-parser-output .reflist .references{font-size:100%;margin-bottom:0;list-style-type:inherit}.mw-parser-output .reflist-columns-2{column-width:30em}.mw-parser-output .reflist-columns-3{column-width:25em}.mw-parser-output .reflist-columns{margin-top:0.3em}.mw-parser-output .reflist-columns ol{margin-top:0}.mw-parser-output .reflist-columns li{page-break-inside:avoid;break-inside:avoid-column}.mw-parser-output .reflist-upper-alpha{list-style-type:upper-alpha}.mw-parser-output .reflist-upper-roman{list-style-type:upper-roman}.mw-parser-output .reflist-lower-alpha{list-style-type:lower-alpha}.mw-parser-output .reflist-lower-greek{list-style-type:lower-greek}.mw-parser-output .reflist-lower-roman{list-style-type:lower-roman}</style><div class="reflist reflist-lower-alpha">
<div class="mw-references-wrap mw-references-columns"><ol class="references">
<li id="cite_note-15"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-15">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">Biographer Edward G. Longacre offers the theory held by some biographers that Grant's parents' decision was based on their recognition of his aversion to music. Longacre, however, also suggests that not pushing religion may have been a form of simple parental neglect.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTELongacre20067_14-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTELongacre20067-14">&#91;14&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-25"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-25">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">One source states Hamer thought the "S" stood for Simpson, Grant's mother's maiden name.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon19673–4_22-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon19673–4-22">&#91;21&#93;</a></sup> According to Grant, the "S." did not stand for anything. Upon graduation from the academy he adopted the name "Ulysses S. Grant".<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198112Smith200124,_83Simon19673–4_23-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198112Smith200124,_83Simon19673–4-23">&#91;22&#93;</a></sup> Another version of the story states that Grant inverted his first and middle names to register at West Point as "Ulysses Hiram Grant" as he thought reporting to the academy with a trunk that carried the initials H.U.G. would subject him to teasing and ridicule. Upon finding that Hamer had nominated him as "Ulysses S. Grant." Grant decided to keep the name as he could avoid the "hug" monogram and it was easier to keep the wrong name than to try changing school records.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEGarland_189830–31_24-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGarland_189830–31-24">&#91;23&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-37"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-37">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">At the time, class ranking largely determined branch assignments. Those at the top of the class were usually assigned to the Engineers, followed by Artillery, Cavalry, and Infantry.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEJones20111580_36-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones20111580-36">&#91;34&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-44"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-44">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">Several scholars, including <a href="/wiki/Jean_Edward_Smith" title="Jean Edward Smith">Jean Edward Smith</a> and <a href="/wiki/Ron_Chernow" title="Ron Chernow">Ron Chernow</a>, state that Longstreet was Grant's best man and the two other officers were Grant's groomsmen.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow201762Smith200173Flood20052007_42-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201762Smith200173Flood20052007-42">&#91;39&#93;</a></sup> All three went on to serve in the Confederate Army and surrendered to Grant at Appomattox.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow201762_43-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow201762-43">&#91;40&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-65"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-65">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">During the Civil War, when Grant's Union supply depot at Holly Springs was sacked in December 1862, he incorporated the strategy of the Union Army foraging the land,<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMiller2019248_63-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiller2019248-63">&#91;59&#93;</a></sup> rather than expose long Union supply lines to enemy attack.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001244_64-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001244-64">&#91;60&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-84"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-84">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text"><a href="/wiki/William_McFeely" class="mw-redirect" title="William McFeely">William McFeely</a> said that Grant left the army simply because he was "profoundly depressed" and that the evidence as to how much and how often Grant drank remains elusive.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198155_79-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely198155-79">&#91;74&#93;</a></sup> Jean Edward Smith maintains Grant's resignation was too sudden to be a calculated decision.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200187_80-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200187-80">&#91;75&#93;</a></sup> Buchanan never mentioned it again until asked about it during the Civil War.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith200188_81-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith200188-81">&#91;76&#93;</a></sup> The effects and extent of Grant's drinking on his military and public career are debated by historians.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFarina2007202_82-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFarina2007202-82">&#91;77&#93;</a></sup> Lyle Dorsett said Grant was an "alcoholic" but functioned amazingly well. William Farina maintains Grant's devotion to family kept him from drinking to excess and sinking into debt.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEFarina200713,_202Dorsett1983_83-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFarina200713,_202Dorsett1983-83">&#91;78&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-179"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-179">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">In 2012, historian <a href="/wiki/Jonathan_D._Sarna" class="mw-redirect" title="Jonathan D. Sarna">Jonathan D. Sarna</a> said: "Gen. Ulysses S. Grant issued the most notorious anti-Jewish official order in American history."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESarna2012b_176-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESarna2012b-176">&#91;170&#93;</a></sup> Grant made amends with the Jewish community during his presidency, appointing them to various federal positions.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESarna2012a89,_147White2016494Chernow2017236_177-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESarna2012a89,_147White2016494Chernow2017236-177">&#91;171&#93;</a></sup> In 2017, biographer Ron Chernow said  of Grant: "As we shall see, Grant as president atoned for his action in a multitude of meaningful ways. He was never a bigoted, hate-filled man and was haunted by his terrible action for the rest of his days."<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017236_178-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017236-178">&#91;172&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-321"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-321">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">Southern Reconstructed states were controlled locally by Republican <a href="/wiki/Carpetbaggers" class="mw-redirect" title="Carpetbaggers">carpetbaggers</a>, <a href="/wiki/Scalawags" class="mw-redirect" title="Scalawags">scalawags</a> and former slaves. By 1877, the conservative Democrats had full control of the region and Reconstruction was dead.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002247–48_320-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002247–48-320">&#91;313&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-331"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-331">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">To placate the South in 1870, Grant signed the <a href="/wiki/Amnesty_Act" title="Amnesty Act">Amnesty Act</a>, which restored political rights to former Confederates.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEKahan201867–68_330-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKahan201867–68-330">&#91;322&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-336"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-336">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">Additionally, Grant's <a href="/wiki/United_States_Postmaster_General" title="United States Postmaster General">Postmaster General</a>, <a href="/wiki/John_Creswell" title="John Creswell">John Creswell</a> used his patronage powers to integrate the postal system and appointed a record number of African-American men and women as postal workers across the nation, while also expanding many of the mail routes.<sup id="cite_ref-333" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-333">&#91;324&#93;</a></sup><sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017629_334-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017629-334">&#91;325&#93;</a></sup> Grant appointed Republican abolitionist and champion of black education <a href="/wiki/Hugh_Lennox_Bond" title="Hugh Lennox Bond">Hugh Lennox Bond</a> as U.S. Circuit Court judge.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017628_335-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017628-335">&#91;326&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-366"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-366">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">An 1870 Congressional investigation chaired by <a href="/wiki/James_A._Garfield" title="James A. Garfield">James A. Garfield</a> cleared Grant of profiteering, but excoriated Gould and Fisk for their manipulation of the gold market and Corbin for exploiting his personal connection to Grant.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012445–46Simon2002248_365-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012445–46Simon2002248-365">&#91;355&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-376"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-376">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">Urged by his Secretary of War Rawlins, Grant initially supported recognition of Cuban belligerency, but Rawlins's death on September 6, 1869, removed any cabinet support for military intervention.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002249_351-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002249-351">&#91;341&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-424"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-424">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">Bison were hunted almost to the point of extinction during the latter 1800s; Yellowstone National Park was the only remaining place in the country where free-roaming herds persisted.<sup id="cite_ref-mF1ZB_423-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-mF1ZB-423">&#91;411&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-435"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-435">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">In spite of Grant's peaceful efforts, over 200 battles were fought with Native Americans during his presidency. Grant's peace policy survived Custer's death, even after Grant left office in 1877, as Indian policy remained under the Interior Department rather than moving to the War Department.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981316_433-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcFeely1981316-433">&#91;420&#93;</a></sup> The policy was considered humanitarian for its time but was later criticized for disregarding tribal cultures.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001541_434-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001541-434">&#91;421&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-446"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-446">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">Details revealed of the 1867 <a href="/wiki/Cr%C3%A9dit_Mobilier_of_America_scandal" class="mw-redirect" title="Crédit Mobilier of America scandal">Crédit Mobilier bribery scandal</a>, implicating both Colfax and Wilson, stung the Grant administration, but Grant was not connected to the corruption.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESimon2002251Chernow2017753Kahan2018114_445-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESimon2002251Chernow2017753Kahan2018114-445">&#91;431&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-455"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-455">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">Greeley died on November 28, 1872, as a result, his electoral votes were split between four candidates. <a href="/wiki/Thomas_A._Hendricks" title="Thomas A. Hendricks">Thomas A. Hendricks</a>, the governor-elect of Indiana, received the majority: 42 electoral votes.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEBrands2012499_454-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBrands2012499-454">&#91;439&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-462"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-462">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">The day after his inauguration, Grant wrote a letter to Colfax expressing his faith and trust in Colfax's integrity and allowed him to publish the letter, but the effort only served to compromise Grant's reputation.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTEChernow2017752–53_461-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChernow2017752–53-461">&#91;445&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-466"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-466">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">As Wilson's death occurred prior to the adoption of the <a href="/wiki/Twenty-fifth_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution" title="Twenty-fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution">Twenty-fifth Amendment</a>, the vacancy in the office of vice president was not filled until the next ensuing election and inauguration.</span>
</li>
<li id="cite_note-487"><span class="mw-cite-backlink"><b><a href="#cite_ref-487">^</a></b></span> <span class="reference-text">When Congress failed to make the Commission's reform rules permanent, Grant dissolved the Commission in 1874.<sup id="cite_ref-FOOTNOTESmith2001589_486-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTESmith2001589-486">&#91;468&#93;</a></sup></span>
</li>
</ol></div></div>
